en: Commentary on the *Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
Scroll One, Part One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master, Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great Wisdom, by Imperial Decree during the Tang Dynasty.
Composed by the founding bhikṣu of Mingci Temple, Pudong Puzhen Gui.
△ Third, the correct explanation of the scriptural text. This has three parts. First, the explanation of the general title:
*The Benevolent Kings’ Sutra on the Prajñāpāramitā for the Protection of the State*.

When Emperor Daizong ruled the realm, he had this sutra translated through successive linguistic intermediaries, intending for himself and the common people to together attain the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

Thus, he wrote in his own preface: "How magnificent! That the protection of the state truly lies in this sutra. I humbly admire the conduct of the Persian [translator] and hope to propagate the teachings of the Tamer (*Vināyaka*).
As for its lofty exposition of the five patiences (*kṣānti*), it sufficiently clarifies the depth of compassion; that it forever dispels all calamities is indeed...

Considering that this is the very foundation of transforming [the world] into purity, it follows that the capacity of Prajñā to protect the state does not require detailed categorization or minute analysis;
its brilliance will naturally be as clear as the sun and moon, and its moisture as pervasive as clouds and rain.
However, when Buddhist scriptures establish their titles, they differ in being single or compound, and may consist of person, dharma, essence, function, cause, effect, or metaphor. Now, following...
Regarding the essence and function of the person and the Dharma, as well as the hidden meanings of the metaphors, there are three pairs of interpretations. First, the pair of person and Dharma:
this refers to the Benevolent Kings protecting their nations; these are the persons who uphold the Prajñāpāramitā, while terms such as "Prajñā" refer to the Dharma that protects the royal kingdom.

This is the king who has secretly realized the benevolent heart and benevolent governance of expedient transformation. He rules over a nation where heaven, earth, the ancestral altars, mountains, rivers, ministers, and subjects are all in harmony.

Such a ruler must rely upon the wondrous gate of the profound and mysterious Prajñā as the level path for transcending the mundane and attaining the Real, and as the golden fortress for protecting the state and securing the realm.
It is the guide for emptying the mind and stilling the境 (objective world), severing transgressions and extinguishing calamities.

This is the Great Sword (Jueque). Nevertheless, when considering the principles and phenomena in general terms, that which protects the land is the phenomenon, while that which is able to protect the Prajñā is the principle.
Thus, regarding these two—essence and function—one must distinguish between essence and function within the aforementioned dharma: namely, Prajñā is the essence.
Translated literally, it is "wisdom" (hui), which refers to the spiritual awakening to the profound mystery and the wondrous realization of the true source, illuminating all dharmas.
This is the wisdom of fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) that accords with emptiness (*śūnyatā*). However, there are three types of this: first, *bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā* (the prajñā of the true mark).
This refers to the true nature that is the object of contemplation, which is precisely fundamental awakening. This nature shares the same source as wisdom;

ignorance is fundamentally exhausted, true illumination is perfectly luminous, and all illusions are entirely detached—this is termed the "true mark. Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The self-nature is pure."
The first is called fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*). The second is the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination, which refers to the wondrous wisdom capable of observation;

this is initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*). This wisdom serves as the basis for both cause and fruit, wherein subject and object are non-dual. It exists yet is not existent; it is forgotten yet is not non-existent. Thus it is termed "contemplative illumination.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Wisdom illuminates the true nature; it is neither existent nor non-existent. The third is the *prajñā* of words and letters.
This refers to the teaching that explains the aforementioned [truth]. As the Sūtra says: "I rely upon the *prajñā* of words and letters to realize the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
It also says: "Dhāraṇī is without words and letters; words and letters manifest dhāraṇī. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states:
"The nature of words and letters is empty; this is itself liberation. Furthermore, the subsequent text says: "All that is proclaimed within the twelve divisions of the scriptures..."
All are thus; there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). Even those who are said to "cultivate letters" are able to realize the true nature of *prajñā*.
This is because the three—wisdom, principle, and teaching—are neither identical nor distinct. They constitute the wondrous Dharma for protecting the nation.
Among the myriad practices performed with a single mind, who could obscure this? Yet some say that the cause is named *prajñā* and the state of fruition is named "wisdom" (*jñāna*), because...
Because Prajñā can sever [delusions], it is so designated during the stage of the cause; in the state of Buddhahood, there is nothing further to sever, and thus it takes the name "Jñāna" (Wisdom).

This is generally the case. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also refers to Prajñā as translated into "Zhihui" (Wisdom). This is because, in the Dharma-nature school, these two dharmas are ultimately the single mind of Prajñā.
Therefore, it is not like the Dharma-character school, which names it "Hui" (Insight) at the stage of the cause and "Zhi" (Wisdom) at the stage of the fruit. Why is this?
Thus, through discernment and decisive resolution, it is uniquely designated as the "eye. Although cause and effect are far removed, how could their wondrous essence differ?
Therefore, whether termed *prajñā* (wisdom) or *jñāna* (knowledge), either may be employed; it is a *pāramitā*, which here means "reaching the other shore."

"Other Shore" (*pāra*) is used as a metaphor. This refers to this sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), which leaves behind this shore of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), crosses over the turbulent middle of afflictions (*kleśa*), and reaches the other shore of nirvāṇa.
This phrasing appears inverted; if one were to adapt the phrasing to include *prajñā*, it should be called "wisdom that reaches the other shore.
This serves to distinguish it from wisdom that does not reach the other shore, and thus it is taken as its name. Vimalakīrti said to all the assembly:

Birth is itself the mark of quiescent extinction; it does not undergo further extinction. It is only because of delusion and inverted views that one perceives birth and death, which is termed "being on this shore.

If one awakens to the fact that birth and death are fundamentally empty and have been quiescent from the beginning, this is termed "reaching the other shore. This is also consistent with the later passage:
"immediately departing" and "immediately arriving," which carries the meaning of "this being that" and "that being this. Thus, we know that Bodhisattvas cultivate both compassion and wisdom together.
Emptiness and existence are illuminated simultaneously. When wisdom guides compassion, one always arrives; when compassion guides wisdom, one never arrives.
Thus, arriving and not arriving are two paths that converge into a single principle. This is just as the *Avataṃsaka* states:
that a bodhisattva does not dwell on the other shore, nor does he dwell in the middle of the stream, yet is able to ferry sentient beings from this shore to the other shore, and so forth. (3)

Regarding doctrine (*dharma*): the words of the sūtra constitute the teaching (*śāsana*), while the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā* (Renwang jing) and others constitute the meaning (*artha*). As for "sūtra," it is the Sanskrit term *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Scripture of Accord" (*kīng-kyǒng*).
"Accord" means to tally with the principle of all Buddhas and to harmonize with the minds of sentient beings; thus, it refers to a teaching that accords with principle and accords with capacity.
If one excludes teachings that do not accord with principle and capacity, this specifically excludes those that are dependent on another (*paratantra*). If [it] accords with principle and...

"Ji" (device/occasion) is a name derived by dependent designation (*tatpuruṣa*). This refers to the teaching that elucidates the meaning of the *Benevolent Kings' Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā* and other sutras;

it is thus an analysis according to the dependent designation compound. If one follows the subsequent text, the emptiness of the nature of words and letters is itself *prajñā*; it is the very essence of *prajñā*.

The compound "holding the function of letters" (持文字用) is a *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) analysis, meaning that its essence holds its functional activity. II. The Virtues of the Translator and the Time:
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, the Śramaṇa Mahāprajñā Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree.
The Li clan ruled with Chang’an as their capital and established the state name of Tang. The "Three Piṭakas" refer to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

This master adopted the name "Fazang" (Dharma-Treasury) based on the state name, thereby using the other to manifest himself; this is an instance of the *dhana-vigraha* (explanatory analysis based on possession).

"Śramaṇa" is a general designation for a disciple of the Śākya. The Sanskrit term is *śramaṇa*, which here means "diligent in cessation"; it is a title for one who cultivates goodness and abandons evil.
This master was the most eminent among the four types of *śramaṇas*. "Great and Vast Wisdom" (*Mahāprajñā*) was the title bestowed upon him.
Following the passing of Emperor Suzong and the accession of Emperor Daizong, he received profound and generous imperial favor.

Upon the completion of his translations of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and the *Ghanavyūha Sūtra*, the Emperor composed a preface for them. On the day the verses were being circulated, auspicious clouds suddenly appeared, and the entire court presented memorials of congratulation. Forever...

The first day of the eleventh month in the first year of the Taiyuan era, an imperial edict was issued granting [Amoghavajra] the rank of *tejin* (Special Advance) and the office of Acting Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (*Hongluqing*), with the honorary title "Great and Vast Wisdom Tripitaka Master.
"Amoghavajra" is the master’s name; in Sanskrit it is *Amogha-vajra*, which in Chinese means "Not-in-Vain Vajra.
Currently, only the two characters "Bukong" (Not-in-Vain) are used, as "Vajra" is abbreviated. He was originally from North India... [he was of] Brahmin... lineage.
He was of the Brahmin caste. Having lost his father at a young age, he followed his uncle to travel and observe the eastern lands.
At the age of fifteen, he became a disciple of the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi, who taught him the *Siddham* phonology from Sanskrit manuscripts. Within ten days, he had mastered it;

the Master marveled greatly at this and thus frequently had him assist in the translations whenever the scriptures were being rendered. Regarding all the treatises on phonology, he accomplished the work in a single year.
The sixth month having concluded, he recited the *Mañjuśrī-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna*; thus, within the one-year limit, he completed it in two evenings.
His quickness and sharpness were all of this nature. Later, he was granted the five sections and three secrets, as well as the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*.

The ritual procedures of the Susiddhi were transmitted in their entirety without omission. Subsequently, when the Master passed away and his posthumous titles had been conferred, [Amoghavajra] recalled the Master’s final instructions and resolved to undertake a distant expedition;
this was the twentieth year of the Kaiyuan era. At the outset of the journey, he experienced a vision of Mañjuśrī manifesting before him.
Along the way, he quelled black winds and great sea monsters; such divine responses were so magnificent that they cannot be fully described. Later, he reached the Master’s [stupa].

"My country, my sovereign subjects, I pay you respectful homage. This exceeds the ordinary protocol. However, as I have abandoned the world for the sake of the Dharma, I have no leisure to calculate worldly glory.

Since then, I have had no fixed teacher; I have extensively sought over five hundred sections of the Secret Treasury, as well as various sūtras and śāstras, the original samayas, the secret mudrās of the various deities, their ritual forms and iconographies, the methods of mandalas, and their insignia."
The nature and characteristics of his realization were such that he left no source unexhausted. He subsequently traveled through the Five Indias, where he repeatedly manifested miraculous responses.

In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he returned to the capital. At that time, a severe drought prevailed. An imperial edict stated: "The timing must not be delayed, yet the rain must not fall too suddenly.
The Master petitioned to establish the ritual of the Peacock Maṇḍala; before three days had passed, the rain fell in abundant measure. One day, a great wind suddenly arose.

His practice was consistently effective. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Treasury of Wisdom" (Zhizang). In the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he was permitted to return to his native country.
In the fifteenth year, an imperial decree ordered him back to the capital to reside at Dàxīngshàn Monastery.

At the beginning of the Zhìdé era, while the Imperial Carriage was at Níngwǔ and Fèngxiáng, the Master regularly submitted secret memorials concerning his well-being. Sùzōng likewise secretly dispatched envoys to seek secret teachings from him.
When the capital was recovered and the rightful rule restored, events unfolded exactly as he had foreseen.

Subsequently, his methods for blessing the state and aiding the people were without exception effective in every instance, hitting the mark a hundred times out of a hundred. The sutras and śāstras he translated total more than one hundred and twenty fascicles.

Seventy-seven sections, along with the catalog and the names of the monastics and laypeople who served as scribes, were compiled; a brief *pūjā-vidhi* was extracted, and upon its completion, it was presented to the throne.
By imperial decree, it was included in the Tripiṭaka. This work originated during the Tiānbǎo era and was finalized in the sixth year of the Dàlì era.
Shortly thereafter, he manifested illness and submitted a memorial to take his leave. An imperial messenger was dispatched to inquire after his health and was granted medicine. Furthermore—

He was granted the title of Kaifu Yitong Sansi (Grand Marshal with Ceremonial Rank Equal to the Three High Officials) and enfeoffed as Duke of Su with a fief of three thousand households. He firmly declined these honors, which were not granted;
he was deeply displeased and said, "The assembly of the Holy Ones is solemnly present, extending their hands to comfort me. When the white moon is full, I shall depart.
How could I, at the moment of death, still covet titles and positions? Thereupon, [he took] the five-pronged vajra bell and ritual mace.

His prayer beads and other personal effects were presented to the Emperor by the imperial messenger Li Xiancheng. Having bathed and positioned himself facing east toward the palace, he entered the state of meditative concentration with his body in the *mahāmudrā* posture and passed away peacefully.
He was seventy years of age and had fifty years of monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-varṣa*). The Emperor suspended court for three days and granted funds for the construction of a stūpa;
an imperial messenger was dispatched by edict to oversee the funeral rites, which were performed with the utmost magnificence and honor. Following the cremation, [the remains were] taken to...
A memorial service was held at the temple. He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of Works (Sikong) and the posthumous name "Great Discerning and Correct, Vast Wisdom Tripitaka Master.

When the funeral pyre was extinguished, several hundred grains of relics were collected; eighty grains were presented to the imperial court. His cranial bone did not burn, and within it was found a single relic.
Half-hidden and half-manifest, an imperial decree was issued to erect a separate stupa within this very monastery. The benefits of his transformative teachings were manifold;

yet, it was the gateway of *dhāraṇī* that most clearly manifested his extraordinary excellence. As for his level on the stages of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), no certainty could be reached regarding its height.

From the beginning, the Xuanzong Emperor continued to honor him with profound respect. Thus, during the Tianbao era, the three kingdoms of West Fan, Da Shi, and Kang led their armies to besiege the West.

Liang [Emperor Gaozong] issued an edict for Emperor Kong to preside over the ritual site. The Master held the incense burner and recited the *Ratnaketuparivarta* (Renwang) secret mantras twenty-eight times.
The Emperor saw some five hundred divine soldiers in the palace courtyard and asked in alarm, "Who are these?
The Master replied, "They are the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa leading his troops to rescue Anxi. Please urgently prepare offerings to dispatch them. On the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month...
On that day, Guo reported: "On the twenty-first day of the second month, about thirty *li* to the northeast of the city, amidst clouds and mist, I beheld divine soldiers of great stature.
As drums and horns blared, the mountains and earth shook and quaked, and the barbarian tribes were struck with terror and fled in disarray.

Within their encampment, there was a golden-colored rat that gnawed the strings of their bows and crossbows until they all snapped. Furthermore, light shone from the gate tower to the north of the city."
The Heavenly King glared in anger, and the frontier tribes fled in great haste. The Emperor examined the memorial from Master Xie;

indeed, after the Master’s passing, he presented each of the imperial edicts bestowed by the three reigns. Thus, receiving honor in life and mourning at death, the transmission of the Dharma to the Western Regions reached its zenith;
such a case is rarely seen in antiquity or today. As for those who translated under imperial decree, it was specifically by the command of Emperor Daizong that this sutra was translated. Therefore—
The preface states: "I am bound by grief like the thorns of the *luan* tree and moved to sorrow by the dew and frost. Receiving and upholding the bequeathed testament, I dare not be remiss or idle.
I have invited a multitude of eminent sages who carry the *śikya* staff, so that the mountain may finally reach its nine-tiered height.

The Duke of the Court, Cao En, has pledged his person to the state and surrendered his life to the Buddha; he assists my true teaching and extends the wondrous gate [of the Dharma] at the south of the Daming Palace."

Taoyuan. Having already provided a detailed translation of the *Huguo Banruo* (Prajñāpāramitā for Protecting the State), this is a brief clarification. The full account is as found in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Song Dynasty).

The appended note states: Regarding the transmission of the wheel of the teachings and commands, in the Land of the East (China), Vajrabodhi is the first patriarch, Amoghavajra is the second patriarch, and Huilang is the third patriarch;
the variations and developments resulting from the lineages that followed them can be understood from this. From here on...
Later, the Qí lineage branched into various schools, all of which claimed to transmit the Great Teaching of Yoga. While they were numerous, why was it that few produced actual results?
This is just as the Yu-jia gave birth to the Ying-long, the Ying-long gave birth to the phoenix, and once the phoenix had descended, it gave birth to common birds.
How could one expect there not to be change and transformation?

△ Section Three: Honoring Antiquity through Textual Analysis. This has three parts: First, the origins and circumstances of the Dharma assembly; second, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (The Lotus Sutra). This has two parts: First, the *Śraddhā-prasāda-anukrama* (The Introductory Chapter on Faith);
second, the title of the current chapter. This has two parts: First, the title of the chapter.
Chapter One: The Prologue (*Nidāna*).

"Prologue" (*xu*) is a term derived from the meaning of "thread" (*xu*). It refers to the beginning or the opening thread. Just as when one pulls a skein, one finds the thread, and by pulling it out, one unravels all the silk from the cocoon;
so too, if one understands the prologue of this sutra, one will penetrate the essential purport of the entire scripture. It is like [the sequence of] clouds first appearing and then...
First rain, then smoke; first smoke and clouds, then fire and rain. The Buddha-dharma is likewise.

Therefore, the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) is explained first to manifest the causes and conditions for the teaching of the Dharma; it is the very beginning of this entire sutra. Why is this so?
It is because, from the gathering of the supportive assembly and the sages and saints of the Three Vehicles, there is manifested the inconceivable, wondrous virtue of shadows and echoes.
The humans and devas of the three realms manifest the true practice of initiating great protection. Next, the assembly of transformations appears;

the manifestation of lands and seats symbolizes that while the mind is pure and phenomena are empty, the source of awakening remains unclouded. The manifestation of causes and fruits symbolizes that while one exhausts the cause and penetrates the fruit, the nature of wisdom shares a single source.
As for the transformational appearance of the eight classes of beings, it demonstrates that the nature of wisdom within the bonds of affliction is likewise [unobscured].
The same applies to the Buddhas who preach the Dharma: they clarify that the ultimate fruit of bodhi is non-dual; these are all the initial manifestations [of their power].
Furthermore, by entering meditative absorption, they demonstrate the stillness and tranquility of wondrous wisdom; by emitting light, they reveal the perfect pervasiveness of the dharma-realm;
by raining flowers, they manifest the inconceivability of causal practice; and by shaking the earth, they shatter the delusive knots of ignorance. These constitute the complete manifestation.

This is the initial thread [of the teaching]. As for such instances as the Great Assembly manifesting doubt, King Bimbisāra posing questions, using music to awaken [the listener], and the light summoning those with karmic affinity—these are the initial threads that assist in its manifestation.

If one grasps this thread, then all subsequent cultivation of causes and realization of fruits, self-benefit and benefiting others, and the protection of the Dharma and the state, will all emerge from this single path. It is just like...
A journey of a thousand li does not begin apart from a single step; a vast and surging river does not originate outside of a single ladle of water.
Therefore, the establishment of titles and the classification of sections are intended to clarify the origins, the principles, and the structural outlines of the authentic teaching of the Dharma.
II. Detailed Explanation of the Sutra. This has two parts. First, the faith and hearing regarding the time and place.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
The ancient masters explained this as follows: "In this manner, I have heard this Dharma from the Buddha," which refers to the time of Ānanda’s compilation of the teachings.
Regarding the chant for the initial ascending of the seat: this was established by the Buddha himself; it need not be explained with profound mystery.

The "speech of a single moment" was likewise established by the Buddha and is commonly used across all sutras, hence it is not specifically pointed out here. Now, according to the *Great Commentary* (Dàshū) by Qingliang, there are three meanings.
First, clarifying the source of its establishment: when the Buddha was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda requested instruction.

Regarding the four matters: it was for these that the Buddha commanded this statement to be placed [at the beginning]. To the four matters thus questioned, the Buddha answered them one by one: first, dwelling in reliance upon the four foundations of mindfulness;
second, taking the precepts as one's teacher; third, the silent exclusion of monks of evil character; and fourth, that at the head of all sūtras, one should establish the formula:
"Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in such-and-such a place," and so forth. Second, the clarification of the establishment [of the sūtra].
The meaning of these words is that there are three purposes for the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: namely, to sever doubt, to quell dispute, and to distinguish from the heterodox.
Regarding the severing of doubt: it refers to the doubt as to whether such scriptural passages were composed by Ānanda himself or spoken by the Buddha.

Therefore, by first stating "Thus have I heard," it is made manifest that this is the Buddha’s teaching and is certainly not his own composition. When Ānanda ascended the seat, his physical marks and signs suddenly [appeared].

Regarding "Thus" (evam): the assembly harbored three doubts concerning the Buddha—whether another Buddha from another direction had come, whether the Buddha was about to pass away, or whether Ānanda would himself become a Buddha.
These three doubts remained unresolved, leaving their hearts as conflicted as ice and fire. Yet, as soon as he uttered "Thus have I heard," those three doubts were shattered like a crumbling wall.
Regarding the third point on the cessation of disputes: it is said that to exhaust the mysteries of the spirit and know the transformations of the Dao can only be expounded by a Buddha;

likewise, only a Buddha can transmit this to future generations. Otherwise, all would be mere conjecture based on individual perceptions and views, from which contradictions and errors would proliferate.
Controversies arise among one another; yet, by examining such statements as these now presented, one knows them to be the Buddha’s true teaching.

Within them, all matters are thoroughly penetrated and profoundly concentrated, encompassing and transforming the realm of sentient beings without ever erring throughout eternity. As the model for the Three Vehicles, how could there be any cause for dispute?
As for the third type, the heterodox and externalists, they are deluded and attached, failing to investigate the source of the mind; their every step leads them into the domain of suffering.
Wherever one encounters the barriers of permanence and annihilation, existence and non-existence, identity and difference, or the four propositions and hundred negations, none can be avoided.

Now, by proclaiming "Thus have I heard," the ultimate and conventional truths are harmoniously integrated, and phenomena and principle are revealed simultaneously. The wondrous essence of the Middle Way is true in every place;

it is not the existence or non-existence of false attachments, nor does it fall into the permanence or annihilation of ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle. Thus speaks the Sage who transmits the Dharma.

To reveal that the Name and Teaching arise from responsive resonance, these words were established; therein lie three intentions. Third, the correct explanation of their meaning consists of six factors:
first, faith; second, hearing; third, time; fourth, the principal [teacher]; fifth, the place; and sixth, the assembly. If these six conditions are not complete, the Teaching will not arise;
it must possess all six to be fully realized, hence the term "accomplishment" (*siddhi*). As for the phrase "Thus" (*evam*): it is...
This refers to the terminology of the Dharma; that is, it points back to the Dharma explained below. This is the accomplishment of faith.
The ancients said that those who believe state, "This matter is thus," while those who do not believe state, "This matter is not thus. Master Zhao said, "Faith is a term for compliance.
Furthermore, it is said that "thus" (ru) is named according to the compliance with the capacity [of the recipient]; therefore, there is nothing that is not received.

"Appellation. This is a general explanation. If one refers specifically to this sutra, then the emptiness of all phenomena mentioned below constitutes "Suchness" (tathatā), and the correct cultivation of the five patiences constitutes "Is-ness" (tathatva).
Question: Why is establishing "Suchness" also called "the accomplishment of faith"? Answer: Faith and Suchness are inseparable in their two meanings;
therefore, it was said previously that "faith is Suchness. This is especially so regarding the Great Dharma of the Buddha.

"The ocean: does one not enter it without faith? Thus, there is indeed a profound reason for the initial establishment of these [terms]. 'I' refers to what is heard; that is, the accomplishment of hearing.

For the Dharma of the Buddha does not enter the ears of the deaf. 'I' refers to Ānanda himself, pointing to the provisional entity composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which is distinct from the 'self' imagined by worldly sentiments.
'Hearing' means the faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*) giving rise to consciousness to listen to the voice of that Buddha."
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "If one merely hears a sound, it pertains only to the ear; if one takes names and phrases as objects, it occurs within the mind.
Now, setting aside the distinction between ear and mind, they are collectively termed 'hearing. If one follows the intent of the sūtras, there is neither speaker nor listener;
only then is it true hearing. Regarding "at one time": it means accomplished at that very moment, for it is difficult to establish transformation outside of the opportune moment.

Because it benefits sentient beings, the teaching and listening are brought to completion. The meeting of teacher and disciple is collectively termed "at one time" (*ekasmin samaye*), which merely distinguishes this from other times.
However, there are differences in the timing of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the sūtras; moreover, the durations of time differ across various regions, being either extended or abbreviated.

Since it is impossible to enumerate each instance individually, a single phrase is used to encompass them all, hence the general designation "at one time. As for "Buddha," he is the principal agent who accomplishes [the goal].

Regarding this: the Sanskrit term is *buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One" (*jue-zhe*). This refers to one who has fully realized the nature and characteristics of both the true and the false. There are three aspects of this awakening:

first, self-awakening to the emptiness of the self (*ātman*), which distinguishes [this awakening] from that of ordinary beings; second, awakening others to the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma*), which distinguishes it from that of the Two Vehicles;

and third, the fulfillment of awakening to the emptiness of both, which accords with original awakening (*ben-ju*) and is termed ultimate awakening (*jui-jing jue*). It is vast, expansive, and boundless.
He is also called the Great Awakened One (*mahābuddha*), supreme and peerless; he is also called the Sublime Awakened One (*sambuddha*) to distinguish him from the bodhisattvas.

Because he is fully endowed with the three types of awakening, he alone is named Buddha. Regarding the ten meanings explaining "Buddha" in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, I shall not cite them here to avoid prolixity.

As for "dwelling in Rājagṛha," etc., this refers to the perfection of the location. In the *Tattvārthā-ṭīkā*, it is said that there are two kinds of dwelling places: first, the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).
This refers to two types of abodes: first, those for converting those in the secular world, such as Rājagṛha;

second, those for presiding over the community of renunciants, such as Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa). By citing Rājagṛha, he distinguishes it from other countries; by citing Vulture Peak, he [distinguishes it from other mountains].
"Mountain. This distinguishes it from other mountains. In the Sanskrit language, it is called Rājagṛha-mahāgara;

this is translated as "Great City of the King's Abode. Here, the word "great" (mahā) is abbreviated. There are many causes and conditions for this city’s name; it is a city belonging to the kingdom of Magadha.
It was due to King Bandhumat, who, believing in false doctrines, vowed to harm a thousand kings. Once he encountered Puming (Samantaprabhāsa), he became confused... [text ends].

His mind opened to enlightenment. He then established himself with the thousand kings in the mountains, where they built a city and erected dwellings; it flourished into a great kingdom, and the governance was passed down through successive reigns.

Because the thousand kings had resided there, it was called Rājagṛha (the Royal Residence). Furthermore, when the houses of the common people within the city were struck by fire seven times, only the residence of the king was spared.
Later, the king issued a decree that all the private residences of the subjects throughout the land should henceforth be designated as "Royal Residences. It did not stop there.

It was burned again, and it was called Rājagṛha (King’s House). There are also accounts such as those stating that the Four Heavenly Kings collectively constructed it, as detailed in the ancient commentaries.
Within and without this city, there were six monasteries (*vihāra*): first, the Bamboo Grove Garden (*Veṇuvana*), and so on, up to the sixth, the Gṛdhrakūṭa Parvata Monastery.
This is translated here as Lingjushan (Vulture Peak). Regarding the etymology, it refers to the fact that during Śākyamuni’s causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*), he acted as a vulture.
Because he raised his parents within this mountain, it was named after him. Regarding its history, to the south of this city lies a *śītavana* (cemetery) where vultures gather;
they consume many of the corpses there. Furthermore, when a person is about to die, these birds fly toward their home and utter mournful cries, as if foreknowing the death.
Thus, it is called Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak). As for its physical form, this mountain...

It has five peaks; the eastern one resembles an elephant’s head, and so on, until the central one, which is like a vulture’s head. Here, the four shapes are omitted, and it is referred to solely by its center.
It is also called Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak). Thus we know that some say this mountain was named after its shape, which is also stated based on its most prominent feature.
However, the places where the Buddha preached the Dharma varied according to the specific intent of each teaching, as in the *Avataṃsaka*, which is circular.

To manifest the Dharma-realm, [the *Avataṃsaka*] traverses all ten locations. To directly reveal the fundamental cause, the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* relies upon the Great Luminous Treasury (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*).
To clarify the meaning of defilement and purity, the *Lotus Sūtra* relies upon the royal city. Furthermore, to clarify the sense of ancestral succession, it relies upon Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*).
Now, as the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme Dharma-gate, it is spoken here on the Sacred Mountain (*Rājagiri*). II. [End of Section] Two.

The enumeration of the great assembly consists of three parts: first, the assembly of the perfected retinue; second, the assembly of the noble ones of the three vehicles; and third, the assembly of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Within the latter, there are further divisions. First is the assembly of those beyond training.
He was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand and eight bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats. Their outflows were exhausted; they were free from further afflictions;
their minds were well-liberated and their wisdom was well-liberated. Possessing the nine knowledges and ten knowledges, they had accomplished what was to be done.
They had fully realized the three contemplations on the provisional and the real, the three contemplations on the gates of emptiness, and had perfected all conditioned and unconditioned merits.
"Along with the great ones below. This raises the category and indicates the number. An ancient master stated that there are four distinct types of assemblies listed in various sutras:
First, the "shadow-and-echo assembly," referring to the bodhisattvas whose great fruits are already perfected; they appear for the sake of causing the True Dharma to abide long in the world.
Second, the "assembly for establishing karmic connections," who, although hearing the teaching in the present, do not yet obtain benefit, but serve as the cause for attaining the Way in the future.

Third, the assembly of initiators: because of these causes and conditions, the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas mutually inspire one another to request the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma for the universal benefit of all sentient beings.
Fourth, the assembly of those who are ready to receive the teaching (the *pratipannaka*): having planted the causes in remote antiquity, they bring the fruit to fruition in this present life;

thus, at the moment they hear the Dharma, they are able to awaken and enter into realization. Furthermore, each of the four assemblies, such as the bhikṣus, possesses their own fourfold manifestations, including the shadow and the echo.
Just as there are shadows and echoes, so too are there those who correspond to the occasion and so forth. "Bhikṣu" is a Sanskrit term that contains three meanings:
first, terrifying Māra; second, a mendicant; and third, one who destroys evil. One is called a bhikṣu to demonstrate the appearance of detachment.

Furthermore, it demonstrates the Mahāyāna path of skillful means, which is shared with the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha). Moreover, among the fourfold assembly, it likewise signifies being far removed [from worldly attachments].
Because it is apart from conditioned activity, it is called "Great. According to the correspondence between the Chinese and Sanskrit translations, *mahā* means "great.

While this designation of "high path and profound virtue" is based on its manifest traces, in terms of principle, it actually refers to the "Three Greats"—the great essence, the great characteristic, and the great function—as being truly great.
Various sūtras state that there were one thousand two hundred and fifty people;

as for this mention of one thousand and eight, it is likely due to a discrepancy in the number, being merely appropriate to the occasion rather than a fixed certainty. Furthermore, the Qin translation states there were eight million billion.
The current mention of "one thousand and eight hundred people" may be due to a variation in the translator’s rendering of the text. The term "and" (*yu*) here carries the meaning of "together.
As the *Śāstra* states: "At one time, in one place, with one precept, one mind, one view, one path, and one liberation"—this refers to them all.
This passage, following the section on the Arhats, praises their virtues; it collectively praises the one thousand and eight hundred people, hence the statement.

All [these] are the elimination of the various outflows (*āsrava*). This specifically clarifies the merits possessed [by this stage]; having already reached the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*), they are neither those in the three fruits nor those in the four paths, but are precisely the fourth fruit, the Arhat.
"Arhat" is a Sanskrit term; it is translated here with three meanings:

first, "slayer of thieves," because the fetters of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* and *vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted; second, "worthy of offerings," because they are capable of acting as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Because the vows are fulfilled, there is no further birth; for the causes of the three realms have ceased, and one does not undergo future existence.

These "outflows" (*āsrava*)—namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*)—all take the deluded consciousness that clings to stillness as their substance.
They are the root of the afflictions of the three realms. They are all called "outflows" because the mind of profound goodness cannot remain entirely unified, but becomes stuck [in delusion].

The profound arising of consciousness flows forth and rushes toward objects; therefore, it is called "outflow" (*āsrava*). The afflictions (*kleśa*)—namely, the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) such as greed, hatred, and delusion—act as the conditions for these outflows.
They injure the *dharmakāya* and oppress the true nature; thus they are called "affliction-thieves.

What is now termed "the exhaustion of outflows and the absence of affliction" refers to the fact that because the root is exhausted, the conditions are likewise non-existent. This is precisely the meaning of "slaying the thieves."
The followers of the Hīnayāna possess concentration but lack wisdom; thus, bound by partiality and deficiency, they have not yet attained liberation.

Now, having exhausted all fetters and enabling the mind to attain mastery, it is said that the mind is "well-liberated. With both wisdom and abandonment fully perfected, one realizes and enters into unimpededness.
Therefore, it is said that through wisdom one is well-liberated. All such as these are Arhats who are like shadows and echoes. The *Vajra-śāstra-yaoyao* states:
"Because the mind is obstructed by the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the mind is not liberated; thus one creates karma, undergoes retribution, and transmigrates through the five destinies."
Due to the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), wisdom is not liberated; one fails to realize one's own mind and does not penetrate the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
Even if one transcends the three realms, one remains stalled at the level of the two vehicles and cannot attain Buddhahood. Now that both [hindrances] are exhausted, mind and wisdom are liberated;

there is no doubt that one will become like a shadow or an echo [of the Buddhas]. Nevertheless, regarding the liberation of mind and wisdom, when categorized according to individuals, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established.
This refers to those whose minds are liberated but whose wisdom is not liberated—the followers of the Two Vehicles; those whose minds are not liberated but whose wisdom is liberated—the Bodhisattvas;
those who are liberated in both respects—the Buddhas; and those who are liberated in neither respect—the ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Regarding the nine knowledges (*jñāna*):

according to the *Dharmasaṃgraha*, the first is the knowledge of the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi-jñāna*), which consists of the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-citta-sthiti*) and so forth. The second is the knowledge of the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi-jñāna*), which consists of the four stages of application (*catasraḥ prayoga-bhūmayaḥ*).

The practices and so forth. Above these, one subdues the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*). 1. The wisdom of the first fruit (*srotāpanna-phala-jñāna*): exhausting all afflictions of views (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) within the three realms and realizing the true truths (*satya*).

2. The wisdom of the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala-jñāna*): abandoning the six grades of afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) in the desire realm. 3. The wisdom of the third fruit (*anāgāmi-phala-jñāna*):

exhausting the remaining afflictions of thought in the desire realm. 4. The wisdom of the fourth fruit (*arhat-phala-jñāna*): exhausting all afflictions of views and thoughts within the three realms. 5. The Pratyekabuddha.

1. Wisdom: It exhausts the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), further eradicating the ten kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). 2. The wisdom of the eighth stage Bodhisattva:

It exhausts the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) of the three realms and cultivates the practices of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). 3. The wisdom of the Buddha-stage: It immediately and simultaneously eradicates the residual habits of the views and thoughts of the three realms.

He sat beneath a wooden Bodhi tree with a bed of growing grass as his seat, manifesting an inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*). Nevertheless, this sutra contains both the wisdoms of the *pratyekabuddha* and the *bodhisattva*;

since their respective bases are both the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) teachings and what they sever are both the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), it does not constitute an obstacle.

The ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are as follows: First is *dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of phenomena). This refers to the untainted knowledge of patience regarding phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma-kṣānti-jñāna*) and the untainted knowledge within the category of patience regarding phenomena (*dharma-kṣānti-jñāna-varga*), which severs the fetters (*saṃyojana*) associated with the Four Truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Second is *anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge).

This refers to the untainted knowledge that severs the fetters associated with the Four Truths of the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*). However, there is no separate analytical observation for severing the fetters of the two higher realms.

1. Knowledge by Inference (anvaya-jñāna): Because it takes as its object only those factors of the lower realms that are abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), it is called knowledge by inference; it is also called inferential knowledge (anumāna-jñāna). 2. Knowledge of Others' Minds (paracitta-jñāna):
It knows the present minds and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) bound to the desire and form realms, as well as a small portion of uncontaminated (anāsrava) minds and mental factors;
it is also called knowledge of others' minds. 3. Conventional Knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna): This refers to knowing worldly, contaminated wisdom. It is also...
1. Knowledge of Names and so forth (*nāma-ādi-jñāna*): This is because it is common to both ordinary persons and noble ones. 2. Knowledge of Suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*):

This refers to the knowledge of the four aspects—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—when contemplating the five aggregates. 3. Knowledge of Origination (*samudaya-jñāna*): This refers to the untainted knowledge that arises when contemplating the four aspects of the causes and conditions of origination as the cause of tainted phenomena.
4. Knowledge of Cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*): This refers to the [knowledge] at the time of realization, characterized by the four aspects of cessation, peace, excellence, and renunciation.

The untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) at the time of practicing the four modes of contemplation (*catasraḥ ākārāḥ*) is the wisdom of the Eightfold Path (*mārga-jñāna*). That is to say, when cultivating [the path], one mounts the correct track of the Path and practices the four modes of contemplation with untainted wisdom.
Now, these four wisdoms regarding suffering (*duḥkha*) and so forth are the model for the Śrāvaka vehicle’s contemplation of the Eight Truths (*aṣṭau satyāni*) and thirty-two modes of contemplation.

Here, the "modes" (*ākāra*) are the subject of contemplation (*ālambaka*), while the "Truths" (*satya*) are the objects of contemplation (*ālambana*). When the four modes of contemplation are exhausted, one Truth is realized.

This is emptiness. Just as it is with the single truth, so it is with the seven truths. This is precisely what is clarified in the *Yuanren lun shu* (Commentary on the Treatise on the Original Person) regarding the reduction of objects (*ālambana*) in seven cycles and the reduction of practitioners in twenty-four cycles.
9. Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*): This refers to having already been able to see suffering, abandon its origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path.
10. Knowledge of Non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*): This is the state where, having already seen suffering, one no longer needs to see it again.

...and so forth. These are they. Apart from these ten knowledges (*jñāna*), there may be the knowledge of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which does not belong to the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Furthermore, among the ten knowledges, the two vehicles possess the first nine, but lack the tenth, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
"That which has been done is finished" refers to the aforementioned matter of realizing wisdom and severing delusions; there is nothing lacking therein. The *Fahua wenju* states:
The causes and effects of the three realms are all matters pertaining to others; the merit of wisdom and abandonment is what is called one’s own benefit.

To attain one’s own benefit is precisely what is meant by "having completed what was to be done," which is the meaning of non-arising. Regarding the contemplation of the three—conventionality, reality, and the real—the term "three" refers to phenomena (dharma) and reception (upādāna).
Phenomenal conventionality refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). As the ancients said: "Form is like a mass of foam"; thus, it is entirely illusory and false.

Therefore, "feeling" (vedanā) is a provisional designation for the four aggregates. As the ancients said: "Feeling is like a bubble; perception (saṃjñā) is like a mirage; mental formations (saṃskāra) are like a plantain tree;
and consciousness (vijñāna) is like a magical illusion. Because these two names [feeling and perception] are combined, they constitute the provisional designation of "name" (nāma).
Since these are empty names and not true names, yet these three dharmas lack substantiality in their own essence and exist only by depending on conditions, sentient beings fail to understand this.

They are falsely grasped as real. When the Noble Ones observe correctly, they see that although things are real, they are empty; since names cannot be found through seeking, how could there be any form or sensation?
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "All dharmas have their distinctions based solely upon deluded thought."
If one is free from discursive thought, then there are no marks of any objective realms. However, these three contemplations are provisional dharmas explained according to the Hinayana teachings;
yet when viewed according to ultimate reality, these three dharmas are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way.
Obstruction and illumination occur at once, and both are forgotten. Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Dharmas produced by causes and conditions—I say they are emptiness."
It is also called "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*) and it is also called the "meaning of the Middle Way. This is it. Regarding the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):

this clarifies the three emptinesses based on the aforementioned three types of provisional designations. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that these are the gates to Nirvana through which one proceeds by means of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

There are three gates, namely the three gates of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth. The gate of emptiness means observing that all phenomena exist falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
thus, there is no self, no person, no agent, and no experiencer. The gate of signlessness (*animitta*) means observing that all phenomena are established through false perception;
within them, there is no bending or stretching, coming or going, movement or stillness, seeing or hearing, nor speech.
It is real, for it is like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, or a shadow. Regarding the gate of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*): this means observing that all phenomena lack intrinsic substance;

even "action" is a delusion, and when the mind is stilled, its substance is empty. Because one makes no arrangements whatsoever, through these three kinds of emptiness, one realizes the three gates of liberation.
Therefore, it is further said that these three serve as the gates. Merit that is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); merit that is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is...

The virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). Thus, in the *lakṣaṇa-yāna* (Characteristics School), it is held that conditioned wisdom (*saṃskṛta-jñāna*) realizes the unconditioned principle (*asaṃskṛta-tattva*).

However, these two kinds of merit (*guṇa*) are distinguished as conditioned or unconditioned based on cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*), respectively. Regarding the term "merit" (*guṇa*): "merit" (*gong*, *guṅ*) refers to the achievement of completion through abandonment and realization;
"virtue" (*de*, *dē*) denotes that which is refined, pure, beautiful, and wholesome. One should distinguish them by means of four logical permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, merit... [text ends]

1. It is virtue but not merit, such as when one accomplishes a task that harms others. 2. It is merit but not virtue, such as when one maintains loyalty and filial piety but has not yet performed a single deed.

3. It is both merit and virtue, such as when one serves the state with loyalty and serves one's parents with filial piety, such that one’s loyalty and filiality become famous in the world and are passed down through generations.
4. It is neither merit nor virtue, such as when one acts to the disadvantage of others and provides no benefit.
The previous [verses] regarding the spreading of ill repute throughout the world and so forth, now possess both aspects; this is the third line.
Bestowing beneficial things upon others and taking goodness for oneself is therefore called "merit. The final line is a summary:

as such actual virtues are present without any deficiency, it says "accomplished," which carries the meaning of being worthy of offerings. Thus, one knows that the name "Arhat" is a general praise. The remaining text...
These are the three meanings explained individually within the definition of the term "Arhat. △ Second, the assembly of those still in training (śaikṣa).
Furthermore, there was an assembly of eight hundred bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were Arhats.
Question: According to the statement that they are all *arhats*, it is very clear that the eight hundred nuns are not *śaikṣas* (those still in training).
Why, then, are they now classified as *śaikṣas*? Answer: The realization and severance [of defilements] by the nuns are not yet profound; most of them remain in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*).

Even the foremost among them, who are *aśaikṣas* (those beyond training), are leaders within the ranks of those in training. Therefore, based on the majority, they are classified as belonging to the category of *śaikṣas*. Even if there are... [exceptions].

The title "Arhat" (羅漢) seems to have no [corresponding] meaning [in this context]. In the text, it first indicates the category, then cites the number, and the final sentence offers a general praise for the virtues of the eight hundred [monks].
As for "Nī," it is a feminine suffix. Originally, there were no women who left the household life;
it was because of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī’s earnest request through Ānanda that the Buddha granted her leave, and subsequently expounded the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭa-guru-dharma*) for her.
She opened the gate of compassion at the site of enlightenment; Māyādevī reverently upheld it with a single mind.
Having escaped the net of karma in the mundane world, her Dharma-eye subsequently became pure. She took charge of the assembly as its presiding leader, and her wisdom-nature was fully enlightened.
Leading eight hundred followers, she headed their practice. Later, Rāhula’s mother also emerged from the toils of worldly existence, her innate faculties being sharp.
Emerging with brilliant clarity, she was destined to realize the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Since her self-benefit was already perfected, she served as the head of the nuns.

These individuals were all like shadows and echoes—attendants who assisted in propagating the transformation [of the Dharma]. Regarding their provisional teachings, it is said that women lack the capacity to achieve the Way, and thus their [access to] the True Dharma is extinguished.
Yet, according to the essential principle, women are all those who equally realize [the truth]; therefore, there is no impairment to the Dharma.
Is it not so that those of such nature were granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? Thus we know that the assembly of nuns all came together;

they did so indeed to receive the Dharma and partake of its benefits, to increase the Path and diminish birth, no different from the Bodhisattvas. Yet those who are nuns today are themselves bewildered and confused;
they do not know what the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) are, nor do they know for what purpose one leaves the household life in this birth.
...this is truly to have cause for shame before one's own heart; how tragic! △ Third, the assembly of Bodhisattvas:
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. Possessing the equality of true wisdom, they had forever severed the obstacles of affliction.

Through skillful means, they gave rise to great practices and vows, benefiting sentient beings by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇacitta*). Universally...

Enveloping all, he possesses the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) and has attained the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). He cultivates the boundless factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and excels in arts and crafts, surpassing all worldly beings.
He penetrates deeply into dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Entering and emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), he manifests immeasurable deeds, subdues the hosts of Māra and his enemies, and illuminates both truths simultaneously. With the Dharma-eye, he perceives universally and knows the faculties of sentient beings. (4)

He possesses the analytical knowledges, the fearlessnesses in proclaiming the Dharma, and the sublime wisdom of the ten powers. He resounds with the thunderous sound of the Dharma, drawing near to the Peerless One (the Buddha).
Thus, he is fully endowed with all such virtues, including the Vajra-samādhi.
"Bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of a Sanskrit term; here it means "a sentient being with the mind of the Way. "Mahāsattva" refers to the "Great Mind of the Way.
As for the designation of their number as "immeasurable," it most clearly demonstrates that those who have fully manifested the Great Mind are numerous.

Thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that Bodhisattvas possess three greatnesses—namely, the greatness of aspiration, the greatness of practice, and the greatness of benefiting sentient beings—which refers to this very point. From "True Wisdom" onwards, [the text] offers praise.
These virtues are all possessed by Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), but are absent in the stage of the worthy ones (*ārya*) prior to the stages.

This is because the subsequent text states that they have "transcended the stage of the foolish" and "are born into the family of the Tathāgata," and it describes them as "abiding in the patience of equality" and possessing "the initial wisdom of signlessness."
It illuminates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), which is of one mark and yet markless; therefore, it is called the equality of true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

It severs all ignorance and extinguishes the craving of the three realms, so that future birth and death will never arise again; thus, it is said to eternally extinguish the obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Taking great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its foremost principle, it gives rise to various great vows and, through the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), cultivates immeasurable supreme practices in every thought-moment. Therefore...

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): these are the virtues of the twofold benefit [for self and others] in this first stage (*bhūmi*). This is because in this stage, while actual wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) effects cessation and realization, expedient means gives rise to practice and vows.

The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*)—namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation—are practiced by abiding in these four dharmas with a vast and pure mind to universally benefit all sentient beings; this is also the practice of benefiting others in the first stage. (4)
The "immeasurable minds" (apramāṇa-citta) are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Because each of these four dharmas is vast and boundless, they are called "immeasurable.
These are the practices and virtues of the second bhūmi; as the subsequent text states: "In the second bhūmi, the four immeasurable minds are supremely quiescent.
Regarding the term "universally covering," this refers to great loving-kindness bestowing happiness upon all, and great compassion [relieving the suffering of all].

Because they uproot all suffering. Regarding the "three types of clear knowledge" (*tisro vidyāḥ*): these are the clear knowledge of past lives, the clear knowledge of the divine eye in the present, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows in the future.
Because they fully know the three periods of time—without past, future, or present—they are said to be "penetratingly discerning.

As for "attaining the five supernormal powers" (*pañcābhijñā*): this refers to the mastery over manifesting the body as large or small and appearing or disappearing at will; with the purity of the divine eye, one perceives everything.
Regarding the various realms of existence: with the purified divine ear, one hears all sounds; with the knowledge of others' minds, one knows [the thoughts of] all sentient beings;
and one is able to know the immeasurable distinctions of their past lives. These are the virtues of the practices of the third stage.

By cultivating the lower [stages], one then cultivates the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment in the fourth stage. This is for the purpose of accomplishing the powers.
The fearlessnesses are the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*). Regarding "craftsmanship" (*śilpa*) and below:

that is, on the fifth stage, one fully contemplates the truths (*satya*) and, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, practices various arts and skills—namely, writing, medicine, poetry and song, drama and laughter, craftsmanship, and incantations.

Regarding heterodox paths and various divinations of fortune and misfortune, there is not a single instance of error; this refers to those who have thoroughly mastered the five sciences on the fifth stage.

As for "profoundly entering" and below: on the sixth stage, one dwells in the three gates of liberation and contemplates all birth and death—how they are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, how consciousness is sown through the accumulation of karma, and so forth, up to birth, old age, and death—all of which arise from attachment to a self.
Ignorance, karma, and their fruits are neither existent nor non-existent; they are of one mark and without marks, for they are non-dual.

This refers to that which is called the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī bhūmi*), wherein, throughout many eons, one practices the hundreds of thousands of samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, thereby attaining the Great Prajñā of boundless illumination.
"Entering and exiting" below refers to the seventh stage (*saptamī bhūmi*), where one dwells in the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) within tranquility.

The cessation-samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the arising of sublime practices: though eternally quiescent, they extensively transform sentient beings; they manifest entry among the śrāvakas while constantly following the Buddha’s wisdom;
they manifest conformity with non-Buddhists and Māras—this refers to those in the seventh stage who conform to the world yet eternally transcend it.
As for "subduing," this refers to the eighth stage, wherein one benefits the entire realm through the wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala*).

Born [into this state], one is sustained by the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Buddhas and attains mastery over the body (*kāya-vaśitā*). Because one destroys the hosts of Māra, it is called "crushing and subduing.

Because one suddenly gives rise to the activity of wisdom (*jñāna-karman*) that equally illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional truths, it is called "shining forth both. This, moreover, is the virtue of the immovable nature of the single *tathatā*-mind.
Under the Dharma-eye school, at this ninth stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes mastery over wisdom and severs the obstacles of non-obstruction; therefore, one is able to...
The Dharma-eye perceives universally. Since this Dharma-eye is well able to observe the conventional world, it is further said that it "knows the faculties of sentient beings.
It attains the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge—of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence—regarding the treasury of the Dharma that is taught.

Thus, in expounding the True Dharma, it is uninterrupted and inexhaustible; consequently, even when faced with questions and challenges arising like clouds, one need not strain to respond as if pouring from a jar. As it is said:
This refers to the perfection of benefiting others through the manifestation of the function of True Suchness (*tathatā*) on the ninth stage.

From "the ten powers" (*daśabala*) onwards, there is praise for the virtues of the tenth stage, which also includes the eleventh stage. There are two kinds of ten powers for a bodhisattva: the first is the power of liberation (*vimukti-bala*).

The power of rescuing from suffering; the power of contemplation; the power of patience; the power of wisdom; the power of severance; the power of hearing; the power of aspiration; the power of fulfillment; and the power of love.
These are from the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*. Second, the power of firm resolve; the power of great compassion that does not abandon sentient beings;
the power of being endowed with great pity; the power of diligence through faith in all Buddha-dharmas; and the power of meditative concentration through reflection and practice.
The power of wisdom that eliminates the two extremes; the power of maturing sentient beings (which is not wearying of birth and death);

the power of contemplating the true mark of phenomena (which is abiding in the patience of the non-arising of dharmas); the power of entering the three gates of liberation; and the power of unimpeded wisdom. This is from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.

Thus, by means of these ten powers of sublime wisdom, in a single moment of thought, one universally observes the births within the realms according to their superior, middling, and inferior faculties, and for them, one preaches the three [vehicles].
By mounting [this vehicle], one enters the sphere of the Buddha’s conduct, his powers, and his fearlessnesses; thus it is said that "the sound of the Dharma thunders like a peal of thunder.

The final two lines conclude with a praise of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), which carries the meaning of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). At the moment when the Vajra-samādhi manifests, one accords with the Tathāgata’s two kinds of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*);
yet, because one has not yet attained the immeasurable [qualities] and so forth, it is specifically called "near. If one were already liberated...
The state is one of both form and formlessness, darkly identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). For one who has returned to non-attainment, how could it be said that [the goal] is near?
Nevertheless, this meaning of praising virtue is all explained by taking the meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) from the subsequent "Chapter on Upholding" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*);
this is most appropriate. Thus, the following summarizes the aforementioned virtues: like the ocean containing the hundred rivers, and like the stars all bowing toward the North Star.

North. Therefore, it is said they are "fully endowed. △ Second, the assembly of humans and devas of the two realms. This has two parts: first, the human assembly; second, the assembly entering the Path.
Regarding the first, the assembly entering the Path, there are two parts: first, the assembly entering the Path through the five precepts.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable assemblies of upāsakas and upāsikās, all of whom had seen the Noble Truths.
*Upāsaka* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "pure male," because within the Buddha-dharma they possess pure faith.
It is also called "male lay attendant" (*jìnshì nán*), because they draw near to the Triple Gem and serve them without fail. *Upāsikā* is likewise a Sanskrit term.
These are called "pure women" (*śuddhikā*) or "laywomen" (*upāsikā*). The character *ni* (尼) is the feminine suffix.

This assembly receives and upholds the Three Refuges to extinguish the causes for rebirth in the three miserable realms, and reverently observes the Five Precepts to prevent the transgressions of the three types of action. As for why they must prevent these:

Abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct guards the bodily karma; the single precept against false speech guards the verbal karma; and the single precept against drinking alcohol guards all three karmas collectively.

By being able to take the Three Refuges, one is immediately freed from the three miserable realms, eliminates the three paths, transcends the three periods of time, and realizes the three insights (*trividyā*).
Furthermore, the three virtues, the three bodies (*trikāya*), and the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*) are all inseparable from these [precepts]. These are the Five Precepts.
Regarding this meaning, the ancient commentaries cite the *Tiewei jing* (Sutra of Tiwei), which states: "One must speak of the five precepts;
one does not mention four or six because five is the correct number for the world.

It is said that in heaven they are the five stars, on earth they are the five sacred peaks, in humans they are the five viscera, in yin and yang they are the five elements, among kings they are the five emperors, and in the world...
These constitute the five virtues (which are the Five Constants). In terms of colors, they are the five colors; in terms of dharmas, they are the five precepts.

Furthermore, the precept against killing is assigned to the East. This East presides over wood, and wood presides over benevolence (*ren*). Benevolence takes the nourishing of life and compassionate love as its essential meaning.
If one upholds this precept without fail, then the five deities of this precept will protect one’s entire person, specifically the liver organ.
Peace. During his life, he nurtured all beings with compassion and extended benevolence to all living creatures. Jupiter moved in its proper course.
At the time of his death, he was reborn in the Four Heavenly Kings’ realm, directly transcending to the higher realms and further accomplishing pure karma.

Had he committed transgressions, Jupiter would have been oppressed and forced back; he would have lost his body and life, forfeiting the love of life in the present and sowing [the seeds for future suffering].
One’s lifespan will be short in the future; how much more so regarding the retribution for this karma of killing, which continues in an endless succession.

Therefore, one should diligently uphold the precept of not killing. The precept against stealing is assigned to the West, because the West presides over metal, and metal signifies righteousness (*yi*).
"Righteousness" (*yi*) refers to following principle and being free from greed. If one upholds it without fail, then the five deities of this precept will protect and assist one's entire person.
The lungs and internal organs will remain peaceful; during life, one will advance through virtue and provide relief to the poor and destitute, while Venus shall manifest auspicious signs.
At death, one will be reborn above in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, or proceed to the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, further receiving its benefits.
One accomplishes meritorious karma. If one violates this precept, it will encounter the planet Venus (Kuja) to bring about calamity;

one’s spirit and vital energy will be exhausted and impoverished, losing integrity and virtue in human society and inviting the curse of "carrying a load on one's back" among the beasts. Furthermore, as for the retribution for the karma of theft, it is never fully requited;
therefore, the single precept against stealing must be firmly maintained. The precept against sexual misconduct is assigned to the South, because the South...
Fire is the master of ritual (*li*). Ritual is defined as integrity and purity without disorder.
If one maintains and receives it without transgression, then these five deities of the precepts will provide secret protection for one’s person. The heart-mind will become clear and concentrated;

in life, one’s advances and retreats will be appropriate, and ritual propriety will vigilantly guard against impropriety. The Fire Star will bestow blessings. At death, one will proceed directly to the Yāma Heaven.

Ascending high to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, one must further diligently cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Should there be a deficiency in its precise observance, one will encounter calamities sent by the Fire Deity and personally suffer the perils of the underworld.
Having disrupted the principles of human relations during life, one shall receive the punishment of the copper pillar after death.

Knowing full well that the retribution for the karma of sexual misconduct has no end to seeking escape, one should understand that this single precept against illicit lust ought to be held fast within the heart. [The precept] against false speech...
The Precept of Speech is assigned to the Central Region. This Central Region presides over Earth; Earth presides over Faith. Faith is defined as sincerity and truthfulness without falsehood.
If one follows [the precepts] with unwavering devotion, then the five deities of this precept will silently protect the body, and the spleen organ will remain healthy and at peace.
Regarding one's life, one’s words will be reliable, one will value promises and honor commitments, and Jupiter (the planet of Earth) will grant its protection.
Upon their death, they are reborn above in Tuṣita Heaven or soar high into the Brahma Heavens; furthermore, they are able to generate merit.

Yet, should they commit even a single transgression, they invoke Saturn and bring about calamity. Through false accusations, slander, and deceitful testimony, they ensnare their own luminous spirits in fraud, and shall receive the punishment of tongue-extraction in hell.
Thus one knows that the karmic retribution for false speech is such that it is easy to sink but difficult to float back up; and yet, false speech—once [committed]...
Regarding the precept: one should maintain it with vigilance. The Precept of Not Drinking is assigned to the North, for the North presides over water, and water presides over wisdom.
Wisdom is defined as not acting contrary to principle; thus, by following [the teachings] without transgression, one serves these five deities of this precept.

The attendant’s physical frame was robust and his kidneys were full. During his life, his provisional and ultimate realization surpassed all others, and his wisdom-illumination was profoundly penetrating, like the brilliant clarity of the water planet (Mercury).
At the time of his death, he was reborn in the Land of Bliss, walking with lofty strides through the Lotus Palace.

Furthermore, one realizes the mastery of severance [from defilements]. Should one nevertheless become immersed in indulgence, it will invoke the influence of the Water Star (Sukra), leading to misfortune;

one’s property will be lost, and by creating turbid karma, one is born as a fool. One attains delusion upon the dark path and ultimately encounters the retribution of irrationality, with suffering states that are endless.
Therefore, know that the precept against the irrationality of alcohol must be firmly maintained. One who is able to maintain it...

Regarding the five precepts, they are clear in their application and unobscured in the mind. Although the four noble truths are not yet fully understood, one nonetheless knows that suffering is impermanent and lacks a self;
that the origin consists of delusions and karma which invite retribution; and that cessation and the path can be realized and cultivated.
Therefore, it is said that all have seen the Noble Truths. Yet, regarding the Five Precepts, those who propagate the Dharma often neglect them and fail to clarify them for those observing the fast.
This is merely because they consider their meaning to be easy to understand. In reality, the profound significance of the Five Precepts is not only unknown to laypeople;
even among those who have left the household life at this time, few are able to grasp their true flavor. Thus, I shall briefly...
I have extracted these ancient meanings and explained them extensively, hoping that those who understand the Way and possess discernment will not weary of these prolix writings.
△ Second, the assembly of the Seven Sages entering the Path:

furthermore, there were immeasurable numbers who cultivated the seven preliminary practices—mindfulness, right effort, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the eight stages of mastery, and the ten... [the list continues].
The sixteen mental applications of the *kṛtsnāyatana* lead to the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Truths.

This first indicates their number. Below the section on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there is praise for their qualities of practice. Since this assembly differs from the previous one, it says, "Furthermore, there are..."
