The seven stages of virtuous practice (*saptakausīdyabhūmi*) refer to the preparatory stages prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the Hīnayāna; they are namely:

the five stages of settling the mind (*pañcavastuprasādhanacitta*), general contemplation (*samantamanasikāra*), specific contemplation (*pratyekamanasikāra*), the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). Regarding "practice" (*caryā*), this refers to the various practices cultivated below, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth;

this praises the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
The five faculties (*pañcendriya*), the five powers (*pañcabala*), and twenty-two categories [of factors], though lacking the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

As for the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), it is excluded because it is cultivated prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as will be explained in detail below under the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*):

first, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as few; second, having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as many; third, having no [perception of] internal forms...
1. Having the perception of form internally, one perceives forms externally that are limited; 2. having no perception of form internally, one perceives forms externally that are manifold;

3. having no perception of form internally, one perceives forms externally that are blue; 4. having no perception of form internally, one perceives forms externally that are yellow; 5. having no perception of form internally, one perceives forms externally that are red;
6. having no perception of form internally, one perceives forms externally that are white. These are called the "Stages of Mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*). If they are excellent...

If it is loathsome, this is called superior knowledge and superior vision. It is like performing the meditation on the great impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to thoroughly treat greed and other afflictions regarding all objects.
As for the ten universal bases (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), they are blue, yellow, red, white, earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness.
They are called "ten" because these ten pervade all places. For example, when one performs the meditation on the blue base, it pervades everything.
Regarding the "spheres" (*āyatana*), the aforementioned "spheres of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*) refers to the ability to subdue objective domains;

these are called "spheres of totality" (*kṛtsnāyatana*), which refers to being extensive, manifold, and all-pervasive. As for the "sixteen mental states," there are four aspects under the Truth of Suffering:
first, impermanence; second, suffering; third, emptiness; and fourth, non-self. Under the Truth of Origination, there are four aspects: first, origination; second... [text ends]... second.

The causes, the three conditions, and the four arisings. Under the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there are four aspects: first, exhaustion; second, cessation; third, excellence; and fourth, detachment.
Under the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), there are four aspects: first, the path; second, correctness; third, the track; and fourth, the vehicle. These constitute the sixteen mental aspects.
Regarding "the realization of the truths through approach" (*satyābhisamaya-prasthāna*), it refers to these sixteen mental aspects which are directed toward the Four Truths.

Clear realization (*abhisamaya*). Just as one contemplates the truth of suffering: first, by means of the aspect of impermanence, one contemplates the causes and conditions of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as arising and ceasing in every new moment;
second, by means of the aspect of suffering, one contemplates the five aggregates as being oppressed by impermanence;

third, by means of the aspect of emptiness, one contemplates the five aggregates as empty because they lack any characteristics such as identity or difference; fourth, by means of the aspect of non-self, one contemplates within the five aggregates...

The characteristics of a self, a person, and so forth are all unfindable. Since the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Truth of Suffering proceeds by means of these four aspects, the same applies to the three remaining truths, such as Origination and so on;
thus it is called "proceeding toward the clear realization of the truths.

However, this "clear" realization belongs to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) and is still categorized as a semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), rather than the true clear realization of the Mahāyāna stages (*bhūmi*). Why is this? Because through that [Small Vehicle] observation, one merely proceeds toward...

Because they pertain to the true principle of the Four Noble Truths, this explains the meaning of the seven types of noble persons according to the Hīnayāna teachings. If explained according to the Mahāyāna, they are: first, the person who has newly resolved their mind;
second, the person who practices with signs (*sanimitta*); third, the person who practices without signs (*animitta*); fourth, the person who practices through skillful means (*upāya*);

fifth, the person of the nature of the seeds of cultivation (*śikṣamāṇagotra*); sixth, the person of the nature of faith (*śraddhāgotra*); and seventh, the person of the nature of the path (*mārgagotra*). All of these abide on the stages (*bhūmi*).
Previously, one who has disciplined the mind and accords with the Path is called a "Sevenfold Noble One" (saptakula-putra). Question:

Regarding the sixteen mental applications (*ṣoḍaśa-citta-kṣaṇa*), how do they correspond to the sixteen stages such as the "Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Dharma of Suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*)? Answer: The "Patience regarding the Knowledge of the Dharma of Suffering" and so forth constitute the final moment of the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

This Patience of Suffering is true illumination; it gives rise to eight patiences and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) beneath the eight truths. What is now referred to as "cultivating the seven noble practices" refers to the stage immediately preceding this.

When one practices the contemplation of the Truths based on causal practice, there are merely sixteen mental states; how could these immediately reach the eight patiences and eight knowledges of the Path of Seeing of the first fruit?
Based on this, it is known that these are not [the true] knowledges and patiences. △ Second, the assembly of kings.
Furthermore, there were sixteen great kings, such as King Prasenajit, each accompanied by several tens of millions of followers.
Here, the number of nations is first cited to identify the kings; the phrase "each with [their followers]" below describes the multitude who came together with them. These are the kings.
The "lord" refers to the sovereign; the "retinue" refers to his attendants. The sixteen countries refer to the first, Vaiśālī, through to the sixteenth, Campā.
One who presides over the throne of supreme authority (*jiu-wu*), governing the world with dignified composure and non-action, is called a king.
That all these have now come to this Dharma assembly shows that what is called ultimate nobility does not reside in national rank or title; rather, it is because...
This was because he desired to honor the Way, protect the Dharma, and safeguard the nation.

Observing King Prasenajit’s subsequent thoughts on the grand strategy for protecting the state, and how the World-Honored One extensively elucidated the profound intent of protecting the Dharma, we know the sincerity with which he sought to protect both the Dharma and the nation.
It was fervent and unceasing. △ Second, the celestial hosts. Part three. First, the celestial hosts of the desire realm.
Furthermore, there were the six kings of the desire heavens, such as Śakra-devānām-indra, together with their retinues of immeasurable devaputras.

"Deva" (Heaven) is so named because it possesses the three meanings of divine efficacy (*śakti*), radiant purity, and sovereignty. This refers to rebirth induced by the superior grade of the five precepts and ten wholesome paths of action.
Although agitation has been eliminated, the taints of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) have not yet been severed; therefore, it is collectively termed the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*).
"Desire" here refers to food, drink, sleep, and sexual desire. Because the intensity of these objects of desire varies, the realm is divided into six heavens.
There is a distinction. As for Śakra-devānām-indra, he is the Lord of the Devas, Śakra. This deity dwells at the summit of the human realm;
neither the sun nor the moon can illuminate his domain, as he rules over the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

He presides over the generation and growth of the myriad transformations of the human world and governs the changes of the Yin and Yang and the Five Elements; there is nothing that does not proceed from him. The character "equal" (等) means "equal to."
Above the Yāma Heaven are the Four Heavens of the Retinue; below them are the eight heavens in each of the four directions of this very heaven, namely:
first, the Heaven of the Peak-Dwellers, up to the thirty-third, the Pure Heaven. Thus, these forty-eight heavens—
These are the ministers and assistants of Śakra Devendra; among them, there are various aides and counselors beyond all counting, hence they are said to be "immeasurable.
△ Second, the assembly of gods in the Form Realm (rūpadhātu).
The four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) include the various Great Brahmā Kings, who are accompanied by their retinues and immeasurable sons of gods (*devaputra*).
Because they have abandoned the defilement of desire yet have not yet exhausted the burden of physical form, it is called the "form realm.

Having already abandoned mental agitation, it is also called "dhyāna," which refers to the state where concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are in equilibrium. These deities experience [rebirth] through the ten wholesome paths of action combined with the cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Birth, however, consists specifically of the six types of conditioned activities (*ṣaḍ-abhisaṃskāra*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). This is the mundane path by which ordinary beings suppress their afflictions.

Within this realm there are eighteen heavens: namely, the three heavens of the first dhyāna, the three heavens of the second dhyāna, the three heavens of the third dhyāna, and the nine heavens of the fourth dhyāna.
They are called "Brahma-heavens" because those born therein reside in the Brahma-world and are free from the defilement of desire.

He is able to lead the assembly of Brahmās and serves as the Great Brahma King. He transformed his appearance to join the gathering and, having attained realization through the sound of the Dharma, sought the path of transcendent cultivation.
As for the omission of the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is merely a matter of brevity; their inclusion is necessarily implied.
△ Third, the various classes of *asura* beings.
The various realms of existence manifest through transformation, including immeasurable sentient beings such as asuras and their diverse retinues.
These "various realms" refer collectively to the five destinies; whether they be ghosts or animals, their past causes may have been praiseworthy, yet now they all appear as transformations.

To participate in this supreme assembly and receive its abundant Dharma benefits is itself a case of one whose discipline is lax while their spiritual vehicle is urgent. Otherwise, one would lack the conditions for liberation and remain self-obstructed;
how much more so, then, would it be to hear the Dharma and gain benefit within this assembly? *Asura* is a term from the Sanskrit language; here it is translated as "Non-God.
Their power of merit is equal to that of the gods, yet they lack divine conduct. Because they possess a preponderance of anger, they are subject to a lightening of their karma.
It is significant that there are four distinct types [of asuras], as clarified in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Thus, we know that the single realm of the asuras may, for the time being, be subsumed within the human or celestial realms by taking only their portion of virtuous retribution. However, if one discusses their experience of suffering, they truly exist below the human realm, equaling the other eight classes of beings.
Question: Regarding the heavenly kings of the three realms and the various destinies of the eight classes of beings, what of their good and evil?
Question: There are differences among beings, and the distinctions between the noble and the base are vast; why then do they all come to participate in this assembly? Answer:

The wondrous wisdom of Prajñā makes no distinction between the holy and the ordinary, nor does it differentiate between good and evil. Sentient and insentient beings are of one essence; nature and non-nature are perfectly realized as one.
Now, as the Tathāgata is about to manifest the principle of this oneness and perfect realization, devas, humans, and those of all other realms are all [invited].

They come here. Even if the devas are in the midst of joy, the asuras are in the midst of anger, the spirits and ghosts are in sorrow, and the birds and beasts are in flight and panic—since they all possess this single body that perfectly accomplishes spiritual awareness, who would not come?

In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is thoroughly investigated that the seven realms of existence are all states of delusion and the marks of conditioned phenomena; within the wondrous, perfect, bright, and non-active fundamental mind, they are all...

Just as flowers in the sky have never had any basis for attachment, one knows that if the true nature of reality (dharmatā) and the original mind are not realized, one will ultimately remain stuck in saṃsāra.
Only if one can hear the Dharma and attain wondrous awakening can one forever sever birth and death. Later, King Bimbisāra praised this, saying:
"Both devas and humans cultivate the practice of renunciation; they are able to train in all the bodhisattva paths. The "Chapter on Bodhisattva Practices" states: [The Buddha] said...

At this time of the Dharma, among the immeasurable assembly of humans and devas, there were those who attained the Patience of Subjugation (*kṣānti*), the Patience of Emptiness and Non-arising, and the stages from the first ground (*bhūmi*) and second ground up to the tenth ground.
Immeasurable Bodhisattvas attained the stage of being an attendant for one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), and so forth.
Based on this, it is known that those who gathered in the Dharma assembly did not do so in vain. 2. The Assembly of Those Who Circulate through Transformations.
Furthermore, there was a manifestation of the pure lands of the ten directions, wherein a hundred billion lion thrones appeared.

The Buddha sat upon them and extensively proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma. Before each throne, a single flower appeared; these hundred billion flowers were adorned with various precious jewels.
Upon each of these flowers, there were again immeasurable transformation Buddhas, immeasurable Bodhisattvas, and the fourfold assembly and eight classes of beings,
all of whom were immeasurable. Among them, each Buddha proclaimed the Prajñāpāramitā,
which circulated and spread throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The assembly listed above consists of those who assist and support [the teaching] in this world. This, however, is the assembly of manifestations that circulate [the teaching] in other worlds.
As for what is called the "circulating assembly," it is because the directions are not limited to a single corner, for there are pure lands in the ten directions;

and because the Buddhas are not limited to a single Buddha, for there are immeasurable transformation Buddhas. Thus, one knows that as a single lamp illuminates a thousand, the circulation [of the Dharma] is inexhaustible. This...
The text has three parts. First, "Furthermore" and below describe the manifestation of lotus seats.
This means that the great assembly in this land sees the manifestation of lotus seats in a pure land. Alternatively, they see those beings not rising from their seats;

although they remain in their own lands throughout the ten directions, they do not hinder the clouds of beings coming to this land to accomplish transformative deeds. All of these are manifestations according to conditions, as it is said:

From the inconceivable source, inconceivable manifestations arise. That which is non-existent yet suddenly appears is called "transformation-manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*), such as the three transformations of the Pure Land described in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The pure lands of the ten directions are the land of real recompense and adornment; they are not the true, quiescent land of light (*prabhāsvara*).
This is because the essential nature of the land of quiescent light is identical to empty space, and it is realized only by those who have attained the ultimate realization.

Because it is not visible [to ordinary perception]. As for the manifestation of ten billion seats, these are the marks of the *adhiṣṭhāna* (recompense-environment) of the Vairocana of the *Avataṃsaka*.
The Buddha sitting upon them is the *mūla-āśraya* (recompense-body). Because he preaches the inconceivable Dharma, it is called the "Essence of the Dharma" (*dharmoddeśa*).
However, since the environment and the body are identical in essence (*yiru*), the Buddha sits upon this seat. Question: Why does this seat manifest in such great numbers?
"Is this indeed inconceivable? He replied: "Vimalakīrti’s room encompasses the celestial phenomena of the universe, and he grasps the great trichiliocosm in his hand;
how could this not be inconceivable? Since it is called 'inconceivable,' you must be careful not to conceive of it with a limited mind.
This is still speaking of the small. Although the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says that 'one is immeasurable and the immeasurable is one,' and that within the small..."
Great! Within the great, the small appears. This extends to the *Avataṃsaka*’s teaching that a single mote of dust contains the entire Dharma-realm, as it is said:

"The tip of a hair can contain all those lands, yet those lands cannot pervade the pores [of that hair]. This is the inconceivable greatness; one must contemplate it with earnest attention and realize it deeply.
Furthermore, that each seat appears upon a lotus flower symbolizes the locus of the emptiness of all phenomena (*dharmas*), wherein each is perfectly accomplished in its wondrous nature.
For this reason, the flowers are adorned with various jewels, symbolizing the accomplishment of the wondrous cause; for each and every adornment represents immeasurable wholesome dharmas.

This further indicates that while *prajñā* is empty, it is in reality not empty. Second, regarding the passage "Among all [the flowers]... and below: the flowers manifest the principal and the retinue.

The transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) are the principals, and the transformation Bodhisattvas are their retinue. The transformation of the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings constitutes the support and protection.
The Dharma assembly represents the wondrous cause. That which relies upon wondrous wisdom for cultivation represents the wondrous cause of the transformation-buddhas and bodhisattvas;

for each and every one arises as a cause and effect that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*). The manifestation of immeasurable fourfold assemblies and the eight classes of beings represents the wondrous cause of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*);
it signifies that according to conditions, all things—whether good or evil, defiled or pure—are brought to completion.

Because all phenomena are thus. Since both the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages are transformations, one knows that everything is ultimately empty, being nothing other than the wondrous nature of sole True Suchness (tathatā).
Therefore, know that the discussions of universal emptiness in the subsequent passages all originate from this;
it serves as the foundational basis for the place where transformations further produce transformations. Third, the "Middle-Lower" section explains the Dharma pervasively.
What is called "the single moon universally appearing in all waters" means that "all waters and moons are subsumed within the single moon.

That each Buddha abides in the true, the responsive, and the transformative, yet none departs from this Way, indicates that there is no other path. That each speaks of this very thing represents that there is no alternative way.
That it flows and pervades everywhere represents that its essential magnitude encompasses the entire dharma-realm. Question: Regarding the manifestation of the Pure Land:
Reaching to the furthest reaches of the ten directions, it may be said that this is the ultimate limit. Yet, simultaneously, there appear billions of seats and billions of flowers are produced;
within each flower, transformation Buddhas, transformation Bodhisattvas, and various other classes of beings appear, all of them infinite in number.

These Buddhas, one after another, preach the Prajñāpāramitā and cause it to circulate throughout the ten directions—this is truly difficult to conceive. Furthermore, one does not know what the underlying reason for this might be. Answer: This...
There are two meanings. First, such manifestations are displayed as a fundamental basis for the subsequent teachings of the Buddha. As the later text states:

"All are empty—the internal is empty, the external is empty, and even emptiness itself is empty because it is empty. It further states: "All conditioned phenomena exist because they are an accumulation of dharmas...
[they] exist up to the tenth stage, and they exist because of the fruit of Buddhahood. All are..."
There is. Furthermore, it is said: "If a bodhisattva dwells in the mark of dharmas, he is not a bodhisattva.
If, regarding all dharmas, one attains immovability—neither arising nor ceasing, neither having marks nor being without marks—one should not give rise to views. Why is this?"
All things are thusness (*tathatā*). The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are also thusness. Based on this single passage, one may follow it wherever one is. For all things are empty;
though one seeks existence, it cannot be found. All things exist; though one seeks emptiness, it cannot be found. All things are thusness;
though one seeks the Middle Way, it cannot be found. To know this is to know the manifested lotus throne, as well as cause and effect, the holy and the ordinary.
Regarding these immeasurable transformations: can they be said to exist? Can they be said to be non-existent? Can they be said to be one or many?

Can they be said to be neither one nor many? Furthermore, it is said that these words and phrases of the Prajñāpāramitā were spoken in common by a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas. Moreover, it is said that these fourteen patiences and ten...
This is the practice cultivated by all Bodhisattvas of the past and present, and that which has been revealed by all Buddhas;
it shall be the same for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the future. Were a Buddha or a Bodhisattva to attain omniscience without proceeding through this gateway, such a thing is impossible.
For the names of the fruits and so forth throughout the ten directions are likewise identical in their dependence upon this.
For this reason, each Buddha individually expounds the Prajñā, which flows throughout the ten directions.
Thus, one should know that these inconceivable manifestations serve as the prologue for the main body of the subsequent text. Second, the manifestations are immeasurable.
Furthermore, it is to manifest the realm of the Perfect and Sudden. This is because the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm is precisely the unique *prajñā* of this sutra;
every single dharma-gate in that sutra consists of the hosts and attendants of the ten directions at the assembly, each proclaiming the non-dual truth.
Now, in this sutra, immeasurable transformation Buddhas each flow forth [the teaching] so as to pervade the ten directions universally. Since the *Avataṃsaka*...
The perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) is itself *prajñā*. Thus, the fact that *prajñā* is fundamentally empty is itself the *Avataṃsaka*.

Therefore, one should know that within each and every transformation flower, transformation Buddha, and transformation cause, there is no hindrance to the production of transformation beings, all of which are likewise immeasurable.

This is precisely the mutual penetration of phenomena and the unimpeded inclusion of the *Avataṃsaka*, manifesting the present *prajñā* as it perfectly accords with the capacities of sentient beings. △ Third, the General [Conclusion].
The assembly gathered.
All those who had come from various directions, such as these, each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.
This concludes the summary of the multitude of Dharma-followers who had come from this world and other realms, supported by his transformations, as they paid their respects.

They prostrated themselves; hence it is called "paying homage at the Buddha’s feet. They proceeded with solemnity and order; hence they withdrew and sat to one side. △ Second, the introductory sequence of the occasion.
This has two parts: first, the manifestation of auspicious omens; second, the determination of the time and its radiance. First, the determination of the time and its radiance.
At that time, on the eighth day of the first month, the World-Honored One entered the sublime samādhi of great tranquility.
From all the pores of his body, he emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that moment, immeasurable devas of the desire realm rained down various exquisite flowers, and the devas of the form realm likewise rained down celestial blossoms of manifold colors, intermingled in a most lovely manner.

At that time, from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), various fragrant flowers rained down; their fragrance was like Mount Sumeru and the flowers were like chariot wheels, descending like clouds and completely covering the great assembly.
Throughout the entire Buddha-world, the earth shook in six ways.

This "Preface of Origination" refers to how, by means of these auspicious lights and omens, the subsequent text initiates the formal exposition of the main doctrine—namely, the thorough elucidation of the profound subtleties of the fundamental intent.
It is also called the "Preface Prior to the Sūtra" or the "Separate Preface," which should be treated according to the separate chapter [on that topic].
Regarding the "first year, eighth day," this refers to the time when this *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* was preached.

According to ancient commentaries citing Paramārtha’s record, the Tathāgata remained in the world for forty-five years and preached three wheels of Dharma, namely: the wheel of turning (*pravartana*), the wheel of illumination (*avabhāsana*), and the wheel of maintenance (*dhāraṇa*).

However, these three wheels have both manifest and esoteric aspects. Esoterically, from the night of attaining the Way until the night of *parinirvāṇa*, he turned the wheel of the Dharma in all three ways.
Manifestly, during the first seven years after his enlightenment, he turned only the turning wheel of the Dharma;

during the thirty-one years following those seven, he turned the illuminating wheel of the Dharma; and during the seven years following the thirty-eighth year, he turned the sustaining wheel of the Dharma.
Regarding the Dharma Wheel: from the time the wheel was first turned until now, thirty years have passed. Up until the twenty-ninth year, other *prajñā* teachings had already been expounded;
it is only now, on the eighth day of the first month of the thirtieth year, that the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* is being taught. Hence, it says "the eighth day of the first month.
This means that this sūtra was preached thirty-seven years after the Buddha attained enlightenment, which would be his seventh year [after his passing].
It is twelve years. Based on this, there should be no further doubt regarding the contents of this sutra;
however, it appears to differ slightly from the common teaching of the five periods throughout one lifetime. Thus, the *Great Commentary on the Avataṃsaka* states:

"The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, relying on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, taught the doctrine of the three wheels of turning, illuminating, and maintaining, which is also largely identical to this [teaching], though the timing..."
The phrasing differs slightly. It means that the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) refers to the teaching of the Four Noble Truths seven years after [the enlightenment];

the teaching of the *Prajñāpāramitā* seven years later constitutes both the turning and the illuminating wheels, because it illuminates existence through emptiness; thirty years later, it fully constitutes the turning, the illuminating, and the sustaining wheels.

Because it illuminates both emptiness and existence simultaneously, it maintains the preceding two [aspects]. However, the refutation of this is explained extensively in the Great Commentary (*Dàshù*).

"Entering the Great" below clarifies the entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*). There are four meanings to entering concentration: first, because unimpeded *prajñā* arises entirely from concentration;

second, because one observes the capacities of sentient beings before administering the medicine of the Dharma; third, because speech is uttered after concentration, such that every word is necessarily true.
This is because it serves as a model for sentient beings; since it must necessarily be thus, the Buddha never has a time when he is not in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Here, the term "entering" is used in this sense. To explain: seeking stillness within movement is called "small," while being still within movement itself is termed "great.

This is the dhyāna of the primary truth (*paramārtha*), wherein quiescence and illumination are simultaneous, transcending all marks while being identical to all phenomena—an unfathomable source that is neither moving nor subject to decay.
"Samādhi" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Right Concentration" (zhèngdìng). It is also called "Right Reception" (zhèngshòu), meaning the experiential enjoyment of right concentration.
It is not comparable to the minor meditative states of ordinary people, and is therefore termed "wondrous.

Since one has already entered this concentration, what is explained in the following sections does not depart from this state but is contained within it. Thus, this serves as the foundation for the subsequent chapters, such as the "Contemplation of the Tathāgata."
[The phrase] "Furthermore, from all parts of the body" clarifies the emission of light. That light is emitted from the pores of the body signifies that this light of wisdom pervades the entire body;

there is no part of it that is not so. That it "universally illuminates the sands of worlds" signifies that the light of wisdom shines perfectly everywhere, for there is no time or place where it is not thus.
Within this, there are two levels of subject and object: first, the pores of the body, which are the locus from which the light is emitted...

"Abiding place. "Two *sāhasra* worlds" refers to the extent of the pervasion of light. One should reflect accordingly that light encompasses both the subject (the capacity to illuminate) and the object (that which is illuminated).

The translation from the Qin period states that "light illuminates the three realms," which speaks in terms of the vertical dimension. The present statement that it reaches "*sāhasra* worlds" clarifies its pervasiveness in terms of the horizontal dimension.
Question: Why does the light pervade the entire body? If it must necessarily do so, why is it that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not [experience it] as well?
"Does he emit light? He replied, "The holy and the ordinary share the same essence; it is only that ordinary beings are deluded and cannot perceive it. As the Great Master Linji said:
"Within each of you there is a true person of no station, who stands at the gateway of your six sense-faculties, emitting light and shaking the earth.
This is intended to bring about immediate clarity regarding the fundamental principle. A monk asked for the reason behind this, and the Master immediately seized him, saying, "Speak! Speak!"
As soon as the monk hesitated, [Linji] pushed him away and said: "The true person of no rank—what is he? A dried-up shit-stick!

This, again, is to avoid the issue face-to-face. For when one realizes it, light shines forth brilliantly; when one does not realize it, the mundane world remains shrouded in darkness. What else could it be?
At that time, rain fell from the desire realm, and many devas offered flowers as an act of worship. These were flowers.
This expresses the causal practice. It reveals the wondrous cause of cultivation based upon the merit of the fruition.
It is called "wondrous" because it takes non-separation from *prajñā* as its cause. "Flowers" refers to the *mahāmāndārava*, the *campaka*, and so forth; hence the term "multitude."
Below the realm of form (rūpadhātu), it rains flowers from within that very realm of form. However, the realm of form transcends the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).

Because of the ultimate sincerity in planting blessings and cultivating causes, it likewise rains [flowers]. Furthermore, they know only the existence of the Buddha; therefore, they offer these [flowers] to Him.

How could they rely on the nature of the Brahma-world and fail to cultivate sublime causes? Since all manner of jewels adorn and embellish them, it is said they are "intermingled with various colors."

This is a mistake. Because it delights the hearts of the multitude, it is said to be "extremely lovely and pleasant. At that time, below the Formless Realm, flowers rained down from the Formless World;
such offerings of the Formless Realm were indeed the most supreme. The trees of fragrance filled the void, heaped up like Mount Sumeru.
The flowers were profuse and large as chariot wheels; this symbolizes that the Buddha’s virtues are sublime and lofty.
Because the true cause gathers like spokes, they descend like clouds, symbolizing the cultivation of wondrous causes and wondrous virtues. They are not produced through deliberate effort.
They cover the entire assembly, symbolizing that these are shared by all sentient beings; it reveals that this wondrous cause should be cultivated with equanimity. Even those without form...

Regarding the "rain of flowers": because it possesses the form-matter that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), these are all the ultimate manifestations of the Buddha’s spiritual virtue.

How could the various devas of the triple world possibly prevent the rain of flowers from falling? From the phrase "Throughout the Buddhas' realms" onwards, there is the auspicious sign of the earth shaking.

Regarding the "sixfold shaking," this refers to: moving, rising, surging, trembling, roaring, and crashing. Thus, the three—moving, rising, and surging—are designated by their physical forms as "movement," while the three—trembling, roaring, and crashing—are designated by their sounds.

Regarding the "movement" [of the earth], there are explanations of it surging in the east and subsiding in the west, or of movement that is partial or universal; these also do not depart from this principle.

As for the mention of the "six types of quaking," this signifies that by relying upon the six consciousnesses, one overturns and destroys ignorance (*avidyā*), thereby directly manifesting wondrous wisdom.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that the mountains, rivers, and great earth are all the result of the binding of ignorance; fundamentally, they are only the One True Reality. Therefore, regarding the quaking of the earth, it is said to be "universal" throughout the Buddhas' lands.
Regarding the world: Question. There are many causes and conditions for the shaking of the earth; why then do you speak directly only in terms of manifesting the destruction of ignorance?
Answer. According to the Āgamas, there are eight causes for the shaking of the earth: first, when the great waters stir; second, when a venerable deity tests its power;
third, when the Tathāgata enters the womb; fourth, when he emerges from the womb; fifth, when he attains enlightenment; sixth, when he turns the wheel of the Dharma... [and so forth].
The time of turning the wheel; the time of teaching the seven breaths; and the time of nirvana. The *Ekottarika Āgama* also lists eight conditions, which are largely identical to these eight.
However, although there are eight conditions for the shaking of the earth, this is merely a general explanation.

If one were to specify them, it is the time of turning the wheel of Dharma among these eight conditions that causes the earth to shake. Since the turning of the wheel of Dharma involves such shaking, then...
To proceed directly to breaking the fetters and delusions of ignorance is most appropriate; for the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is undertaken solely because ignorance persists.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the shaking of the earth treats three kinds of afflictions:

first, to treat those sentient beings born in the heavens who are attached to celestial blessings, the earth shakes their palaces to cause them to give rise to weary detachment and to arouse the mind that seeks the Dharma; second, to treat...
Sentient beings who commit evil do not recognize impermanence; they indulge their minds and let their wills run wild, thereby causing the earth to shake.

To cause them to abandon evil and follow good, one employs three methods to subdue sentient beings of pride. Alternatively, through the power of mantras, one may cause a slight earthquake, which might give rise to a mind of arrogance.
Seeing this, he was greatly moved and realized that his own power was inferior. Is this not also a means of subduing the three kinds of afflictions?

Presenting the canopy: this refers to one who has given rise to the inconceivable realm. "Wu-gou" (stainless) means purity; "cheng" (to name) refers to the appellation.
This is none other than the ancient Buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa manifesting his traces, entering the dust to assist in propagating the Dharma transformation.

This is he who borrowed the seat from King Dīpa, took rice from fragrant soil, encompassed the celestial phenomena within his chamber, and grasped the great trichiliocosm with his hand—clarifying the non-duality of the ultimate truth.
Within the pure realm, the afflictions are manifested within the kingdom of Vaiśālī; this is indeed the inconceivable transcendence [of the Buddha].
Śāriputra was foremost in reputation and virtue, and first in wisdom. Observing the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra, he was the first to receive his prediction of enlightenment;
how could he have been a mere śrāvaka? Subhūti was foremost in understanding emptiness; when the Prajñāpāramitā discusses emptiness, he is the most [profound].
The foremost [disciple], who is still one of those who have entered the ocean of the jewel-bright emptiness, manifests as a śrāvaka; he is also one who acts through skillful means.
Maitreya is one whose benevolence flourishes in the present world and whose compassion reaches into future kalpas, and is thus the one who shall succeed the Buddha.
Siṃhanāda is one who proclaims fearlessness and is likewise a companion of the Dharma-body; therefore, King Bimbisāra questioned each of them individually.
This can be called "one who knows the music playing together with one who knows the music. Regarding the phrase "at that time the assembly [remained silent] below":

this clarifies that the assembly had no response. This has two meanings. First, regarding the manifestation of traces: it means that the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā* is such that the myriad dharmas are tranquil and still, realized only by the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment;
thus, he reveals it from his entire being. This demonstrates that only a Buddha can know it, and therefore the assembly could not fathom it.

Furthermore, regarding the second point, the perspective of the esoteric intent (*samdhāya-bhāṣita*): it means that the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) is fundamentally empty and all things are suchness (*tathatā*).
Since the World-Honored One has manifested these auspicious omens to clarify this truth, the great assembly then realized its wondrous subtlety through silent cognition;

thus, they were unable to provide an answer. This is what is meant by "speaking in silence" and "silence in speaking. When the Great Gate of Giving is opened, there is no obstruction. How could it truly be that [the assembly] was incapable?
Answer: Second, awakening through the performance of music.
King Prasenajit and others, sustained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, performed extensive musical performances.
The various devas of the desire and form realms each played immeasurable celestial music, the sound of which pervaded the trichiliocosm.
Master Zhaoming said: "The whirlwind topples the mountains, yet they remain eternally still; the rivers rush together in their flow, yet they do not move.
This means that the spiritual culmination of the Perfected Person is boundless; though amidst movement, they are eternally still.

Now, when the World-Honored One enters meditative concentration and manifests auspicious signs, such that the various devas of the desire realm produce music whose sound reaches throughout the great trichiliocosm, this is truly because they rely upon the Buddha's supernormal power.
One seeks for the Buddha to emerge from samādhi so that he may promptly send down seasonal rain to moisten and save all that is withered and parched.
Otherwise, even when a woman before the Buddha enters samādhi, no one can awaken her to emerge; this must await Wangming.
How much more so when the Buddha enters the dhyāna-concentration of Great Quiescence—a clear wave within the ocean of profound wisdom, a full moon of luminous nature within emptiness? Thus we know:

The Buddha’s manifestation of auspicious omens and the assembly’s performance of music are likewise instances of the mutual resonance between the path and its response. △ Second, the Universal Enlightenment through Radiance.
This has two parts. First, the manifestation of transformation through light.
At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted immeasurable, incalculable rays of light. These radiance-rays were of various colors, and within each ray appeared a precious lotus flower.
Each flower had a thousand petals, all of which were golden in color, and upon each was a manifested Buddha proclaiming the essentials of the Dharma.
Previously, light was emitted from the hairs of his body to signify that the light of wisdom manifests throughout his entire being;
now, that he emits light reaching as far as incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) numbers signifies that the light of wisdom transcends all measure.

For when wondrous wisdom forgets the realm of conceptualization, how could numerical calculation possibly reach it? That its radiance is of various colors signifies that the illumination of wisdom proceeds according to the truths and conditions.

They are not the same. This refers to contemplating emptiness, the provisional, and the middle within all phenomena. The light of wisdom is immeasurable; such wondrous practice is difficult to fathom.
Therefore, within each ray of light, precious lotus flowers appear. This signifies that from wondrous wisdom, various causal practices arise.
Although causal practices are myriad and diverse, the awakened mind is non-dual; hence it is called the "Thousand-Petaled Golden [Lotus]."
Form (*rūpa*). This, moreover, is gathered back into a single source by means of the wondrous cause.

This very wondrous wisdom and wondrous cause constitute the essence of attaining Buddhahood and the wisdom for expounding the Dharma; therefore, it is said that above there is a transformation Buddha who proclaims the essentials of the Dharma.
This is precisely the Buddha emitting a single ray of light, wherein wondrous wisdom is fully manifested. Cause, effect, practice, and realization are all inseparable from this single illumination.
However, Prajñāpāramitā transcends the four propositions and uniquely reveals the true emptiness; therefore, it clarifies only that there is a manifested Buddha who preaches the Dharma.
This demonstrates that the responsive manifestation is not the true Buddha, nor is it the one who preaches the Dharma; thus, it is called the "transformation body" (nirmāṇakāya).

Yet, it is only the true body of the ultimate reality (dharmatā) that reveals the fundamental quiescence, which is the true Buddha. △ Second, the light shines upon those with karmic affinity. Part two: First, [the introduction].
This collectively reveals the universal benefit.
This light of the Buddha appears universally throughout the buddha-fields of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, manifesting for all who have a karmic affinity with it.
The bright sun rises in the heavens; it does not conceal its radiance for those who lack sight. Yet, those who are not blind naturally behold the Buddha’s light pervading all realms.
It does not conceal its radiance for the sake of sentient beings; rather, it manifests for those with whom there is a karmic affinity.
Thus we know that those people of today who do not see the Buddha’s light, and those who do not hear the True Dharma, possess no affinity and are self-obstructed.

How great indeed is the significance of having such an affinity! △ Second, specifically clarifying the assembly that has come. This has two parts. First, indicating their directions and listing their names.
In those Buddha-lands of other directions: in the east, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantaprabha;
in the southeast, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Padmapāṇi; in the south, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vigatāśoka; in the southwest, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Prabhāsa;
in the west, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Caritramati; and in the northwest, the Bodhisattva Ratnajaya.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samaha; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vijayagrāha of the north;
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Virajaska of the northeast; the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Priyagrāha of the zenith;
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Padmavijaya of the nadir—each accompanied by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—all came to this place.
The Buddha’s light shines once, and the Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all arrive together;
this symbolizes that the light of wisdom is perfectly penetrating and not confined to a single corner. Its intelligence is bright and vast, not possessed by a single person alone.

Yet, as the names and meanings of the Bodhisattvas differ according to their respective directions, they too are illuminated by our Buddha’s radiance; this serves to manifest the symbolic intent of the Dharma being established according to those various regions.
How could this be in vain? "Universal Radiance" (Puguang) refers to the pervasive clarity of the body and wisdom, illuminating the entire dharma-realm as one.
Its manifestation in the East symbolizes that within movement there is immovable, wondrous wisdom. Since the East corresponds to the trigram Zhen, it is the image of the stirring of thunder;
yet, being called "Universal Radiance," it is entirely free from delusion and darkness, and is neither coming nor going. Therefore, its essence is eternally quiescent.
"Stillness" means that within movement there is immobility. "Lotus-Handed One" refers to grasping the Dharma-treasure; it signifies the mutual penetration of cause and effect.

His traces manifest toward the southeast, which also symbolizes wondrous wisdom, for he has successfully realized the fruition of the cause. Now, the southeast corresponds to the trigram Xun, which represents the image of wind;
yet he is called "Lotus. This indicates that the flower itself is the fruit. Furthermore, he is called "Handed. *Note: The term "Lotus-Handed One" (Padmapāṇi) is a common epithet for Avalokiteśvara.*
The hand is able to grasp objects; this symbolizes wisdom that causes cause and effect to interpenetrate, representing the image of the power of wind causing blossoms to open and fruit to form.
"Free from sorrow" means that spiritual clarity is devoid of all traces, such that there is no entanglement of grief whatsoever. He manifested his traces in the South.
Thus, the Li hexagram is empty in its center, which signifies the absence of substantiality; hence it symbolizes "leaving behind sorrow.

As for "radiance," it refers to the brilliance of virtue and wisdom being clearly manifest and unobscured by the dust of defilement. Its manifestation in the southwest corresponds to Kun, representing the source of life;

this illustrates that wisdom takes the principle of life as its task, which is what is meant by "having clarity. Hence it symbolizes Kun. "Practicing wisdom" means that not a single thing is left in ignorance, and [wisdom pervades] the myriad...
He practices true illumination and manifests his traces in the West. The trigram Dui represents marshes and the breaking or crumbling of things;

its imagery is also like that of one who appears foolish and lacking in wisdom. Therefore, it is essential to practice wisdom, so that amidst the breaking and crumbling of birth and death, one may have clear realization within all phenomena.
"Jewel Victorious" (Baosheng) refers to the inexhaustibility of inherent virtue and the overflowing of the treasury of wisdom; he thus manifests his traces in the West.

The North represents *qian* (heaven) and vigor. Its symbolic image is one who walks the Path with self-strengthening and ceaseless effort, manifesting the supreme treasure of spiritual clarity and vigor that can remain lively within a single void; this symbolizes *qian*.
As for "superior reception," it refers to wisdom receiving objects without deficiency; it manifests its traces in the north. *Kan* (water) is...
Deficiency. Its symbol is water, which flows everywhere without fixed direction and is never subject to deficiency;
this represents wondrous wisdom, which does not abide within the symbols of the myriad dharmas. "Free from dust" means that the single mind is clarified and not defiled by worldly passions.
It manifests its traces in the northeast, where *gen* (艮) signifies the way of cessation and completion; its symbol belongs to earth, yet it causes movement.

It is not so; this represents the profound, eternal, and wondrous wisdom that is consistent from beginning to end. "Receiving with joy" means attaining benefit through deep cultivation and entering meditative absorption with mastery;
however, as the fruit is realized from this [practice], it is shown to proceed from above.
"Superior lotus" means the fragrance of the myriad practices and the successful cultivation of the six perfections; however, as the cause precedes the fruit, it is shown to proceed from below.
[The names and directions] above are all based on the inexhaustible, wondrous response of Prajñā. Thus, the Buddha emits light that illuminates lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
those who call upon his name from the ten directions signify that they are all present at the Dharma assembly. These are the assembly who initiated [the teaching].
If it were not so, then establishing names and directions would merely serve to manifest the formal discourse, and the whole would be a futile exertion. My humble view is as follows:
This is what the Mother says; it refers to the various [attendants] below, namely the assembly of kinsmen. △ Second, making offerings and prostrating to the Buddha:
Holding various incenses, scattering various flowers, and performing immeasurable music, they made offerings to the Tathāgata.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew silently to sit, joining their palms in reverence and contemplating the Buddha with single-minded focus.
Incense, flowers, and music are the ritual implements used for making offerings; they serve to express one’s devotion and also to symbolize what has been realized.

This is because the virtues realized by the Bodhisattvas are already fragrant, and thus flowers are held to represent them; and because the sublime causes have already been cultivated, and thus flowers are scattered to represent them.
As for the offering of music, the *Lotus Sūtra* clarifies that the realization of the Buddha-way is not brought about by minor conditions.
...the Tathāgata, who is the very Buddha being offered to. Now, there are many kinds of prostration;
this is the third, the respectful prostration, because one prostrates with the five limbs touching the ground and reverently clasps the feet.

It is also the fourth, the signless prostration, because at the time of the correct prostration, one enters deeply into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), transcending the marks of names and words. Nevertheless, although there is no [subject] capable of...
Universally directing body and mind so that they pervade everywhere like a shadow, one pays homage to that which is beyond homage.
Although one pays homage to all things, one is in fact paying homage to the true Buddha—the Dharma-body within one's own person—and does not seek it outwardly.

Eventually, at the moment of a single prostration to the Buddha, whether internal or external, all is the same *bhūtatathatā-prajñā* (the wisdom of the true mark). This is further the arising of function: internally contemplating the true mark while paying homage to the Buddha.
To collect the mind and concentrate the spirit is called "silence. To stand upright and wait for the Dharma is called "sitting back. Joining the palms is to gather the mind within;

this is the desire to receive and uphold the wondrous principle of the Middle Way. Be reverent in the regulation of bodily posture so that there is no deficiency, and respectful in the commitment of the will with utmost sincerity.
Having long admired the perfect sound, one stretches the neck for the rain of Dharma, like a hungry person thinking of food or a thirsty person waiting for water.
Thus, with the three karmas applied with diligence, he single-mindedly contemplates the Buddha; his compassionate voice pervades all, and his mercy fills the world of men.
This concludes the account of how this supreme Dharma assembly was brought about.

△ Second, the correct exposition of the profound and subtle. Part Two: First, the brief introductory outline of the sections.
From here below, the main body of the scripture consists of six chapters, which are divided into four parts. First: Protecting the Buddha-dharma from within; revealing that principle is empty.
The Profound [Treatise] consists of three sections. First, the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata," which clarifies the practice of self-benefit and answers the first question.
Second, the "Chapter on Bodhisattva Practice," which clarifies the practice of benefiting others and answers the second and third questions.

Third, the "Chapter on the Two Truths," which clarifies the correct principle that serves as the basis for the two types of protection: the protection of the nation and the manifestation of the excellence of the Dharma.
1. Benefit: namely, the fifth chapter, "Protecting the State. 2. Repaying Kindness through Offerings: revealing that the fruit is inconceivable; namely, the sixth chapter, "The Inconceivable.
3. The Manner of Propagating the Sutra: revealing that practice is inexhaustible; namely, the seventh chapter, "Receiving and Upholding."

...Thus it is. △ Second, the explanation of the text according to the topical outline. This has four parts. First, protecting the Buddha-dharma internally. This has two parts: first, briefly opening the two types of protection;
second, the title of the present chapter. First, the brief opening of the two protections. Second, the title of the present chapter.
Chapter Two: Contemplating the Tathāgata.
Following the appearance of the auspicious light-omen of the Tathāgata, this section clarifies the profound intent of Prajñā as the fundamental source for both internal and external protection.
Thus, emerging from samādhi, [the Buddha] anticipated the King’s thoughts; based on the conditions of the King’s resolve to protect the nation, [he spoke] in two parts.

Regarding the sincere request for protection, herein we first clarify the protection of the fruit: its ultimate aim lies in the salvation of sentient beings. One clarifies the truth by not dwelling on signs;
one carries out transformation while contemplating the emptiness of the essence. Wisdom and principle are non-dual; sentient beings and Buddhas are as one.

Next, we clarify the contemplation of the body as being far removed from all signs, such that it ultimately transcends both mind and speech—this is called right contemplation. Therefore, it is termed "Contemplating the Tathāgata."
This chapter, however, concerns *vipaśyanā* (contemplation), which is the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination (*guan-zhao*). The Tathāgata is the *prajñā* of the true nature (*shixiang*).
That the Tathāgata is identified with the true nature is because the Qin translation titles this section the "Chapter on Contemplating Emptiness" (*Guan-kong-pin*).

Thus, we know that when the principle follows the wisdom, it is translated as "Tathāgata," and when the wisdom follows the principle, it is translated as "Contemplating Emptiness. The *Vajracchedikā* states: "The Tathāgata is the suchness (*tathatā*) of all dharmas."

The meaning is this: that which takes suchness as its meaning is the Tathāgata. Thus we know that the wondrous wisdom of signlessness contemplates the true mark of phenomena as, in sum, neither arising nor ceasing, neither departing nor coming;
it transcends existence and non-existence, merging in secret identity with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
It is eternally severed from self and person, equalizing all within wondrous emptiness. This clarifies its truth: the ten thousand objects are one suchness.
Investigating their conventional nature, all conditions exist as illusions. This Bodhisattva is correctly practicing the contemplation of the Middle Way;

how could they be compared to the stagnation and immersion of ordinary people and the Hinayanists, or to the simultaneous discourse on existence, non-existence, heterodoxy, and false attachments to permanence or annihilation?
Contemplative observation is its function, while the true reality (*dharmatā*) is its essence. Without attaining this essence, one cannot give rise to this function. Without...
This is the attainment of function. It does not manifest this essence; rather, by subsuming function back into essence, both object and wisdom are forgotten, and essence and function are non-dual.
If one transcends function from essence, then detachment and presence are simultaneously accomplished, achieving both at once through simultaneous negation and illumination.

This is what is meant by "function takes all essences as its root" and "essence follows after function. Although essence and function are two, they do not depart from the single Prajñā. However, it must not be...
To grasp this as being real—what does that mean? If one attempts to reconcile it through the view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*), one is killed by the demon of the view of existence.

If one adopts the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*), one is killed by the demon of the view of emptiness. At this point, the path of names and words is cut off; the intellect and mind can no longer peer into it. All dualistic extremes are unable to enter it.
If one attempts to reconcile it through the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), the calamity is the same as with the two extremes; for it is neither empty...
There is. Furthermore, it cannot be called "middle. Ultimately, what can it be called? Here, the *śakara* eye cannot peer into it;
the thousand hands of Great Compassion cannot grasp it. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Even if there were a single dharma that surpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa, I would still say it is like an illusion and like a dream. This is it.
...Indeed. △ Second, the correct interpretation of the sutra text, in three parts. First, anticipating the intent of the request:
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi, sat upon the lion throne, and addressed the great assembly, saying:
"I know that the sixteen kings and others have all formed this thought: 'The World-Honored One possesses great compassion and universally brings benefit and happiness to us, the various kings.'"
What is meant by "protecting the nation"?

The Buddha knew that the time had come to teach the two protections of Prajñā; therefore, he arose from samādhi. However, there is no time when the Buddha is not in a state of meditative concentration.
That he is now said to "enter and emerge" is for the sake of demonstrating a model for sentient beings. The lion throne symbolizes the Buddha preaching the Dharma.
Fearlessness is like being a lion among men. "The great assembly" refers to those for whom the teaching is intended.

When a king possesses a kingdom, the mandate of Heaven and the hearts of the people depend upon whether order or chaos, security or peril prevail. If he attains the Way, the mandate of Heaven will be favorable and the hearts of the people will submit.
If he loses the Way, Heaven will turn against the seasons and things will run contrary to principle. Therefore, governance and disorder are the pivotal mechanisms for protecting the state.
It is merely a matter of shifting one's focus within the single mind. For this reason, as soon as the Buddha emerged from samādhi, he directed his attention toward Prajñā;

the King immediately thought of making a request, yet his mind was hesitant regarding the protection of the state. Thus we know that as for the essentials of protecting the state, who else could achieve it were it not through the wondrous benefits of Prajñā?
Furthermore, that the Buddha knew the King’s thoughts and requests is what is meant by the saying: "When one digs a pond..."
Waiting for the moon: once the pond is completed, the moon comes of its own accord. How could this be like the saying, "How can I know the hearts of others, that I might measure them"?
The ancient commentaries state that sixteen kings intended to inquire about the causes and conditions of protecting the kingdom.

Based on the previous passage where the Master of Jetavana was entreated by this king, we now understand that the intent of the invitation extended to all sixteen kingdoms; it is simply that the inquiry could not be made [individually].
[The request] is many. A request must necessarily have a patron. Let us tentatively take this king as the primary one;
however, the Buddha knew that the intent of the request was not limited to a single person, and thus, in principle, it pertains to sixteen kings.

Thus we know that the inquiry regarding mindfulness and the protection of the state serves as the prologue for the subsequent "Chapter on Bodhisattva Practice," the "Chapter on the Two Truths," and the "Chapter on Protecting the State. △ Second, a brief opening of the admonition.
Listen, sons of good family. I shall now first explain for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the protection of the fruit of Buddhahood and the protection of the practices of the ten stages.
You all should listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
According to the subsequent text, he does not abide in the practice of transformation. Since all beings and Buddhas are empty, he does not cling to names or appearances.

Equalizing wisdom and principle within a single nature, he protects the fruit of Buddhahood. Relying upon the five stages of patience (*kṣānti*) in his cultivation, he brings universal benefit to both himself and others.
Abiding for many kalpas, one correctly transforms others; practicing both the provisional and the ultimate simultaneously is the protection of the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Now, as for the two protections for kings—which have not yet been requested—the Buddha himself first explains them.

These two matters, the protection of the Buddha-fruit and the protection of the ten stages, are intended to clarify that these two protections serve as the foundation for external protection. If one were to speak only of protecting the state, then [there would only be] peace and harmony.
At that time, the minds of people were prone to arrogance and complacency; indulging in deluded thoughts, they lost their true nature and became oblivious to the principles of reality.

As days passed, they drifted into chaos and disorder, remaining unaware of their plight. Therefore, the Buddha first opened the two protective methods for transcending the world, enabling them to know that all phenomena are identical to Suchness (tathatā) and that everything is empty everywhere.
By means of this, one may directly exhaust the ocean-like nature of the causes and practices leading to the fruit of Buddhahood. However—
Later, one cultivates the field of merit known as Prajñā; by means of this, there is ample capacity for protecting the state.

Thus, we know that opening the two internal protections also serves as the foundation for the external protection of the land. "You all," and so forth, is an admonition regarding listening to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which says:
"If you listen to the Dharma with a conditioned mind, this Dharma will also be a condition; it is not the attainment of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Now...

"Exhorting those who listen attentively": this means that one must not listen to the Dharma with a distracted mind. Only by ceasing discursive thought and eliminating external conditions—eating and drinking with ease—will one have a share in the Dharma.
"Listening attentively" refers to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); "reflecting well" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);

and the meaning [of the latter] contains the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Thus, the exhortation to listen encompasses these three types of wisdom. △ Third, receiving the exhortation and praising the offerings.
At that time, the great assembly, including King Prasenajit and others, having heard the Buddha’s words, all praised him together, saying, “Excellent, excellent!
They immediately scattered immeasurable exquisite jewel-flowers, which transformed in mid-air into precious canopies that covered the entire assembly,
reaching everywhere without exception.

In the *Lotus Sūtra*, when the sons requested vehicles, the elder, knowing his own wealth was immeasurable, bestowed upon each of them a great white ox-cart, which exceeded what the sons had hoped for.
Now, because you, O Kings, have recollected and requested the causes and conditions for protecting the state, the Buddha has first shown you the two protections that transcend the world;
these likewise exceed what you kings had hoped for, and thus you rejoice and praise them as excellent.

To make offerings to and thus highly praise such a virtuous one is indeed to know with faith that the Tathāgata has proclaimed the *prajñā* and revealed the wondrous wisdom inherently possessed by every person.
Therefore, an ancient commentary cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, stating: "The Buddha taught the *prajñā* so that innumerable sentient beings shall continue the Buddha-wisdom.
It further cites Nāgārjuna’s explanation: "It is able to shatter the various [afflictions] of sentient beings."
The afflictions are capable of bestowing the unsurpassed Great Dharma upon all Buddhas; this is precisely the intended meaning.
The scattering of exquisite jewel-flowers symbolizes that cultivation arises in dependence upon the nature, with the myriad practices blooming in full fragrance.

The transformation of these flowers into a canopy that universally covers the void symbolizes unconditional compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*), which, like the sky’s universal covering, delivers all beings and brings coolness to all categories of existence. Thus, one should know that the Buddha taught this.
Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, it has long been understood that each chapter yields specific benefits. △ Second, the detailed explanation through question and answer, in two parts.
First, the formal inquiry by the appropriate recipient:
At that time, King Prasenajit rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha as follows:
He said, "World-Honored One, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva protect the fruit of Buddhahood? How does he protect the practices of the ten stages?
When Confucius asked about filial piety, Zeng Shen rose from his seat to respond, thereby demonstrating the supreme reverence he held for the dignity of his teacher’s Way.

How much more so when requesting the Great Dharma that transcends the world! He would immediately sacrifice his life for the sake of the Dharma, offering his own body as a bed and seat—this is what he finds sweet.
It is the mind. Thus, the King, though possessing a body as weighty as ten thousand chariots, paid homage to the Sage who looks down from the heights of the Four Great Elements;

and though his ambition was set upon the position of the Nine-Five (the Emperor), he prostrated himself before the Sole Honored One, the Tamer of Men on the Ten Stages. This was because two matters—protecting the state and protecting the Dharma—were most urgent.
Whether it be worldly or world-transcending matters, that both types of conditions are held fast in the heart is precisely what has brought this about; how could it be in vain?

This is also because he has enriched the world with the Way, rather than seeking to subdue the world through national rank or power. He is truly an ancient Buddha manifesting in the world to extensively benefit all living beings.
This further inquiry is performed with the three karmas of body, speech, and mind in full sincerity, as previously described by the Bodhisattva.
In full, it is called *bodhisattva*. This translates as "Awakened Being. There are three interpretations:

first, "awakened" refers to seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above, while "being" refers to transforming sentient beings below; second, "awakened" refers to self-benefit through abandonment and realization, while "being" refers to benefiting others through compassion;
third, "awakened" refers to having already abandoned [afflictions] and realized [the truth], being able to awaken to one's own mind, while "being" refers to... [sentient beings].

This refers to those who have not yet severed [afflictions] nor realized [the path], and who still possess remaining objects of perception; it points to the person who is able to practice and protect.
The following clarifies the dharmas that are to be practiced and protected. The intent of the question is: "We pray that you will protect the nation.

The Buddha first opened up two forms of protection, which represents the height of his compassion. However, regarding the two types of cultivation—causal and resultant—it is not yet known by what dharma one should cultivate.
By what means is one protected? This is why he asks this question. For the Buddha has revealed two forms of protection;

he merely cited their fundamental source, whereas the King asks how they are practiced, thereby deepening the teaching to guide its flow. This is what is meant by "joining the beat to form a measure" and "the striking and the singing proceeding together.
It is exactly like this. II. The Tathāgata’s Response. (Four parts. First, clarifying self-benefit. Answer:
The first question has three parts: First, the correct contemplation of the principle of emptiness. Second, the correct exposition of true emptiness. This has two parts:
First, stating the thesis and providing the formal explanation; second, the formal explanation itself. This has two parts: First, indicating the realm of those to be converted.

The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit, saying: "Those who protect the fruit of Buddhahood—the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—should abide in this manner, teaching and transforming all beings born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, and by transformation."

The phrase "protecting the fruit of Buddhahood" (*buddhatva-phala*) restates and confirms the preceding question. "All bodhisattvas" refers to the bodhisattvas of the five subsequent stages of patience (*kṣānti*);
"all" is a term denoting plurality and diversity, and thus it is known to point to those in the five stages of patience mentioned below.

The phrase "should be thus" (*evam eva bhavitavyam*) points back in reverse to the following passage: "not dwelling on the marks of form, not contemplating form as such," and so forth; that is to say, "one should be thus."

This refers to dwelling in or not dwelling in the characteristics of form and so forth, while teaching and transforming sentient beings. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When seeing arises, form is manifested; when clarity sees, perception is formed. It continues:

"Among the four modes of birth, the egg-born arise solely through perception; the womb-born are due to emotional attachment; the moisture-born are induced by contact; and the transformation-born respond through separation.

This clarifies that the four modes of birth are based on false delusion, with deluded awakening as the cause; they are summoned and induced by deluded karma, resulting in different ways of taking birth.

Thus, there are four [modes of birth]. However, devas are born by transformation (*upapāduka*); ghosts (*preta*) undergo both womb-birth and transformation; birds and dragons undergo all four modes of birth;
and humans likewise undergo all four. Therefore, the ancient commentary states: "At that time, among humans, those born from the womb were the sons of Viśākhā;
those born from thirty-two eggs were the bhikṣus Mahāparvata and Kṣudraparvata; and those born from moisture were the maiden Āmra."
The birth from qi (moisture) occurs. At the beginning of the kalpa, all humans were born by transformation; thus, these four modes of birth differ in their scope and application.
Nevertheless, they pervade the three realms and equally encompass the nine classes of beings, in accordance with the intent of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
What is now called the "four births" is merely a brief indication; in meaning, all must be fully present. Birth from an egg is placed first because the *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies its four conditions.

This is based on the fact that conditions (*pratyaya*) generally occupy the primary position. If, however, one bases it on the mind, the sequence follows the principle of flowing from the fundamental source toward its manifestations.

Question: When the protection of the fruit (*phala-rakṣā*) is explained as the fruit itself, the name and the reality correspond. Now, you designate "protection of the fruit" but explain it by means of "birth through transformation" (*upapāduka*).
Why is this? Answer: The protection of the fruit lies precisely in the saving of sentient beings. If one does not save sentient beings, how can the protection of the fruit be manifested? Moreover...
The ocean of fruition transcends words; what could be protected? It is by relying on provisional words for protection that one can manifest the protection of the fruition.

Thus, the causes and effects of delivering sentient beings are established through the true mark (*dharmatā*). Therefore, in the "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Vimalakīrti (Vimukticandra) and Vajragarbha represent cause and fruition respectively;
likewise, while the stages of the cause may be described, the ocean of fruition remains beyond words. Question: Regarding those born from eggs, moisture, or the non-conceptual (*asaṃjñin*)...

Regarding the formless realm of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), how is it transformed? Answer: There are three causes and conditions: first, for those born in a difficult place, one waits for the proper time;
second, for those born in a non-difficult place who are not yet matured, one brings them to maturity; third, for those already matured, one brings about their liberation.
△ Second, the wisdom that performs the transformation. This has two parts. First, correctly contemplating the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*).

One does not contemplate the marks of form, nor does one contemplate the suchness of form. This applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; to self, person, knowledge, and vision; to permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

to the four means of attraction and the six perfections; to the two truths and the four truths; to the powers, the fearlessnesses, and so forth—indeed, to all dharmas, even up to bodhisattvas and tathāgatas.
In this same way, one does not contemplate their marks, nor does one contemplate their suchness.
The first two phrases take "form" (*rūpa*) as the primary example; the subsequent categories of sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, serve as illustrations for all phenomena.

That which the eye perceives is form; its definition is that which possesses substantiality and resistance (*sapratigha*). There are eleven such factors, namely the five sense organs and the six sense objects.

When subdivided, these consist of the two types of form—shape (*saṃsthāna*) and color-appearance (*varṇa*)—each of which has many varieties. The physical body, which is the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*) of sentient beings, is what is called the provisional borrowing of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

This is because one regards [all beings] as oneself. Therefore, while the intent in saving sentient beings lies in benefiting and delivering them, engaging with the mundane world values the forgetting of the self-centered mind.

For all sentient beings, their physical forms and appearances are like illusions; for a Bodhisattva, they neither dwell upon nor observe them. Thus, throughout one’s life, one saves sentient beings, yet there are no sentient beings to be saved;
throughout the day, one performs transformations, yet there is no transformation to be performed. When things come, one responds in accordance with them, like a mirror manifesting images.
"Neither beauty nor ugliness exists. The *Vajracchedikā* says: "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* says:
