contemplating the ultimate, it is not the ultimate, for it is the conventional that is the ultimate; contemplating the conventional, it is not the conventional, for it is the ultimate that is the conventional.

The conventional does not deviate from the ultimate; by means of the conventional, one realizes the ultimate. The ultimate does not deviate from the conventional; by means of the ultimate, one manifests the conventional.

Therefore, it is said that they are "simultaneously illumined" and "equal. As for "supernormal powers," this refers to employing the wisdom of the ten powers to pervade unspeakable worlds, universally bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings according to their needs.
As for "vow-wisdom," this refers to fulfilling the hundred [thousand] perfections over the course of a thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

The ten thousand great vows are directed toward the fruit of Buddhahood. Nevertheless, although the single mind of True Suchness is eternally concentrated and unmoving, one manifests through transformation-birth (*nirmāṇa*) in order to protect the practices of the eighth stage.
△ Ninth, the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwells in as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in ten million billion asaṃkhyeya worlds,
acts as a Brahmā king of the third dhyāna, cultivates as many gates of Dharma-illumination as there are atoms in ten million billion asaṃkhyeya worlds,
and transforms all sentient beings through the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
The number of worlds abiding in this ninth stage is such that it cannot be clarified by calculation or reckoning; this is because the power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) of this stage is so vast.
Nevertheless, it is not yet in accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), because numerical quantity still persists.
The Brahmā King of the Third Dhyāna is the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In the world-system of this heaven, both body and mind are entirely perfect and pure. Pure.

The accomplishment of virtue brings about the manifestation of supreme reliance and leads to the bliss of nirvana; thus it is so named. Regarding "cultivating the hundred [virtues]" below, this clarifies the method of cultivation.
This too is merely a provisional description based on the stages of practice;

in reality, at this stage, one possesses great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the power of cultivation, fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), and mastery over realized wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*), such that throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one can manifest as many forms as the sands of ten million Ganges Rivers.

This refers to the infinite treasury of the Dharma and the fulfillment of benefits through the spiritual power of all Buddhas. Regarding the phrase "by means of the four [analytical knowledges]," it speaks of transformational birth (*upapāduka*).
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "When the Bodhisattvas of this stage have attained the true essence, they manifest its true function;

whatever they illuminate and respond to is entirely *tathatā* (suchness); therefore, it is called 'Universal Wisdom' (*Samantaprajñā*). These Bodhisattvas possess the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and act...
The Great Dharma Master expounds immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* phrases and meanings without end. As the subsequent sutra states:
"In a single *kṣaṇa*, throughout unspeakably many worlds, he explains all the questions and difficulties of sentient beings with a single voice, causing them all to rejoice.
This is precisely the meaning of the transformational birth of the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*). However, as for wisdom...

This refers to the "Unobstructed One," who, through a mind skillfully responding to phenomena, responds universally and without fixed direction. The four wisdoms are those of Dharma, Meaning, Eloquence, and Joy.
By means of these, one transforms and nurtures sentient beings in order to protect the practices of the ninth stage. △ Tenth: The Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
If a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields and becomes a Great Brahmā King of the Fourth Dhyāna, acting as the lord of the three realms;
if they cultivate the unspeakably unspeakable Dharma-illumination gate and attain the Samādhi of Exhausted Principle;
if they act in accordance with the sphere of activity of the Buddhas, exhausting the source of the three realms and universally benefiting all sentient beings, just like the realm of a Buddha.

From the initial generation of the mind of faith, for a hundred million *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he has extensively accumulated boundless factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and extensively increased boundless great wisdom.
Therefore, he is able to dwell in these unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
having reached this stage of the causal path, there is nothing further to be added. This Great Brahmā King is none other than Maheśvara, the Great Sovereign.
"O Heavenly King, this one is the lord of the triple world because his divine power is vast and his wisdom is supreme;

he is able to know the number of raindrops that fall during seven days within the triple world. The phrase "cultivation is not inferior" clarifies the practice of cultivation, meaning that this practice also increases according to one's stage.
The phrase "attaining the principle" and below clarifies the birth by transformation (*upapāduka*), meaning that the merit of practicing on this ground has been completed.
Having fulfilled the training and conduct, it is called the "exhaustion of principle. The wondrous cloud of the compassionate shade covers the ocean of nirvana;
possessing the substance yet being subtle, it is said to be "identical to the Buddha. Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root of delusion and karma within the three realms;

since ignorance is exhausted at this stage, it is called the "exhaustion of the source. Great compassion is fully pervasive, performing the Buddha-work with a mind free of conditions (*anālambana-citta*), according to [the needs of beings].

Because it causes those who are so destined to enter the Buddha-way, it is called "universal benefit. Because this stage accords with the two fruits of the Buddha’s twofold transformation (āśraya-parāvṛtti), it is called the "Buddha-realm.
These are all the spheres, practices, and virtues at the culmination of the stages, which were absent in the preceding stages.
One also cultivates these for the purpose of protecting the practices of the ten stages. △ Third, the conclusion clarifies the identity of the path.
This is the manner in which Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas manifest in the bodies of various kings to perform the work of transformation and guidance. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions do likewise;
having realized unsurpassed enlightenment, they constantly and pervasively benefit and bring joy to sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.

The previous question asked, "How does one transform sentient beings? This concludes the answer with the words, "This is called equality," and so forth. Now, as for the result being identical to the cause:

this is because cause and effect are mutually pervasive. Thus, the benefit and happiness that transform sentient beings exist simultaneously and in the same place, whether in the causal stage or the resultant stage.
Because it cannot be separated [from the preceding], the conclusion is thus expressed: △ Second, the recitation of verses in praise of the Buddha. Part three.
First, the assembly’s offering at that time.
At that moment, the entire great assembly rose from their seats, scattering unspeakable flowers and burning unspeakable incense.
They made offerings, paid homage, and praised the Tathāgata. At that time, King Prasenajit, standing before the Buddha, praised him in verse:
"Flowers manifest the cause; incense manifests the virtue. The superior abiding in the realm and the cultivation of the Dharma— All are ineffable. Thus, this is the ground of the cause."
The ground and its virtue—both are ineffable. △ Second, the King of Aṅga praises in verse. This has three parts: first, a general eulogy of the Triple Gem;
second, a specific eulogy of the activities of the Triple Gem; third, a specific praise of the purity of the Buddha’s three karmas. First, the eulogy of the Buddha’s three karmas being pure.

The World-Honored One, the Guide, the Vajra-body, who turns the Wheel of Dharma with a mind and conduct of quiescent extinction, and whose eightfold perfect resonance expounds and reveals the supramundane;
he alone is the Honored One. He guides the deluded and points toward awakening, serving as a model for humans and devas; therefore, he is called the "World-Honored One, the Guide. This...
The sovereign upon which the three karmas depend. Below, the three karmas are clarified. The "Vajra-body" refers to the body-karma;
this indicates the Dharmakāya, which is called the Vajra-body because the essence of the Dharmakāya is like empty space, transcending all hundred negations.
The four propositions are perfectly transcended, for they differ from all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, which undergo transition and change.

This may also be designated as the *saṃbhogakāya* (Response Body), because the response does not depart from the Truth (*dharmatā*). As it is said: "This body of mine is now both eternal and the Dharma.

Mental activity is quiescent; this refers to the mental karma. That is to say, wondrous wisdom accords with principle; it is taught that the Response is without mind, which is not the same as delusion.
The mind [is so called] because it undergoes arising and ceasing. Eighth is the "Discerning Perfect Sound" (*pratisaṃvid-svara-saṃpatti*), which pertains to the vocal karma.

"Discernment" (*pratibhāna*) refers to responding to objects with swift agility. Regarding the eight perfect sounds, the *Brahmayu Sūtra* states: first, the most excellent sound; second, easy to understand;
third, harmonious; fourth, soft and supple; fifth, unerring; sixth, not feminine; seventh, dignified; eighth, deep and far-reaching. These sounds are called "perfect."
This means: if a sound is not all-pervasive, it is not perfect; if a sound is equally pervasive, its melodic cadence is lost. Thus, that which is perfect is not [ordinary] sound.
Now, the Buddha does not disrupt the cadence while being equally pervasive, nor does he move from his pervasiveness while the cadence varies.

This is the Tathāgata’s perfect sound (pratyekabuddha-ghoṣa), which is not within the realm of the mind or consciousness. "Turning the Wheel of Dharma" refers to the aforementioned five levels of patience (kṣānti) and so forth.

The Dharma: because it crushes and destroys all hindrances through the five patiences (*kṣānti*), it is "expounded. This refers to the sound of the teaching that explains the dharma of the five patiences.
"Turning the wheel" pertains to the internal, thus following the mental action (*manas-karma*); "expounding" pertains to the external, thus following the vocal action (*vāk-karma*).

If categorized according to the Three Jewels, the aforementioned three actions constitute the Buddha Jewel; the turning of the wheel of Dharma, from the perspective of that which is turned, constitutes the Dharma Jewel. Below...

This is the Saṅgha Jewel. If categorized according to the three wheels, these correspond respectively to the supernormal powers, the knowledge of others' minds, and the instructions of the three types of action.
Furthermore, ancient commentators explain these three phrases as the fivefold perfections: first, the World-Honored One’s perfection of majestic virtue; [and so forth].
Second, the two guides are fully endowed with wisdom. Third, the three vajra-bodies are fully endowed with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Fourth, the activities of the mind are quiescent; they are fully endowed with liberation. Fifth, they turn the wheel of the Dharma; they are fully endowed with the transformation of others.

However, these differ in wording but are identical in meaning to the three karmas; therefore, they are recorded here in brief. △ Second, praising the assembly for gaining benefit upon hearing the Dharma.
At that time, one hundred trillion beings attained the Way; devas and humans alike cultivated the practice of renunciation, able to train in all bodhisattva paths.

As stated in the *Qixin lun* (Awakening of Faith): "That is to say, when the Tathāgata was in the world, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties, and the person who could preach [the Dharma] possessed both form and mind."

The karma is supreme. A single utterance of the perfect voice is understood equally by those of diverse natures. This clarifies that both the time, the occasion, the speaker, and the listeners are supreme;
therefore, it is easy to enter the Path. The benefits gained from this present sutra are likewise so.

As for the assembly at that time—namely, the followers of the three vehicles, humans, devas, and others who attained the Way—it is said that one hundred trillion beings obtained benefit upon hearing the Dharma of the Five Patiences. This refers to those who obtained benefit.

Such instances are numerous. Yet, while the sublime joy of devas and humans cannot, by itself, rectify the mind’s deliberations or lead one toward Bodhi, upon hearing this Dharma once, one is suddenly able to grow weary of worldly clamor with the mind and cultivate the supramundane with the body.

This is because the Three Karmas of the Tathāgata are so preeminent that, upon a single sight of his physical form or a single hearing of the True Dharma, deluded thoughts are eliminated and the true mind [is revealed].
It is also a manifestation. Yet, although the bodies of devas and humans are subject to desire, they remain free from desire within that desire;

though they dwell amidst defilement, they are not stained by it—this too is a practice of renunciation. Furthermore, the path of the Bodhisattva does not transcend self-benefit and the benefit of others.

One practices according to the five stages of patience (*kṣānti*) for the sake of self-benefit; one delivers sentient beings by relying on provisional positions for the sake of benefiting others. Therefore, upon hearing this Dharma...
All of them practiced that Way; this is what is meant by receiving it from the Buddha and practicing it within oneself. If one were to assign these to the five fruits:
the fact that the assembly attained the Way at that time is the fruit of dominance (*adhipati-phala*); their collective cultivation of renunciation is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*);
and their ability to practice the Great Way is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), because they practiced this Way by hearing this Dharma.
△ Second, five verses on the profound and mysterious nature of the Five Patiences. Part Three: First, the shared basis of cause and effect.

The Dharma-gate of the wondrous merits of the Five Patiences: Verse 14. Bodhisattvas are able to clearly and thoroughly understand the practice of the Patiences within the stages of the Ten Worthies and the Ten Sages.

The first phrase praises the dharma of patience (*kṣānti*), manifesting its excellence. The following two phrases praise its inclusion within the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), wherein both self-benefit and benefit for others are attained;

hence it is called "merit" (*guṇa*). Because its contemplative cultivation is profound and subtle, it is called the "wondrous dharma" (*saddharma*). Because it gives rise to what is preeminent, it is called a "gate" (*mukha*).
As for "thoroughly realizing," this means that all bodhisattvas, from the beginning to the end, penetrate the cause and encompass the fruit, thereby attaining realization and severance.
Transformation and benefit. Because one does not depart from these five patiences (*kṣānti*), the practice within patience is that upon which the noble ones (*ārya*) rely;
by means of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*), they advance toward realization. △ Second, the solitary transcendence of the stage of fruition.
Only the Buddha alone can exhaust the source.

"Only" has the sense of exclusion and selection. To truly reach the ultimate and exhaust all delusions—only the Buddha is capable of this; for while the causes [of other beings] provide only partial realization.
Thus, if a single principle has not reached the realm of ultimate exhaustion, the stages of causal cultivation (*hetu-bhūmi*) will remain fragmented.
If all obstacles have not been thoroughly severed at the source of delusion, then as a Buddha, one is eternally pure and liberated, a state of inconceivable quiescence (*śānti*).

Having crossed the ocean of existence upon the vessel of compassion, one reaches the shore of the two benefits; having cut through the dense forest, one enters the precious abode where the ten thousand virtues are perfectly fulfilled. It does not merely...
Entering the subtle and exhausting the source, one likewise emerges from the truth and goes against the current.
Thus, only a Buddha is able to reach such profound and far-reaching depths. △ Third, the inclusion of the Three Jewels.
The ocean-like assembly of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—the treasury of the Three Jewels—encompasses immeasurable merit within it.
This single essence of the Three Jewels does not depart from the five levels of patience (*pañca-kṣānti*); thus, the immeasurable merit of the Three Jewels is likewise fully contained therein.
Indeed, these are the five levels of patience: the contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional is the Buddha Jewel; the upholding of the correct norm is the Dharma Jewel... [and so forth].

Cultivation is itself the Dharma Jewel; not contravening True Suchness (Tathatā) is the Sangha Jewel. It may be said that it is like space encompassing form, or like a treasury universally containing all.

How wondrous are the Five Patiences! Are they not the very root and foundation of all causes and effects? II. Separate Verses on the Five Patiences. Five parts. First, verses on the Patience of Subjugation (Vōjin).
Two sections. First, the direct verses on the stages of patience. Two sections. First, verses on the stage of the Ten Faiths (Jūshin).
When a Bodhisattva of the ten wholesome paths arouses the Great Mind, they forever part from the ocean of suffering in the wheel of the three realms.

Those of the lower grade of the minor wholesome deeds become *kṣullaka-rāja* (minor kings), while those of the upper grade of the ten wholesome deeds become *cakra-vartin* (wheel-turning) kings with iron wheels.
Indeed, it is not easy for one to be capable of arousing this mind. The *Awakening of Faith* states that it is based upon sentient beings of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
By the power of the perfuming of their roots of goodness, they believe in the retribution of karma and are able to give rise to the ten wholesome actions.
Disgusted by the suffering of birth and death, they seek unsurpassed bodhi and encounter various Buddhas, personally receiving and making offerings to them.

They practice the mind of faith for ten thousand kalpas until that faith is perfected; therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct them to resolve their minds [on enlightenment], or do so through great compassion.

Therefore, one is able to spontaneously generate the aspiration for enlightenment; or, because the True Dharma is about to perish, one is able to spontaneously generate the aspiration through the causal conditions of protecting the Dharma.

The former [part] proves the first phrase, and the latter proves the second phrase. Thus, those who have achieved the generation of the aspiration through faith enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and never again fall back;
this is called abiding within the lineage of the Tathāgata, in correspondence with the primary cause.

However, regarding the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith, it is extensive as the ten types previously mentioned, but in brief, there are three: first, the straightforward mind, because one correctly contemplates the single reality of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma;
second, the profound mind, because one delights in accumulating all virtuous practices; and third, the mind of great compassion, because one desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the arousal of the mind through the ten wholesome paths, which seeks deliverance from the three realms.
Although one has not yet attained liberation from the realms (*dhātu*), one is already able to leave behind the evil destinies; therefore, it is said that one is "permanently parted" from them.
The ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*) do not exceed the three of body, four of speech, and three of mind. If they are cultivated with a superior mind, the goodness belongs to the superior grade.

If cultivated with the two lower minds, the goodness belongs to the middle or inferior grades. This is because there are distinctions in the arousal of the mind—such as being focused or distracted, respectful or negligent—and thus the ten wholesome actions [are differentiated].
There are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior grades. As for the "Kings of Scattered Millet," these are kings scattered throughout Jambudvīpa who are as numerous as millet seeds.
A Wheel-turning King of Iron (Cakravartin) is one who rules over a single Jambudvīpa, such as King Aśoka.
△ Second, the verse on the stages of Abiding, Progressing, and Orientation.

The stage of the lineage of practice (*śikṣāgotra*) is the copper wheel over two continents; the stage of the nature-lineage (*prakṛtisthagotra*) and the stage of the lineage of the path (*pratipannakagotra*) are the silver wheel over three continents;
and the firm-virtue universal monarch (*dharmarāja cakravartin*) is the gold wheel over the four continents.

The first line of the verse praises the abiding stage: that is to say, by the power of the roots of goodness cultivated through perfuming, one practices the ten stages of conduct and beholds the Buddha.

Regarding the Dharma and the Saṃgha: because they give rise to the bodhicitta, they are called the "cultivated seeds. The copper wheel is that which arrives in accordance with the king’s meritorious response;
it governs two continents, which refers to the limits of the territory over which this king exercises his transformative influence. The next line praises the stages of practice.
The silver wheel likewise arrives in response to his meritorious karma; it governs three heavens, which refers to the realm of the king’s transformative influence.

Furthermore, "nature" (*gotra*) refers to the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā*). Specifically, the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) at the stage of lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), and the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) at the stage of middle patience, become established as a nature through repeated practice;
thus they are called "lineage-nature" (*gotra-bhāva*). Now, within the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (or *Yingluo jing*), there are six natures, which are also termed the "six wisdoms. The six natures are:

the nature of practice (*śikṣā-gotra*), the nature of lineage (*gotra-gotra*), the nature of the path (*mārga-gotra*), the noble nature (*ārya-gotra*), the nature of equal enlightenment (*samabhisambodhi-gotra*), and the nature of wondrous enlightenment (*sudarśana-gotra*). The six wisdoms correspond to hearing and reflection.

Cultivating the signless means the illumination of stillness and the stillness of illumination. The two phrases concerning the "knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*) eulogize the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*).

This constitutes the cultivation of the superior Patience of Subduing (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), entering the Path of Equality; it is called the Nature of the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā-gotra*). As the subsequent text states: "This Bodhisattva dwells within firm patience."
Contemplating the nature of all phenomena, he attains the state of being without arising or ceasing; therefore, he is named the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) of Firm Virtue.
This king mounts this wheel to transform and guide the four continents. As for the golden wheel, it likewise arises through the power of this king’s merit.
The seven treasures refer to the woman, the jewel, the wheel, the general, the minister, the elephant, and the horse. △ Second, the specific verse on patience:
Virtue. Second. First, the summary of the preceding stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

"The thirty persons of the noble embryo of subduing patience" refers to the ten abodes (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*)—the three types of worthy ones (*sattva*) prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).
They have not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, nor have they realized the principle; they are merely able to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), but are not yet [able to eradicate them].
Because it severs [afflictions], it is called "Patience of Subjugation" (*vinirdhāvana-kṣānti*); for by means of the wisdom of patience, one is able to subjugate the afflictions.

The thirty stages of mind (*triṃśat-citta*) serve as the womb for the ten noble ones (*daśārya*), and are therefore called the "Noble Womb" (*āryagarbha*). Regarding these thirty persons, the preceding section on the "Nature of the Cultivated Seed" (*paripuṣṭa-gotra*) states:

"This is the mind of the Bodhisattva’s nourishment, serving as the Noble Womb. The subsequent section on the "Nature of the Path-Seed" (*mārga-gotra*) states: "It is able to realize the equanimity of the noble ones."
This refers to the aforementioned grounds. This very point is the intent [of the verse]. The following line concludes the stages upon which patience relies;

that is to say, there are ten stages each for the positions of abiding, practice, and heading toward. △ Second, the verse on subsequent excellence has two parts. First, it clarifies the arising of cause and effect.
The Buddhas of the three periods of time have trained therein; there is nothing that does not arise from this Patient Acceptance (*kṣānti*).
It gives birth to the root of all bodhisattva practices. Therefore, it is difficult to give rise to the mind [of awakening] and difficult to have faith.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "All worthy sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Now, likewise...
It should be said: all causes and effects take the wisdom of the patience of submissiveness (*vinaya-kṣānti*) as their gateway for the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
This is because this patience is the staircase for entering the Path and the pivotal point for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is called the "root.

Furthermore, the practice of a Bodhisattva is fundamentally based upon the patience of submissiveness, and this patience is perfected through faith (*śraddhā*); thus, this patience [is the foundation].
It is not difficult; it is the arousal of the bodhicitta that is difficult. This is like the source of the king of all grains, which is the myriad streams.
As for the myriad streams, they do not arise from difficulty; rather, it is the initial drop of water that is difficult. Regarding why faith is difficult:
an ancient commentary states that once faith is aroused, one enters the ten abodes of the Perfect Teaching and immediately severs ignorance.

Yet ignorance is vast and solid; it cannot be severed by anything other than the threefold contemplation within a single mind. The wisdom capable of severing it arises from the stage of the ten faiths;
this is why the difficulty of attaining such faith is extolled. △ Second, clarifying the characteristics and functions of the mind.
If one attains the mind of faith, one will certainly not regress; entering the first stage of the path of non-arising, one brings equal benefit to both self and others.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s initial aspiration for enlightenment.

This refers to if one attains the aspiration for enlightenment according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one will certainly not fall back; that is, one does not descend into the gradual stages but immediately enters [the path].
The path of the first stage consists in being born into the family of the Tathāgata at this stage and for the first time realizing True Suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is called "non-arising.
The third phrase refers to entering into the practices of the two benefits (self and others) within the first stage, as one abides in the patience of equality (*samatā-kṣānti*) at this stage.
There are no two marks. Through the wondrous function of skillful means, the two benefits are sovereign; thus they are called "all-pervasive equality.

The concluding phrase that summarizes the title can be understood accordingly. Question: Regarding "one whose faith does not regress," does this refer to the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), or rather the intent of the Separate Teaching (Biejiao)?
The ancient commentary answers: If considered according to the Separate Teaching, it refers to the gradual progression from the ten stages of faith (shixin) without regression.

One ascends to the Stage of Joy. If we speak according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), a Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths is immediately non-retrogressive and thus ascends to the First Abode (Prathamavihāra).

Since the First Abode of the Perfect Teaching is equivalent to the First Ground (Prathamabhūmi) of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), both the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the subsequent scriptural passages likewise treat the Ten Abodes as the Ten Grounds.
This is the specific doctrine of the Tiantai school; in reality, it is from the very first arousal of the thought of enlightenment (prathamacittotpāda).
At that moment, one attains perfect enlightenment; having penetrated from the cause to the ocean of fruition, how could this merely be an entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*)?

Furthermore, how could it even be a matter of discussing whether there is regression or no regression? As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states: "If the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, then your six sense faculties before you will function interchangeably.
From within this mutual functioning, one can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine dry-wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*), wherein the perfectly luminous and refined mind..."

The transformation arises from within, like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli. Thus one transcends the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and dedication, as well as the four minds of application.
Through the diamond-like samādhi practiced by Bodhisattvas, one attains the perfect clarity of equal enlightenment and enters the Tathāgata’s ocean of wondrous adornment.
Having perfected Bodhi, one returns to the state of non-attainment; this is the excellent proof. Thus does the aspiration arise.
Regarding those who may fall back or regress, the *Awakening of Faith* also contains this meaning. That text states:

"If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are slight and whose afflictions have been deep and heavy for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha and are able to make offerings to him..."
Nevertheless, they may give rise to the seeds of humans or devas, or give rise to the seeds of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas).

Even if there are those who seek the Mahāyāna, their faculties are not fixed; they may advance or retreat. Some may make offerings to various Buddhas for less than ten thousand kalpas, yet within that time, encountering the right conditions, they may also resolve their minds [for enlightenment].
This is what is called resolving the mind upon seeing the physical marks of a Buddha, or due to making offerings.
The assembly of monks may resolve their minds [for enlightenment] in various ways: perhaps they are taught by one who follows the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) to resolve their minds;

or they may learn to resolve their minds by following others. Such resolutions of mind are entirely indeterminate; encountering adverse conditions, they may suddenly fall back and lose them, descending to the stage of the Two Vehicles (Dvayāyāna).
According to the intent of the treatise, it is clear that their delusions are heavy and their virtues are meager; they seek erroneously and seek perversely, being full of great hesitation.
When riding [in the vehicle], if the practice has not yet reached fulfillment and one encounters adverse conditions that cannot be overcome;

or if one perceives the Buddha through form (*rūpa*), dwells upon signs (*nimitta*) while making offerings to the Sangha, and follows inferior teachings to imitate the traces of others—those who resolve their minds [for enlightenment] in such ways will all fall back and lose it. As for those whose resolve is necessarily non-retrogressive, this has already been cited from the treatise in the section on the initial resolution.
Generally speaking, through internal and external cultivation, long-standing roots of goodness, and the cultivation of supreme merit—

In the field of cultivation, when one has perfected the practice of superior wisdom and understanding and is capable of generating [the resolve], upon encountering a superior condition—whether by relying on the power of others or through one's own strength—one generates these ten minds.
There is no loss regarding what lies below, and there is gain regarding what lies above; ultimately not regressing, one enters the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Knowing this, it is understood that not only does the resolve generated at the completion of faith become non-regressive, but even...

Regarding the five stages [of the *pañcavastuka*], even those who abide in the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā*) and possess both superior seeds and superior practice will certainly not fall back.

As for those whose roots of capacity have arisen, even small virtues can lead to the Buddha-way; however, for those who merely follow after traces, even great practices find it difficult to transcend the causal mind.
The Great Sage, according to the capacities of beings, spoke of those with the nature of the seed-lineage (*gotra*) who might still fall back into hell, based on their initial state.

Regarding the intent of the teachings: there are those who say that even during the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa one may still fall back; this is spoken according to the intent of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

There are those who say that one may fall back from the stage of the Ten Abodes (daśabhūmi-kuśala-mūla); this is also spoken according to the intent of the Initial Teaching (Śrāvaka-yāna). There are those who say that one may fall back from the Ten Faiths (daśa-śraddhā);

this is also spoken according to the provisional teachings of both the Initial and Final Vehicles. However, if one speaks according to the awakening of the mind in the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti/Avataṃsaka), it is wondrously transcendent.

[This is] a classification. What is it that can be regressed? However, regarding the statement in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that those prior to the seventh stage among the ten stages may regress—this refers to cases such as the Devaputra Viśuddhanetra, the Prince Dharmamati, and Śāriputra, who, while seeking to enter the seventh stage, encountered adverse conditions and thus fell back to the level of ordinary beings, becoming holders of great false views.
Alternatively, these may be manifestations of skillful means (upāya) intended to demonstrate regression.
There are those who fall away; thus, there are those who are startled and urged forward by this teaching for those who have not yet studied it. Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* further states:
"As stated in the sūtras, some say that there are those who fall back and descend into evil realms; however, this is not an actual falling back.

It is merely for the sake of inspiring those beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and are indolent, so as to cause them to become courageous and diligent. Furthermore, once these bodhisattvas have resolved their minds..."
Thereafter, they remain far removed from cowardice and never ultimately regress to fall into the stages of the two vehicles.
Even upon hearing that it requires immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) periods of diligent toil and difficult practices to attain *nirvāṇa*, they do not become discouraged.

This is because, through faith, they know that all phenomena have been *nirvāṇa* by their very nature from the very beginning. Based on this, one should understand those who, having resolved their minds [on enlightenment], might otherwise regress and fall away.
It cannot be that his retreat was real; rather, it must have been a skillful manifestation of a temporary retrogression, is it not?
*Commentary on the Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomiduo Jing*, Scroll 1, Section 2;
*Commentary on the Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomiduo Jing*, Scroll 1, Section 3.
Translated by the Tang Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Mahāvaipulyajñāna Amoghavajra by Imperial Decree;
composed by the founding Bhikṣu of Mingcihui Temple, Zhupi Zhenhui of Shu.

△ Second, the verses on the patience of faith (śraddhākṣānti). Part two. First, the actual verses on the patience of faith. Part three. First, the verses on the patience of the first stage (prathamabhūmi). Part two. First...
The verse describes the functions of the respective stages:

The Bodhisattva of Joy is a Wheel-Turning King; First illuminating the principle of the equality of the two truths, he transforms sentient beings through provisional means as he travels through a hundred lands, Planting seeds of pure giving to benefit all living beings.
The first verse of the hymn refers to the stages [of the bodhisattva path]. However, as for the Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), he takes lapis lazuli as his wheel.

If one were to designate the first stage (*bhūmi*) as that of an iron-wheel-turning king, this would be merely one interpretation within the provisional teachings (*neyārtha*). Yet, since it is stated that he dwells in a hundred buddha-fields, how could it be fixed that an iron-wheel-turning king rules over only a single world-system?
Furthermore, although those from the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) up to the first stage are collectively termed "wheel-turning kings," [their specific designations vary].

Furthermore, they differ according to whether they are made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*). Moreover, the dimensions and boundaries of their wheel-marks (*cakrāṅka*) are distinct:
the iron wheel is one *krośa* in width; the copper wheel is two *krośas* in width; the silver wheel is three *krośas* in width;
and the gold wheel is four *krośas* in width. According to this, if it were a lapis lazuli wheel, its width would be—

It should be ten times larger than the golden wheel. For since there is a difference as vast as that between heaven and abyss between the stages of the sages and saints, the dimensions of the wheels must naturally be vastly different.
*Krośa* has the same meaning as *yojana*. The second line of the verse refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) realized therein.
This refers to the *sarvatraga-tathatā* (all-pervading suchness). Regarding the term "equality," it means abiding in the patience of equality (*samatā-kṣānti*).

By means of signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*), one illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as equal in its single characteristic; for it is neither characterized nor non-characterized. The three lines of verse describe the transformation through compassionate mind.

Since this stage is metaphorically assigned to the position of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), it is called "expedient transformation. Abiding in a hundred Buddha-fields, one brings benefit to sentient beings.
Because it is born [into this state], it is called "wandering" (*yǒu*). This four-line verse describes the practice cultivated on this stage:

within the *dānapāramitā*, one constantly practices it in every thought-moment; while other perfections are not neglected, they are simply mentioned according to their predominance. △ Second, the verse on the merit of entering the stage.
The prajñā that enters into principle is called "abiding"; the arising of merit while abiding is called a "ground.
In the first abiding, one mind possesses all virtues, remaining unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

The first two lines of the verse describe the names of these noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*), which differ according to their designations. By means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one realizes suchness (*tathatā*).
"Principle" (*li*). Entering by relying on this principle is called "abiding" (*zhu*); this refers to its beginning.

Because one accumulates prior dharmas until they reach the state of perfected reality, and because all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon this, it is called "ground" (*di*); this refers to its culmination.

Thus, the two names "ground" and "abiding" are like the distinct designations for "eyes" and "pupils. In antiquity, "ground" was associated with the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), while "abiding" was associated with the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This is correct.

This reveals that the first dwelling (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is precisely equal to the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*); each is merely the perspective of its own school.
Thus, an ancient said: "The Buddha-ground is like a royal city; there are three types of people who enter this royal city."
The road to be traversed was five hundred and fifty *li* long. One man rode a divine steed and could arrive in less than a day;
another rode a lame donkey and could arrive in ten days; the third was lame and could not arrive even after thirty days.
Although these three men all reached the royal city, their speeds differed. This was because of the road they had traveled.
The distance is the same at five hundred and fifty *li*. Whether one’s faculties are gradual or sudden, the entry into and realization of the Buddha-stage is likewise so:

some may require the passage of kalpas before they can enter and realize it, while others may be able to transcend it suddenly in a single thought-moment. Although the sudden and gradual differ, the stages of cultivation are identical.
The three phrases [of the verse] manifest the union of the names of the Grounds (*bhūmi*) and the Abodes (*vihāra*), for by means of the One Mind, the three [wisdoms] are sustained.
Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Because it is able to fulfill all virtues, it is called "abiding" (*vihāra*); because it possesses all virtues, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).

Based on this, the two names "ground" and "abiding" are identical; this is indeed the authoritative word of the Sage (*āptavāda*). As for those who claim that "ground" and "abiding" are as different as heaven and abyss, why is this?
The fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*) states that the practice of this ground cannot [be overcome] by the demons of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra-māra*).
Because it is unshakeable; because it is free from "I" and "mine"; and because it is without fear. For in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there are no two characteristics;
therefore, it is unshakeable. △ Second, the verse on the patience of the second stage.
The Bodhisattva Vigatamala, King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, manifests forms throughout the six realms and a thousand lands.
His foundation of ethical discipline is pure and perfectly complete; he is forever free from the faults of transgressions and errors.
He is the true nature that is signless and objectless, without essence, without birth, and without duality in its illumination.

The first two lines of the verse commemorate this stage as being situated in the state of *upapāduka* (miraculous birth). This refers to the cultivation of the practice of great compassion for the benefit of others.

The final four lines clarify the function of self-benefit: the severance of delusion and the realization of truth. "Precepts" (*śīla*) here refers to the threefold pure precepts (*tri-vidha-śīla*) and so forth.
In this stage, one upholds the precepts; being tranquil and purely wholesome, one is free from the defilement of breaking them, and is thus said to be "pure and perfect.

However, the characteristics of the precepts are manifold and cannot be fully enumerated. In brief, they consist of restraint and observance, the cessation of transgressions, the severing of evil and the prevention of wrongdoing, and the subduing of the three karmas—each leading to individual liberation.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that among the ten perfections, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is particularly predominant.

It is not that other [virtues] are not cultivated; they are simply mentioned according to their conditions and their predominance. To act with deliberate intent is called a "deliberate transgression" (*saṃcintya-āpatti*);

to act without such intent is called an "unintentional transgression" (*abhrānta-āpatti*). On this stage, the ten wholesome paths of action are fully cultivated and the ten unwholesome paths are forever severed;

therefore, it is said that one is "permanently free from all faults. Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "On this stage, one protects even the blades of grass; how then could one be willing to kill a living being? Regarding oneself...
One is able to relinquish everything; how could one dare to take what is not rightfully theirs? One also develops a sense of weariness toward one's own wife and household;

how could one be willing to seek out external sexual misconduct and the like? Based on this, one would not even commit an unintentional transgression, much less a deliberate one. As stated above, this refers to severing delusion.

The following clarifies the realization of the ultimate truth (*tattva*). This stage realizes the most supreme *tathatā* (suchness). When this principle manifests before one, the nature of identity and difference ceases;
the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is signless, and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is no longer a condition for perception.

It is the nature of pure, singular reality. Because this nature is empty, quiescent, and profoundly still, it is said to be "without substance. Because it is primordially and spontaneously perfected, it is said to be "unborn. Because it is a single characteristic of equality, [it is thus described].
There is no dualistic illumination. To say "non-dual" means that it is not only when wisdom takes an object as its condition; even at the moment of understanding, they are always inherently one.

This is because suchness and wisdom are mutually identical; furthermore, there is no wisdom apart from suchness, nor is there suchness apart from wisdom. Subject and object are both obliterated and forgotten.
It is neither like nor wisdom; this is the wondrous state of non-duality and the absence of non-duality. 3. Verses on the Patience of the Third Stage:

The Bodhisattva Luminous Radiance, King of the Yāma Heaven, Manifests forms to travel to ten thousand Buddha-fields, Skillfully attaining mastery in samādhi, With the freedom of appearing and disappearing, endowed with the three insights (vidyās).
The first two lines clarify the manifestation of transformative activity by assuming various forms according to one's station;

that is, through immeasurable skillful means in accordance with their vow-power, they demonstrate the joy of the Dharma in response to the minds of sentient beings. The next two lines clarify the cultivation of practice:

*samādhi* refers to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments. One who is "skillfully proficient" therein employs the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) characteristic of this stage in successive order.

Because they accord with and are fully endowed with supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they possess mastery over concealment and manifestation; that is, they attain the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). They manifest bodies of various sizes:
when manifesting as large, the large appears and the small is concealed; when manifesting as small, the small appears and the large is concealed. Therefore, they are further said to possess "mastery.

As for the "three knowledges" (*vidyā*), based on the patience regarding the signless (*animitta-kṣānti*), they fully know the three periods of time; because there is no going and no coming, they are called "knowledges."

This is because it can destroy the ignorance regarding the three time periods (*traiyadhvika*). Now, the "three knowledges" (*tisro vidyāḥ*) refer to three of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*):

the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*). In this stage, the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*) is cultivated preeminently;

there are also passages concerning what is abandoned and what is realized, though they are merely abbreviated in the verse. △ Second, the summary conclusion on the patient acceptance of faith (*śraddhākṣānti*).

The Joyful, the Stainless, and the Radiant; Able to extinguish the afflictions that bind one to form, Fully observing all actions of body, speech, and mind, The nature of phenomena is pure, its illumination perfect in every way.

The first line summarizes the names of the stages. Although there are three levels of stage, they are grouped together because they equally cultivate faith and patience (*kṣānti*). The second line [describes their function].
A summary verse on the afflictions to be abandoned in the three stages and the bondage of form, which is the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).

In the first stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the conceptualized attachment to phenomena; in the second and third stages, one gradually abandons the innate attachment to phenomena. To distinguish this in detail, each of these three stages abandons one hindrance and two delusions (*moha*).
As stated in the *Awakening of Faith* regarding the six types of defilement: namely, the "defilement associated with non-interruption" (*asamuccheda-saṃprayukta-kleśa*).

One attains the Ground of Pure Mind because one has ultimately abandoned this defilement. This defilement is the third among the six coarse [defilements], namely the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*), which is the discrimination of the clinging to dharmas (*dharma-grāha-vikalpa*).
It is also called the defilement associated with discriminative cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*).

Because it is ultimately abandoned from the Ground of Possessing Precepts (*śīlavatī-bhūmi*) up to the Ground of Skillful Means of the Signless (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*), this defilement corresponds to the first among the six coarse [defilements], the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

This refers to the innate clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). That which is able to extinguish it is through the patience of signlessness (*animitta-kṣānti*), because one contemplates that form is itself emptiness, and because the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature.
The third phrase refers to the arising of delusions and the creation of karma, which does not transcend the three types of action (*trikarma*).
Therefore, by fully contemplating the three actions, body and mind become pure; one guards the mouth like a jar and restrains the mind like [a gate].
In the city [of the Dharma], benefiting oneself and others is free from error. As for the term "contemplation" (guan):

it is because one realizes that form is itself emptiness, and that the three karmas are themselves the true mark (dharmatā). The fourth phrase refers to the principle realized, which is none other than the Middle Way.
Some say that the principles of the Three Truths are clearly distinct; such is the view of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles. However, since contemplative observation is already...
It is emptiness, it is the provisional, and it is the Middle. The principle of the truths is likewise the True, the Conventional, and the Middle.
This so-called subject of observation and object of observation is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers: though they merge, they are not one; though they separate, they are not divided.

The perfect pervasiveness of the nature-wisdom is thus. △ Third, the verse on compliant patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Part two. First, the actual verse on compliant patience. Part three. First, the verse on the four [truths].
The Earth-Patience;
the Bodhisattva Jvalanaprabha of Great Diligence; the King of Tuṣita roaming through billions of lands;
with true wisdom of quiescent cessation and the wisdom of skillful means, he penetrates the principle of non-arising and illuminates both emptiness and existence.
The first two lines concern the stages of practice and transformation; "this heaven" and "this land" refer to the locations where these stages of practice and transformation take place.

"Great diligence" refers to tireless effort in benefiting both oneself and others. Since among the ten perfections of this stage, diligence is practiced with particular emphasis, it is praised here in this verse.
The latter two lines concern the subject and object of realization: true wisdom realizes the principle, yet in its illumination of the nature of reality, both subject and object are forgotten.
Emptiness and existence are non-dual; therefore, it is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*). Expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) refers to the provisional wisdom for delivering sentient beings.

On the stages of the bodhisattva path (*bhūmi*), the two benefits—self-benefit and benefiting others—are cultivated simultaneously. Without the provisional, one cannot engage with the mundane world; without the ultimate, one cannot realize the principle. Thus, both types of wisdom are required.
The principle of non-arising is *tathatā* (suchness), which is realized by ultimate wisdom. Emptiness and existence refer to the two truths: the ultimate truth and the conventional truth.

That which is illuminated by the wisdom of skillful means is called "penetration" (*dá*) when it is profoundly clear and deeply entered; it is called "illumination" (*zhào*) when there is profound contemplation and thorough vision.

This is the distinction between the two wisdoms of skillful means and reality (*upāya* and *bhūta*). The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states that at this stage, clarity reaches its ultimate limit and awakening is full, like a great mass of fire.

Because all objects of perception are shadows that are entirely incinerated and severed, this is also a genuine proof of the realization of the principle of non-arising through the quiescence of true wisdom.
△ Second, the verse on the patience of the fifth stage.
The Bodhisattva Duryodhana attains equanimity; The king of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven contemplates the hundred billion realms as empty space, observing them with the truth of non-duality.

The first two lines and the fourth line [of the verse] praise the vast manifestation of his conduct and transformation according to his station. The third line praises... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a verse concerning the Bodhisattva Duryodhana. The final "third line" is left incomplete in the source.)

The two characteristics of movement and stillness are, in this stage, observed as they truly are as emptiness; because the mundane and the supramundane are equal in their single characteristic, it is called "contemplating with clarity.
As the subsequent text states: "In accordance with the pure, equal, and non-differentiated characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā)."
This is precisely its meaning. If one takes the following phrase as part of the meaning, then by means of the contemplation of the Truth of Emptiness (*śūnyatā-satya*), movement is itself stillness;
manifesting forms within the six realms of existence, stillness is itself movement. However, this meaning of contemplating the Truth is merely one aspect of it.

Regarding this stage, the details concerning the practice, cultivation, abandonment, realization, all similarities and differences, and the meaning of that which cannot be reached, are not clarified here because the verses are too concise.
△ Third, the verses on the patience of the six stages.
The Bodhisattva Abhimukta, Sovereign King, Illuminates and perceives that the characteristics of dependent origination are non-dual;
The light of his supreme wisdom pervades everywhere, Traveling to billions of lands to transform sentient beings.

The first and last lines of this verse describe the deeds of transformation performed while abiding in the respective stages. The second and third lines refer to the stages themselves upon which he relies.
The practice of cultivation refers to attaining the superior compliant patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*) on this stage and abiding in the three gates of liberation.

One is thus able to exhaust the causes of accumulation and the karma of accumulation within the triple world, as well as the coarse manifestations of active conduct. Therefore, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination through this truth:
they all exist because of attachment to a self; in reality, they are neither existent nor non-existent, being a single mark that is markless—the wondrous, profound, perfect, and limpid nature.
There is no duality. The light of ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*) is precisely the sixth perfection, that of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Because this stage specifically cultivates it, wisdom becomes perfectly clear and complete, its boundless radiance illuminating all phenomena. △ Second, the summary of abandonment and realization.
The Ground of Blazing Wisdom, Difficult to Conquer, and Manifesting Presence; It can sever the three obstructions and the delusions of the mind;

through the wisdom of emptiness, it is tranquil and free from objective conditions, observing with non-referential contemplation; It reflects back upon the emptiness of the mind and its immeasurable objects.

The first phrase concludes the name [of the ground]. The second phrase concerns the obstructions to be severed: "the delusions of the mind" refers to the failure to achieve liberation within the mind.

The *Awakening of Faith* states that the "defilement associated with discriminative cognition" (*vikalpa-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*) is severed; this also refers to the innate grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha-āveṇika*).

However, phenomena are not empty or quiescent, because phenomena arise from the arising of the mind. If the mind were empty and quiescent, phenomena would naturally be clear, still, and of one suchness.
What is it that deludes the mind? If these three stages of the path are analyzed in detail, each eliminates one hindrance and two types of ignorance.

As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "In the fourth stage, one eternally severs the subtle views of self and phenomena; in the fifth stage, one severs the hindrance of seeking nirvāṇa with the inclination of the Lesser Vehicle;
in the sixth stage, one severs the coarse manifestation of the causes and karmic accumulations of the triple world. This...
These are likewise all delusions of the mind; therefore, they are expressed in this verse.

The third and fourth lines mean that in these three stages, one attains the contemplation of the Middle Way, wherein one does not give rise to notions of existence or non-existence while contemplating all phenomena. The wisdom of emptiness is tranquil, whereby one realizes the emptiness of all dharmas.
Right contemplation is concentrated and still, realizing there is no discrimination; hence it is called "without conditions" (*anālambana*). As it is said:

Although one contemplates emptiness, one does not give rise to the notion of emptiness. This is the fourth phrase. That is to say, at the very moment of correctly contemplating emptiness, the object is not empty.
If one were identical with emptiness, one would be stuck in emptiness. Because it is empty yet capable of existence, it exists while being precisely emptiness;
this is the subtlety of correct contemplation. However, the meaning of contemplation has many facets and cannot be fully revealed by a single word. To seek its essential point:

"Different paths lead to the same destination. Regarding the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) of Tiantai, there are the doctrines of sequential and distinct practice (*kramika-bheda*) and simultaneous and perfect integration (*yugapat-samanta*).

In the distinct contemplation, one first contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then the provisional (*prajñapti*), and finally the middle (*madhyama*). In the perfect contemplation, mentioning one immediately includes the three; speaking of the three immediately includes the one.

However, practicing through the sequential and distinct method may be accessible to those at the stage of the Three Worthies (*tri-vidha-puṇya-kṣetra*). Practicing through the simultaneous and perfect method can only be cultivated by those at the stage of the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*). Now, this sutra...
This refers to the meaning of "perfect cultivation. It is because, although one contemplates non-arising (*anutpāda*), one simultaneously illuminates immeasurable objects.
In the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, there are likewise distinctions between practicing calming and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) either singly or in tandem.

What is called "calming" (*śamatha*) means to bring to rest all objective appearances, in accordance with the meaning of the contemplation of *śamatha*. What is called "insight" (*vipaśyanā*) means to discern causes...

Because it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of *vipaśyanā* regarding the phenomena of dependent origination and arising-and-ceasing, one gradually cultivates these two meanings without separation, so that they manifest simultaneously.
However, if practiced singly, there is correct *śamatha* without *vipaśyanā*, or correct *vipaśyanā* without *śamatha*;
whereas when practiced as a pair, correct *śamatha* is itself *vipaśyanā*, and correct *vipaśyanā* is itself *śamatha*. This sutra refers precisely to this dual practice.

This is the meaning of cultivation. The preceding phrase, "emptiness-wisdom has no object," is contemplation within cessation (*śamatha*). The following phrase, "further illuminating all objects," is contemplation within cessation.
If explained according to the *Fajie huanyuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source of the Dharma-realm):

taking emptiness as the gate means that by encompassing the truths and wisdoms, everything is empty; this is the contemplation of true emptiness beyond all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Taking non-obstruction as the gate...

To encompass both existence and non-existence, as well as the subjective and objective, without obstruction, is the contemplation of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena (*li-shi wu-ai guan*).
Taking "containing" as its gate, it encompasses both the one and the many, emptiness and existence, such that they interpenetrate;

this is the fusion of the object and the wisdom, the subject and the object—what is called the contemplation of universal containment (*zhou-bian han-rong guan*). Question: According to the above correlation with the *Dharmadhātu Contemplation*, this is still a general indication. If one were to correlate them specifically...

"How is it that they now coincide in a single track? He replied: "When the wisdom of emptiness in this present sutra is tranquil, there is an absence of subject and object, and all characteristics are severed;

this is identical to the meaning of the first contemplation on true emptiness. When the wisdom of emptiness in this present sutra, being tranquil, again illuminates all objects, and at the very moment of this illumination, everything is tranquil;
this is identical to the meaning of the second contemplation on the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena."

Now, when the wisdom of emptiness in this sutra is tranquil and encompasses all subject and object, and when it universally permeates and reflects back upon all objects, it contains both the mind and its objects within emptiness while they remain distinct.
This is identical in meaning to the third contemplation on universal inclusion.

Thus, one should know that when the sages of the stages above the earth contemplate all phenomena, their wisdom as the perceiving subject and the principles as the perceived object must necessarily be like this. △ Four.

Verses on the Patience of Non-arising (Anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Three [sections]. First, verses on the patience of the seventh stage. Two [parts]. First, verses on the characteristics of the stages and practices.
The Bodhisattva of Far-reaching Progress (Dūraṃgamā), King of the First Dhyāna, Abides in the patience of non-arising within the signless;
his skillful means are entirely equal, Constantly transforming sentient beings across billions of lands.
The first and last lines of the verse describe the stages of practice and the gathering of beings through transformation. The second and third lines praise the two types of beneficial conduct:

the upper line refers to self-benefit, and the lower line refers to benefiting others. This means that on this stage, one cultivates the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), perceiving not even the slightest mark of arising or ceasing in any phenomenon.
Reaching the ultimate limit of true suchness (*tathatā*), one transcends all extremes; though following along with the world, one is ever-transcendent.

Therefore, it is said that one dwells in the signless (*animitta*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "In the seventh stage, one enters deeply into the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

In this stage, one dwells in cessation while initiating practice; one dwells in wisdom while practicing compassion. One manifests as a follower of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) while cultivating the Buddha-wisdom above;

one appears as a heterodox practitioner while upholding the True Dharma. Thus, it is called "skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*). Nevertheless, movement and stillness are of one suchness, and heterodoxy and orthodoxy [are likewise unified].
They observe equally; small and great are non-dual. Wisdom and compassion function together, both being entirely equal.

This also signifies the realization of the virtue of effortlessness (*anābhoga*), which differs from the sixth stage where observation is subject to interruption. Thus, the practice and cultivation are as described. II.
Verse on the Extent of the Severing of Afflictions.
Entering the stage of the Immovable Dharma-stream, one is forever free from the segmentation of birth and death, transcending all realms of existence;
constantly contemplating the ultimate truth, one illuminates non-duality. For twenty-one lifetimes, one practices the conduct of emptiness and tranquility, following the path;
yet the ignorance of attachment to the Dharma remains as a subtle habit. Only the Great Being on the Stage of Far-Reaching can sever this alone.

The eighth stage is adjacent to the ultimate; therefore, it is called "entering. The second phrase clarifies the cessation of birth: because one has not yet transcended the *sambhogakāya* (recompense body), it is termed "segmented" (*paricchinna*).
Upon the exhaustion of this present body, one immediately enters the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body); hence, it is said that [birth] is forever non-existent.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage have not yet discarded their physical bodies; yet it is said they "enter the stream of Dharma," at which point they sever the [segmented birth].

"Transcending all realms of existence" (*bhava*) means that by means of the correct contemplation of the Middle Way, one enters the stream of the Dharma equally and is no longer subject to any obstruction.

"All realms of existence" refers to the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). Because the realm of segmented birth (*paricchinna-bhava*) has not been severed, one does not transcend these realms of existence.

This is a preliminary description of the merits from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward; it is certain to be thus. If, however, it is considered from the perspective of the path of realization (*sākṣātkriyā-mārga*), [the meaning is as follows].

Thus, it is appropriate that from the first bhūmi onward, having severed the coarse aspects of the two types of grasping and realized true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), one should no longer receive the retributive fruits of the triple world.
However, this is discussed here in terms of specific distinctions; therefore, it is only from the seventh bhūmi onward that one is able to act in this manner.

Because it is effortless, spontaneous, and uninterrupted, it is called "constant contemplation. This is because at this stage, one is able to enter into the simultaneous contemplation of both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*).
The ultimate and the conventional are viewed as identical; matter and mind are of one essence. Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), even the slightest difference is inadmissible;

thus, there are no two distinct characteristics. This verse summarizes what is realized. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) to the seventh, each possesses three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—of abandonment and realization, which constitute twenty-one births.
This also corresponds to the fact that each stage has three distinct mental states: entering, abiding, and emerging.
It is for this reason. Nevertheless, throughout the process of birth after birth, one should always observe the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) with wisdom, seeing all things as empty and quiescent;

this constitutes the practice. This is not the same as those who contemplate emptiness while remaining attached to existence and the like. The latter two phrases refer to the limits of severing delusions.
Although one has already severed all delusions of the three realms prior to the seventh stage, one’s own wisdom is still not yet perfected, and one remains attached to the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, it is said that the ignorance of the habitual tendencies of attachment to the Dharma that accords with the Path is completely severed at this seventh stage (*bhūmi*).
Thus, it is said that only the Great Being (*mahāsattva*) of the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṃgamā*) is able to sever it.

This is because, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, the defilement associated with discriminative knowledge (*vikalpa-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*) is only ultimately abandoned upon reaching the Stage of Skillful Means regarding the Signless (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*); this refers precisely to the innate clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-sahaja*).
At this point, [the afflictions] are exhausted; yet ignorance is also abandoned to some extent, for it is only upon reaching the stage of a Tathāgata that it is ultimately abandoned.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that those on the "Far-Reaching Stage" (*dūraṃgamā bhūmi*) are not said to possess afflictions because all afflictions no longer function;
however, because their pursuit of the wisdom of a Tathāgata is not yet fulfilled, they are, according to the present sūtra, practitioners of the Dharma that accords with the Path.
Affection is a true testimony. △ Second, the verse on the patience of the eighth stage:
The Bodhisattva Immovable is a king of the second dhyāna; Having attained a transformation body, he is eternally sovereign.
Within millions of lands as numerous as motes of dust, He transforms sentient beings according to their various forms.
Fully knowing the immeasurable kalpas of the three periods of time, one is eternally unmoving within the primary truth (*paramārtha*).

The first phrase designates the name and indicates the stage: because it is the single mind of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "unmoving. Second, the "King of Dhyāna" refers to the king who occupies this stage.
"Attaining transformation" below clarifies the compassion of transformative birth (*upapāduka*). Regarding the term "transformative change," it signifies mastery, as previously [stated].

There is no further division into segments; now there is the transformation-body (*pariṇāma-kāya*). The ancients said that one alters the coarse body into a subtle substance and transforms a short lifespan into a long one.
Coming and going through birth and death is like a mere play; therefore, it is called "sovereignty. Question:

It is the doctrine and principle that those in the ultimate fruit of the Two Vehicles transcend the suffering of the triple world and undergo birth as a transformation-body. Now, regarding the stage of the Sage at the eighth ground, it is ultimately... [no further]... (Note: The source text appears to be truncated here).

Regarding the Path of Effort (*prayoga-mārga*): from the perspective of the Hīnayāna, this stage is as vastly different as heaven and earth. How can it be said that one first undergoes the transformation of the basis (*parivṛtti*) at this level?
Answer: There are two points of view. First, within the noble stages of the Mahāyāna, there is no separate practice;

rather, the methods of the Śrāvaka vehicle are employed as a provisional means to reveal the relative depth and shallowness [of the Mahāyāna path]. This is just as the seven stages of the spiritual friends (*saptakalyāṇamitra*) in the Hīnayāna correspond to the three provisions (*trisaṃbhāra*) in the Mahāyāna.

The four preparatory stages (*prayoga*) constitute the provisions. In the Hīnayāna, the fruit of *srotāpanna* is termed the "Path of Seeing" (*darśanamārga*), because one first abandons the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and enters the stream of the noble ones (*ārya-srotas*).
In the Mahāyāna, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is likewise called the "Path of Seeing," as it is the initial realization of suchness (*tathatā*).
The second, third, and fourth fruits of the Hīnayāna, as well as their respective paths of approach, are termed the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

In the Mahāyāna, from the second bhūmi up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), these are likewise termed the stage of cultivation. Furthermore, the three fruits of the Hīnayāna are called "Non-returners" (*anāgāmin*);

because they have completely severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and will not be reborn in the lower realms, they are so named. This is analogous, for example, to the seventh bhūmi in the Mahāyāna.

Thus, they are eternally without segmentation and transcend all realms of existence (*bhava*). The four fruits [of the Śrāvaka] exit the three realms and undergo transformational birth (*pariṇāmika-janman*);
this is also analogous to the Mahāyāna eighth stage, where one undergoes transformational birth and manifests through sovereign emanation.

However, while the traces of their names, designations, and stages are the same—whether Small or Great Vehicle—there is a difference as vast as heaven and earth regarding their realization and cultivation. This may be understood.
It is attained through the mind; therefore, it is said that there is no separate cultivation for the Great [Vehicle], which relies upon the Small [Vehicle] to clarify its meaning.

Second, the followers of the Small Vehicle sever delusions and realize the truth, seeking only liberation from the three realms. The śrāvakas who incline toward quiescence pursue their own benefit, regarding the cultivation of the view of transformation as a substantial reality.
The bodhisattvas in the noble stages of the Great Vehicle benefit others; therefore, they retain their delusions to moisten and sustain their rebirths.
He manifests entry into the triple world and shares the sufferings of the people, his intention being to practice transformation through teaching.

If he were to desire to prematurely sever the *pariccheda-śarīra* (the body of分段, or "segmented" existence), his wisdom would be superfluous while his compassion would be insufficient, making him equal to those of the Two Vehicles. Therefore, it is only at the eighth stage that he first receives the *pariṇāma-kāya* (the body of 變易, or "transformative" existence).

Although the name "transformative" is the same, in the Lesser Vehicle it refers to the quiescence of the realm of rebirth (*yoni*), whereas in the Great Vehicle it refers to the saving of sentient beings. Furthermore...
These cannot be discussed as being on the same level. Generally, those who study the teachings must not be indiscriminate.

The first two lines praise dwelling in a land through transformation-birth; because at the eighth stage one pervades unspeakably many great trichiliocosms to benefit sentient beings according to their needs, one specifically manifests forms identical to those beings.
The latter two lines clarify wisdom, for in a single thought-moment [one is universally...]
One contemplates immeasurable kalpas as being devoid of past, future, and present; thus it is said that "all is known," which refers to the perfect contemplation of the three periods of time.

If one were situated in either extreme or the middle, then each phenomenon would abide in its own characteristic, and thus there would be movement. On this stage, however, one abides in the cultivation of signlessness (*animitta*).
Because the merit of the Middle Patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*) is pure, one cannot be moved by the two extremes. This is what is called the single mind of True Suchness (*tathatā-citta*).
△ Three verses on the patience of the ninth stage.
Bodhisattva Śubhamati, King of the Third Dhyāna, Is able to manifest within a single moment throughout a thousand Ganges-sands of worlds;
He eternally abides in the practice of unconditioned emptiness and stillness, And realizes the Buddha-treasuries as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in a single thought-moment.
The first line of the verse refers to the stages; the second line refers to the sphere of transformation.

This means that in a single moment of thought, within unspeakable realms, one can answer the difficult questions of all sentient beings and manifest a hundred trillion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) supernormal powers.

The third line means that this stage abides in the supreme *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena), extinguishes the characteristics of mind and mental states, and realizes wisdom.
Sovereign. Although he manifests true function, he ever abides in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); this is what is meant by being "in the present moment yet beyond the kalpas.
If one connects this with the meaning of the preceding phrase, then he universally manifests at once while eternally dwelling in emptiness and stillness;
