The humble [author] maintains that this question is King Bimbisāra’s follow-up to the previous section on the "Contemplation of the Tathāgata," specifically from the passage beginning with "contemplating the true mark of the body; contemplating the Buddha is likewise.
That section had, for the time being, elucidated the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—and the two wisdoms of contemplation of the true mark and contemplative insight. Now, first...
This uses the truths to challenge the [notion of] wisdom. Subsequently, both truths are manifested together as being neither one nor two.
Therefore, the question is raised: "Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth? If one says there is not, then wisdom should not be dual;
if one says there is, then wisdom should not be singular. The intent of the challenge is that if conventional truth does not exist within the ultimate, then there would be only...

The ultimate truth is but one. Since there is only the single ultimate truth, wisdom should likewise consist only of the single wisdom of the *prajñā* of the true nature (*dharmatā*), and there should not be two wisdoms—the wisdom of the true nature and the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Now, since wisdom actually exists as two, how can it be said that the conventional does not exist within the ultimate? If one says that the conventional exists within the ultimate, then there would be an ultimate...
Regarding the two truths of meaning and conventionality: since there are two truths, there should likewise be two types of knowledge;
it should not be that there is only one kind of knowledge. Since there is only one kind of knowledge, how could the conventional exist within the ultimate?
If so, is the fruit of the correct wisdom of *prajñā* one or two? One should also say: is the fruit of the ultimate and the conventional one or two?
"There are two. Thus he asks, "What are these things? This above passage raises the truths that are the objects of observation to challenge the wisdom that observes them.

Wisdom is divided into two according to its essence and function; the truths are divided into two according to principle and phenomenon. The essence of wisdom and the essence of the truths are fundamentally neither one nor two.
King Ajātaśatru asked in terms of their function, hence there are "one" and "two"; the Buddha subsequently answered in terms of their essence.
Therefore, it is said that they are neither one nor two. Since there is neither speaker nor listener, how could there be one or two?
II. The Tathāgata’s Response.
The Buddha said: "Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of King Dragon-Light (Nāgaprabha), you already asked about this meaning. I now..."
There is no speaking; you now do not listen. This absence of speaking and listening is precisely what is called "one meaning and two meanings.
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
In the response, he first recounts his former inquiries. Since his past causes were already profound, his pursuit of the Way became even more earnest.
Without relying on these prior practices, how could one have been able to investigate and clarify this matter? The Buddha spoke of this in order to manifest his past traces.
"I have no inferiority. Next, he answers the core meaning of the question: that both speaker and listener are empty, which is non-duality;
yet speaking and listening remain distinct, which is non-identity. However, this wondrous state of neither speaking nor listening is the discourse on neither identity nor non-identity.
Such realms are truly difficult to conceive. Therefore, Subhūti remained silent, offering neither speech nor demonstration, while Śakra praised him for his excellent teaching.
Regarding *Prajñā*, Master Zhaoming said: "Śākyamuni closed his chamber in Magadha; Vimalakīrti sealed his mouth in Vaiśālī.

This was because they took the Principle as their divine guide, and thus their mouths remained silent. They accomplished what could not otherwise be accomplished; all of this was to illuminate that there is no speaking.
If one knows there is no speaking, then one knows there is no listening. Is it not the case that where there is neither speaking nor listening, one attains [the truth]?

This is the principle of "one and not two. The final two lines admonish the listener and grant permission to speak; that is, one must not listen to the Dharma of true reality with a mind of arising and ceasing.
△ Third, citing evidence from past teachings. This has three parts. First, the formal presentation of the two truths.
This has three parts. First, clarifying the two truths of non-action.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
The signless ultimate truth In essence is not created by self or other; Conditioned existence, like an illusion, Is likewise not created by self or other.
This verse answers by means of the simultaneous transcendence of the ultimate and the conventional, wherein emptiness and existence are of one flavor.
This sufficiently clarifies the Buddha’s intent, demonstrating that the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual. Since they are non-dual, how could they fall into the state of being distinct?

The first two lines clarify the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the latter two lines clarify the emptiness of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Within the ultimate truth, the first line establishes its essential nature.
That which is called "signless" (animitta) is so because its essence is devoid of signs such as defilement and purity, or existence and non-existence.
That which is called "ultimate truth" (paramārtha-satya) is so because it transcends the mundane, merges with the real, and is empty, luminous, wondrous, and absolute.

The following phrase means that this principle is not something realized by a "revealing cause" (vyañjana-hetu), and thus is not self-made; nor is it something produced by a "generating cause" (janana-hetu), and thus is not made by another. It is primordial...

It is manifest and perfected, transcending all dualistic oppositions and far exceeding the realm of thought and deliberation. The latter two lines mean that all phenomena do not exist apart from form and mind;
their arising is entirely dependent upon causes and conditions, such as the eye being produced through nine conditions and so forth.

Thus, the Treatise states: "Causes do not produce, because they arise through conditions; conditions do not produce, because they arise through causes. Furthermore, a Sūtra says: "All phenomena arise from..."

Regarding dependent origination and so forth: although phenomena arise dependently, they exist while their nature is eternally empty of self-existence, comparable to a magical illusion—appearing yet not real.
When one investigates their fundamental root, they are originally not produced by causes and conditions; thus the Treatise states, "All phenomena do not arise from themselves," and so on.

From this we know that in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), things are fundamentally empty and causal conditions lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). Thus, the ultimate and the conventional are harmoniously integrated, forming a single, undifferentiated whole.
It is of one flavor; therefore, both [texts] state that its essence is not produced by self or other. This is as the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says:
"Observe the phenomena of the world that can be made—what among them is indestructible? Yet, one never hears of empty space becoming rotten or decaying. Based on this:

That which is produced by action is subject to destruction; that which is not produced is indestructible. Now, since both the ultimate and the conventional are said to be unproduced, this further clarifies that the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.
This is the principle of non-duality, wherein the appearance of waves is nothing other than water.

Nevertheless, that both the ultimate and the conventional lack a creator is because they fundamentally lack substantial reality; it is simply the single principle of the nature of phenomena being empty of self-nature through the convergence of conditions.

If this is explained in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), one establishes the contemplation of the three absences of nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) with respect to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). First, regarding the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), one establishes the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*);
that is to say, it is not produced by self or other, and because deluded thoughts arise and perish, there is in reality no arising or perishing.

Second, regarding the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), one performs the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda-vipaśyanā*); that is to say, the defiled and pure aspects of the dependent nature arise from conditions and lack [intrinsic] existence.
Nature (*svabhāva*). Because it is not created by itself or by another. Third, regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one practices the contemplation of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
That is to say, being devoid of the former two [natures], ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is likewise not created by itself or by another.

Question: Regarding the principle that ultimate emptiness and conventional existence are without a creator, what is the distinction? Answer: The proponents of heterodox views hold different conceptions of a creator; some, for instance, cling to a primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
They take this as their primary principle; some maintain that Brahmā creates all beings, while others hold that time, space, atoms, primordial chaos, or spontaneity are likewise produced by an agent.

However, the true teaching of the present age—in which both the ultimate and conventional truths are simultaneously extinguished—is utterly distinct from the deluded calculations of heterodox outsiders.

Nevertheless, even the provisional teachings regarding ritual practice are confused by the notion of an agent; those of the Two Vehicles sink into emptiness, being solely terrified of conditioned phenomena.
Sentient beings are all unable to realize that their own minds are of one suchness, in which the ultimate and the conventional are non-dual.
Therefore, when the Buddha answers regarding the two truths, he first clarifies "non-action" (anabhisamskāra); there is indeed a profound reason for this. II. Clarifying the Two Truths of Non-nature.

The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without nature; In the ultimate truth, it is empty like space. All existents are illusory phenomena, existing through the collection of the three provisional designations.

The first half [of the verse] clarifies the True, and the second half clarifies the Conventional. In the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*, it is clarified that True Suchness is unchanging while following conditions.

There are two meanings: the conventional meaning of the establishment of phenomena and the ultimate meaning of the emptiness of essence. Within these two meanings, the ultimate is unchanging while the conventional is the emptiness of essence;
the ultimate follows conditions while the conventional is the establishment of phenomena. The purport of this verse is likewise similar to this.
The *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is precisely true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That which serves as the nature of the myriad phenomena is, fundamentally, without nature;
it is only in the sense that when it correctly accords with conditions, it remains unchanging, that it is said to be "without nature.

As for the "Tathatā of ultimate emptiness," "emptiness" refers to its essence being fundamentally empty, while "suchness" (*tathatā*) refers to its being one and the same across all phenomena. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All phenomena, from the very beginning..."

Come! It is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, and so forth, up to being indestructible; it is solely this one mind, and is therefore called *tathatā* (suchness). Yet that *tathatā* is devoid of characteristics;
it is precisely the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) of the present moment. That *tathatā* is equanimity; it is precisely the meaning of "thus" (*tathā*) in the present moment.

The second half [of the verse] refers to the fact that at the very time of accomplishing the task, its essence is empty. "All existences" (*bhava*) refers to the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*). It is an illusion.

There are phenomena (*dharmas*). This refers to the causes and effects of the three realms, both the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), which manifest according to karmic conditions; therefore, they are called "illusory existence.

The "three provisionalities" (*tri-vidha-prajñapti*)—namely, the provisionalities of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*), of sensation (*vedanā-prajñapti*), and of name (*nāma-prajñapti*)—collectively refer to all phenomena within the three realms, which arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
It is also like the phenomena of illusion: through the conjunction of spells and cloths, appearances arise that can produce the three types of conventional existence (*prajñapti*).
All phenomena thus produced are equally unreal; therefore, one knows they exist only conventionally. Thus Master Zhao said: "If true existence were truly existent, then there would be no cessation.

However, these two meanings of emptiness and existence mutually establish one another: because the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is empty and such-like, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is illusory.
There is. Because all existents are illusory designations while the ultimate truth is emptiness-as-such, one knows that true emptiness and illusory existence do not obstruct one another;

only when they mutually constitute each other can they be said to coexist and yet be simultaneously extinguished, with appearance and disappearance being unimpeded and existence and non-existence being sovereign.
One may reflect upon this accordingly. △ Third, clarifying the perfect fusion of the two truths.

There is no non-existence, for there is no ultimate reality; it is the emptiness of the supreme meaning of cessation. All phenomena exist through causes and conditions; such is the meaning of existence and non-existence.

Thus, the ancients said that the true is not distinct from the conventional. It is the conventional itself that is the true; the true has no essence apart from the conventional. The conventional is the true. The true has no essence. The conventional...

There is no separate conventional [truth]; it is precisely the ultimate that is the conventional. Because it is precisely the ultimate that is the conventional, the conventional has no intrinsic substance.

Therefore, it is said that there is no "non-existence" regarding the non-existence of reality. However, this first phrase follows from the two preceding verses, both of which state that both the ultimate and the conventional are empty.
Here, one wishes to clarify that both truths exist, thereby demonstrating the unimpeded coexistence and sublation of the two truths as the perfectly interfused two truths.
Furthermore, the first "non-existence" (*wu*) here serves to thoroughly sweep away the previous notion that there is no second truth (*advaya-satya*).
This means that the prior claim—that neither the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) nor the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) truly exists—is logically untenable. Why is this?

If one were to say that the ultimate and conventional truths are eternally non-existent, that would constitute the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). Therefore, what follows clarifies that both truths exist, so as to avoid falling into such an error.
To eliminate the view of nihilism, the Buddha taught that it is not the case that both the ultimate and conventional truths are truly non-existent.

This is because the ultimate is not separate from the ultimate; it is the conventional itself that is the ultimate. Since the ultimate exists as the conventional, how could the ultimate lack a real essence?

Likewise, the conventional is not separate from the conventional; it is the ultimate itself that is the conventional. Since the conventional exists as the ultimate, how could the conventional [lack a real essence]?

Is there no conventional essence? Therefore, it is said that there is no "non-existence" within the ultimate truth; this means that non-existence does not exist [as a substantial entity]. The following three phrases re-explain the meaning of the first phrase:

the phrase "quiescence" clarifies the ultimate (the True), the phrase "dependent origination" clarifies the conventional (the mundane), and the phrase "neither existence nor non-existence" concludes both together.
For the emptiness of the ultimate truth is the emptiness of that which exists; emptiness is eternally not empty, while all phenomena are illusory existents.

It is existence that is itself emptiness; existence is eternally non-existence. Its subsistence and its dissolution are sovereign, as the two truths are fused as one. Thus it is said that the meaning of existence and non-existence is such.
However, the two truths are elucidated in terms of the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*), whereas existence and non-existence are designated in terms of their phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Because existence and non-existence are distinguished based on those two truths, the three preceding verses may speak of "signlessness" and "lack of intrinsic nature," or of "original existence" and "illusory existence," or of "emptiness"—these various names for verbal designations differ, yet their underlying meaning is the same;
otherwise, one would easily become confused. If one perceives their fundamental principle, then none of these [expressions] will be incorrect. Therefore, the ancients...
The Commentary states: "The two truths of the ultimate and the conventional are, in essence, a single wondrous principle that is fundamentally without differentiation;

therefore, they are described by the term 'one fundamental non-existence. Thus, there is no nature and no marks; no self and no other; no existence, no non-existence, and no absence of non-existence; neither duality nor non-duality;
neither action nor non-action—all such things are entirely absent. To speak of them as 'one fundamental existence' refers to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*)."

They are primordially existent. The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is primordially existent; causes and conditions are primordially existent; all phenomena are primordially existent; existence and non-existence are primordially existent; the two truths are primordially existent;
the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) are primordially existent. There is nothing that is not existentially present.

Yet, when expressed through the single emptiness, there is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of reality (*tattva-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the non-duality of the two, and the emptiness of illusions and transformations as well.
As for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is entirely the ultimate truth: from the perspective of oneness, all are one; from the perspective of duality, all are two;

from the perspective of existence, all exist; from the perspective of non-existence, all are non-existent; from the perspective of being correct, all are correct; from the perspective of being incorrect, all are incorrect;
when explained through various distinct names, all are explained by various distinct names; and even with coarse words...

To speak in detail, these are all instances of coarse and subtle speech. When the preceding verse-lines are interwoven and examined, they are almost impossible to clarify through conventional ethics or categorical definitions;
rather, they directly manifest the inexhaustibility of the wondrous principle and fully reveal the self-nature of *prajñā*.
According to the meaning of the ancient commentaries, this refers to the Tathāgata’s solemn illumination of the *dharmatā*.
The single dharma of interpenetration serves as the gateway; every dharma fully converges upon this one dharma.
It is like the North Star, around which all the stars revolve. How marvelous is this ancient commentary! II. Directly answering the question. (Three parts) 1.
Contrasting Principle and Wisdom to dispel the notions of identity and difference.
Existence and non-existence are fundamentally two, like the two horns of an ox; yet through illuminating understanding, one sees they are not two.
As the *Great Commentary* states:

"The principle pervades phenomena; the boundlessness of the dependent origination of the one and the many is such that phenomena attain fusion with the principle. Through a thousand [phenomena], [the principle is revealed].

They are subsumed within one another without obstruction. Now, if we consider them according to the meaning of their distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) are far apart;

thus, there is a distinction between them, like the two horns of an ox—neither of which can be missing. However, from the perspective of mental contemplation, the ultimate and the conventional are of one essence;
their characteristics are simultaneous. The Two Truths stand alone and tranquil beyond the realm of verbal teachings; this is what is meant by "constantly [abiding] within understanding."

They are inherently one. Yet, if one examines their conditions and objects (*ālambana*), then within the conventional that is identical to the ultimate, the characteristics of the conventional remain distinct;
and within the ultimate that is identical to the conventional, the true nature is ever-manifest. Thus, while they share a single flavor, their thousandfold differences remain utterly non-identical.
This is what is meant by "the truths are eternally two. One should know that the first two lines clarify this through both the dharma and its analogy, establishing the meaning of duality. Third.

The four phrases [of the tetralemma] employ wisdom to dispel principle, clarifying the meaning of non-duality. The four phrases employ principle to dispel wisdom, clarifying the meaning of non-identity.
Since they are neither identical nor dual, then emptiness and existence are no longer fetters; thus, what is called the Middle Way is made manifest herein.
2. The Relative Dispelling of Clinging Attachments through Wisdom and Principle.
The mind that understands perceives non-duality; seeking duality, it cannot be found. This does not mean that the two truths are individually unattainable;

rather, it is because ordinary people cling to "one" or cling to "two" that they are bound by phenomena and unable to penetrate to a thorough understanding. When the mind that understands is perfected in clarity, [all such attachments vanish].
Thus one knows that the essence of phenomena is neither identical [to its attributes] nor separate from them; therefore, non-duality is perceived.
As for perceiving non-duality, it is because when one seeks duality, it cannot be found. Yet, this non-duality means that the two truths are one;
it does not mean they must be called "one," for even "one" is unattainable. If one were to insist on "one," then "one" would be just like "two."

Furthermore, this is a phenomenon that falls within the realm of numerical reckoning. Thus, the *Dharmapada* states: "Even 'one' is not [truly] one," for the purpose of destroying all numerical reckonings;
this is precisely what is meant. Master Sengzheng said: "Right and wrong are mutually dependent; therefore, there arise the names of the 'True' and the 'Conventional.'"

If one truth is taken as the real, then one knows that the two statements constitute the provisional; this is also the meaning of this [passage]. △ Third, the meaning of entering the Real through the correspondence of wisdom and principle:
Within understanding, there is always only one; within the truths, there are always two. To thoroughly comprehend this oneness and duality—

Because true entry into the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is itself wisdom, wisdom and the principle are eternally one. Because wisdom is itself the principle, the truths are eternally two.
Thus, we know that wisdom and the principle are one; to falsely seek them as two is like seeking water outside the waves or searching for light outside the mirror—how could one know?

How profound is this wisdom! If one can thoroughly comprehend it, then through this mysterious understanding, one awakens to and enters the cavern of principle and wondrously realizes the source of truth.
It is like space merging with space, or water poured into water. The ancients said: "A pair of solitary geese fly high across the vast earth;
a pair of mandarin ducks stand alone by the pond. This is the mysterious mirror of the eternal oneness and eternal duality of principle and wisdom. △
The three [verses] establish the preceding meaning. First, regarding existence and non-existence according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):
Arising as an illusion within conventional truth, It is like flowers in the sky, Like a shadow, or like the optical illusion of falling hairs;
Through causes and conditions, it exists as a phantom.

The first line cites the phenomena to clarify that all dharmas are not real, arising from the deluded mind. The second and third lines employ metaphors to clarify that although things appear to exist, they are not substantial:
flowers in the sky are originally without arising or ceasing, yet those with diseased vision falsely grasp them as real;
reflections in water cannot be seized, yet the ignorant and obstinate recognize them as true; a mass of hair never actually spins, yet the observer sees it as such.
This cycle is like the way sentient beings falsely conceptualize all phenomena; how could they know that causes and conditions are like illusions and are ultimately unreal?
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "The three realms are false and deceptive, produced solely by the mind. Apart from the mind, the six sense objects do not exist;
even to the point that when the mind arises, phenomena arise, and when the mind ceases, phenomena cease. This accords with the intent of the present sutra, though that [text] relies on...
Arising from the True to produce the delusive: this demonstrates that their illusory transformations lack substantiality, which is what makes them distinct.

Thus we know that illusory existence is like flowers in the sky; the principle of emptiness is fully revealed. The appearance of hair-tufts before the eyes, echoes, and shadows sufficiently illustrate dependent origination.

To awaken to true emptiness is to not dwell in any phenomena; to contemplate illusory existence is to exhort one’s own practice. This wondrously accords with the numinous and subtle wisdom, penetrating the Unmanifest in its hidden depths.
In the realm of birth, how could existence and non-existence, or the ultimate and the conventional, even be worth mentioning? 2.

The Sage perceives existence and non-existence as illusory transformations; the deluded commoner calls illusory transformations "true reality. To the illusionist, the illusory phenomena are seen as true reality, yet both illusion and reality are entirely non-existent.

The physical and mental, the supported and the supporting, existence and non-existence of cause and effect, and the conceptual measures of ordinary beings and sages—all arise as illusory manifestations following conditions from within the single mind.
Now, to use this deluded mind to discriminate deluded objects is precisely to see illusion through illusion.

To see illusion with illusion is not the way of the wise. Because they realize that the mind is but mind, it is said that "the deluded person is called the truth of illusion. This refers to the illusionist.

Thus one knows that illusion has no inherent nature; therefore, both reality and illusion are entirely non-existent. This is like the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which states that seeing an optical aberration is not itself a disease.

What is called "non-existence" does not mean actual non-existence; it refers to what the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* calls the extinction of the illusory phenomena, whereby the illusory mind also ceases.
Because the illusory mind is extinguished, the extinction of the illusion is also extinguished; that which is not illusory does not undergo extinction—this is precisely the meaning.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*’s response by the Buddha to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding the two truths, the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*), is largely identical to this scripture; I shall not cite it here to avoid prolixity.
△ Third, the conclusion establishing right contemplation.
If one thoroughly understands such dharmas, one will immediately comprehend the meaning of both the one and the many.
One should apply this contemplation universally to all dharmas.

What has been clarified above is that the ultimate and conventional truths are observed together; emptiness and existence are non-dual; and the truths and wisdom follow one another. This is capable of—

Since both [subject and object] are simultaneously extinguished, one is able to be dual yet non-dual, and non-dual yet dual; with "one" and "two" being mutually sovereign, this constitutes the true Two Truths.
If a person can comprehend this, then whether it be "one" or "two," there is no need for laborious interrogation. Thus it is said: "One immediately understands the meaning of 'one' and 'two.
As for the "three phrases," they refer to extending [the principle] by analogy; thus, all dharmas that are without marks are likewise [to be understood].
That which is subsumed under the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is such; all that pertains to causes and conditions is subsumed under the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

To know that all phenomena do not transcend these two truths is to know that all phenomena are neither one nor two, and thus cannot be conceptualized through the conventional designations of existence or non-existence.
Therefore, it is said: "One should contemplate in this manner. Upon reaching this point, what is called "knowing the absence of speech and hearing" is realized.
This is what was taught and explained. △ Fourth, the explanation establishing the two truths. Part two: First, clarifying the two meanings of "permanent.
"Great King, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) while transforming all sentient beings."
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This refers to abiding in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) while initiating sublime practices;
though eternally quiescent, one extensively transforms sentient beings. However, this meaning is not yet complete. It should be stated as follows:

it is compassion within wisdom that transforms all sentient beings, and wisdom within compassion that abides in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This principle is as Master Zhao said: "the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena."

What is called *prajñā* (wisdom) is the ability to remain without manifesting [in form]; this is the merit of *upāya* (expedient means). Adapting to transform sentient beings is what is called *upāya*;
remaining unstained by worldly entanglements is the power of *prajñā*. △ Second, clarifying the meaning of "constant unity" in three parts:
first, stating the capacity and the reason to clarify unity.
The Buddha and sentient beings are one and not two. Why is this? Both "sentient beings" and "bodhi" are empty.
Because sentient beings are empty, one can establish that bodhi is empty; because bodhi is empty, one can establish that sentient beings are empty.
The following passage clarifies the meaning of non-duality through the emptiness of both sentient beings and Buddhas.

In the *Avataṃsaka*, it is taught that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are without distinction. The Commentary states: "Within the minds of sentient beings, all Buddhas realize the Truth in every thought-moment;
within the minds of all Buddhas, sentient beings become Buddhas at every instant. This is the perfect principle of the non-duality of sentient beings and Buddhas. Why is this so?
Objection: The Buddha has already attained the perfect clarity of Great Enlightenment, whereas sentient beings remain in a state of delusion like a long night;
how can you say they are non-dual? Explanation below: Sentient beings exist through defiled conditions, while Bodhi is realized through pure conditions.
Although defilement and purity differ, both equally rely upon causes and conditions. Yet these causes and conditions are themselves empty; subject and object are non-dual. This non-duality...

The essential point is this: since they are fundamentally identical within the single suchness (tathatā), one may place the emptiness of beings (pudgala-śūnyatā) within the emptiness of wisdom (jñāna-śūnyatā), subsuming that which is transformed (the object) within the transformer (the subject);
or one may place the emptiness of wisdom within the emptiness of beings, subsuming the transformer within the transformed. There is nothing that cannot be thus accommodated;
it is like water and milk being inseparable, for their luminous essence is non-dual. △ Second, clarifying oneness by means of the relationship between the object and wisdom.
All phenomena are empty because they are empty of emptiness. Why is this? Because *prajñā* is signless, both truths are empty;
that is to say, from ignorance up to all-knowledge, there is no self-characteristic and no other-characteristic. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), one sees nothing to be seen.
Whether there is practice, one does not grasp or cling; whether there is no practice, one also does not grasp or cling. It is neither practice nor...
One does not practice; nor does one grasp or cling. Regarding all dharmas, there is no grasping or clinging at all.
The first two phrases belong to both [the preceding and the following]. This serves as a transitional passage that concludes what precedes and gives rise to what follows.

If it concludes what precedes, then the subject and object of both sentient beings and Buddhas are entirely empty. Because they are empty, the characteristic of emptiness itself is set aside; thus, the two are non-dual. If it gives rise to...

The latter [term] "emptiness" (śūnyatā) refers to the object (*ālambana*), while the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). This means that because the object is empty, wisdom is also empty; thus, it is called the "emptiness of emptiness.
Although both belong to two categories, the meaning of the latter is more extensive. Why is this? [The text] poses a question:
Given that all phenomena (*dharmas*) are arrayed before one's eyes, for what reason are both sentient beings and Buddhas empty? [This is the *prajñā* section.]
[The Master] explains: First, he explains one meaning. That is to say, because the upper realm is empty, it reveals that wisdom is empty;

because wisdom is empty, both the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti) are simultaneously extinguished. Words are forgotten and thoughts are cut off—this is precisely what is meant by "the brilliant sun eclipsing the radiance of all other lights."
When Mount Sumeru falls, the heights of the surrounding peaks vanish; upon reaching this state, what dharma could possibly not be empty?

Yet, that Prajñā is signless (animitta) is because its essence is itself signless and is not comprised of manifold signs. From here on, the text proceeds by successively addressing difficulties to provide a further explanation.
This section clarifies emptiness in terms of delusion and awakening; the intent is that when all dharmas are clearly seen as empty, the characteristic of emptiness becomes manifest.
However, Prajñā is signless (*animitta*). Of what signs is it signless? What is the extent (*pramāṇa*) of its emptiness? Therefore, the commentary states:
"That is to say, from ignorance (*avidyā*) onwards, everything is empty and empty; how could there be any signs? Here, "ignorance" refers specifically to the cause of delusion.
"Omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) is spoken of in reference to delusion regarding the fruit. Thus, in the interim, there is neither self nor other;
this *prajñā* is devoid of characteristics throughout both delusion and awakening from beginning to end. When realized within the principle of wisdom (*jñāna*), it is seeing without seeing;

truly, there is neither subject nor object. This *prajñā* is devoid of characteristics at the moment of realization and entry. "Self-characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) refers to the intrinsic essence of *prajñā*.
"Other characteristics" refers to the teaching on ignorance and so forth. Regarding the phrase "If there is... and below, it concerns not clinging to clarity or emptiness.
An ancient said: "Prajñā is like a great mass of fire; one cannot enter from any of its four sides. He also said: "Prajñā is like a cool pond; one may enter from all four sides.
This is because dwelling in characteristics and grasping with attachment brings about great harm and keeps one far removed from Prajñā.

Therefore, it cannot be entered [in this way]. If one does not dwell upon or grasp at signs (*nimitta*), then internally the parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature) is extinguished, and externally the paratantra-svabhāva (dependent nature) is forgotten;
all things become equally the perfectly luminous *prajñā*. What, then, could not be entered? Thus, if one practices by means of this, one immediately ascends to the highest stages;
if one does not practice by means of this, one remains ignorant of the treasure of one's own house. It is not a matter of practicing or not practicing, but rather of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Conforming to the Middle Way, one realizes that regarding all phenomena, their worldly characteristics are eternally abiding;
this is the measure of the merit of non-attachment, which is identical to empty space—how could it be anything trivial? To act is to practice the profound path of Prajñāpāramitā.
△ Third, clarifying oneness by means of defilement and purity.
When a bodhisattva has not yet attained buddhahood, they take awakening (bodhi) to be affliction; when a bodhisattva attains buddhahood, they take affliction to be awakening.
Why is this? Because in the ultimate sense (paramārtha), there is no duality. All Buddhas and Tathāgatas, as well as all phenomena, are entirely suchness (tathatā).
This first section presents a dual heading regarding defilement and purity: that when one is deluded, the entirety of purity is defilement; and after awakening, the very defilement is purity.

Although the moments of delusion and awakening differ, the source of defilement and purity is non-dual. It is like being deluded and mistaking south for north; upon awakening, it is realized that south *is* north.
There is a difference between delusion and awakening, yet there is no duality between south and north. Why is this so? [End of quote]

Objection: Afflictions (*kleśa*) and enlightenment (*bodhi*) are like a benevolent person and a tyrant who do not function for one another, or like fire and water which do not serve as causes for one another.
For what reason, then, are defilement and purity entirely identical? The answer is explained below in two senses: first, from the perspective of principle (*li*), they are one and without duality;
second, from the perspective of realization (*zheng*), all phenomena are suchness (*tathatā*). By virtue of this, the entirety of defilement is transformed into purity.
To cause the deluded to awaken: this very thing is that; that very thing is this. There is no other path. △ Second, clarifying that the preaching of the Dharma is non-dual.
This has three parts. First, the request made by those whose faculties are suited to the teaching.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying: "How is it that the Buddhas of the ten directions and all bodhisattvas do not depart from words and letters, yet practice the true mark?"
The questioner’s intent is as follows: Since it was explained above that all phenomena (dharmas) are empty, then written characters do not exist.

How is it, then, that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not depart from written characters yet practice the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa)? For the true mark is signless (animitta), whereas written characters leave traces.
Because "existence" and "non-existence" are diametrically opposed, this question was asked. △ Second, the Tathāgata’s response. This has two parts.
First, clarifying the teaching on emptiness.
The Buddha said: "Great King, 'letters' refers to the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas," and so forth.

Whether it be parables, historical narratives, birth stories, vaipulya sutras, or marvelous discourses—all that is proclaimed, whether in sound, speech, or written characters and phrases, is entirely suchness;
there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*). If one grasps at the marks of words, that is not the true mark.
First, the titles of the sūtras are listed; however, these twelve [categories] collectively encompass the entirety of the Tathāgata’s teachings throughout his life.

They are all explanations given according to the occasion, adapted to the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, like administering medicine based on the specific ailment. In reality, there is no fixed dharma; therefore, all are empty.
*Sūtra* is called "Scripture in Accordance with Truth" (*kṣepa-sūtra*); *Geya* is called "Verses in Response" (*geya*); *Vyākaraṇa* is called "Prophecy" (*vyākaraṇa*).
Gāthā is called "Verses. Udāna is called "Spontaneous Utterances. Nidāna is called "Origins. Avadāna is called "Parables.
Itivṛttaka is called "Past Occurrences. Jātaka is called "Birth Stories. Saṃyukta-āgama is called "Connected Discourses."
*Vaipulya* means "Extensive. *Adbhutadharma* means "Marvelous. *Avadāna* means "Parables. *Upadeśa* means "Exegesis";
their meanings are explained elsewhere. From "All that... below, it clarifies that all speech is suchness (*tathatā*). Now, when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma...
Because the triad of name, phrase, and syllable (nāma-pada-vyañjana) functions in harmony to constitute the essence of the teaching, sound (*śabda*) is a substantial dharma (*dravya-dharma*).

However, these three—name, phrase, and syllable—are conventional designations based upon sound; that is to say, names express intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), phrases express distinctions (*viśeṣa*), and syllables are the characters (*akṣara*) that serve as the basis for both.
Yet, the very emptiness of the nature of syllables is *prajñā*. Therefore, both speech and written characters are all suchness (*tathatā*), and they are one.
There is nothing whatsoever that is not the true mark (dharmatā). This means that one practices the true mark without clinging to words and letters.

Thus, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "The nature of words and letters is detachment; there is no detachment apart from words and letters—this is liberation. This is precisely the meaning of this passage. Furthermore, it says:
Dhāraṇī is devoid of words, yet words manifest dhāraṇī; this is to perceive the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) through words themselves.
This is precisely the *prajñā* of words—profoundly mysterious and wondrous. If one were to take it as something inferior, then clinging to it would deviate from the truth.
Qingliang said: "Use the sacred teachings as a clear mirror to reflect upon one's own mind; use one's own mind as a lamp of wisdom to illuminate [the darkness]."
The profound purport of the sutras is such that one must first hear the teaching before one can contemplate it; only by letting go of the finger can one perceive the moon.
This is what is meant by not clinging to words while practicing the true reality (dharmatā). To grasp [the teaching] is merely to seize upon the words themselves.

Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, in its commentary on emptiness, uses the metaphors of wind and painting, stating: "Wind is a metaphor for sound; painting is a metaphor for names and phrases. Neither of these...
It may be accepted, for these teachings are all in accord with realized wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*). They are not like the wind in tree leaves or a painting on a wall;
they are to be seen and heard only through the path of teaching. Furthermore, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"If any dharma were even as much as a hair's breadth not empty, then the Buddhas would not appear in the world, nor would they ever preach."
All dharmas are empty by nature. Furthermore, the subsequent sutra asks: "What is called the true mark of all dharmas? It says:

"It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty and non-existent. As explained in the aforementioned sutras and treatises, it is clarified that the characteristics of words and letters cannot be grasped.
II. Explaining the Cultivation of Emptiness. This has two parts: first, the actual exposition of the practice.

Great King, as for the cultivation of the true nature (*dharmatā*), cultivating the true nature according to its words is the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas and the fundamental mother of the wisdom of all sentient beings.
This is precisely what is called the essence of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). When the Buddhas have not yet attained Buddhahood, it serves as the mother of their wisdom;

when the Buddhas have already attained Buddhahood, it becomes omniscience itself. It is the nature of that which has not yet been attained, and [the perfection] of that which has already been attained.
This constitutes wisdom.

This passage has two parts; the first concerns cultivation based on causes. As stated above, "words and letters cannot be grasped," for to grasp them is to contradict the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
This says that one does not seek liberation apart from words and letters, because the very nature of words and letters is emptiness.
If one practices according to the text, one will intuitively realize the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); thus, the very letters are themselves the true reality.
Now, as for true reality, it is the truth encountered in every phenomenon; how could it be a mere empty word? Therefore, it is said that one "cultivates true reality.

To cultivate true reality is to practice according to the words as they are; it is not necessary to depart from the words. Nevertheless, while the teaching reveals the principle, it is through the principle [that the teaching is realized].
When wisdom arises, the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished; because it exists within words and letters, it is further said that these are the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Question: Words and letters are provisionally established based on sound. Why, then, does one cultivate the true mark (dharmatā) in accordance with words and letters? Answer:
Lingyun attained awakening upon viewing blossoms, and Xiangyan realized the source of the mind while striking a bamboo; both reached a profound understanding of the mind’s origin.

Yet, written words are no less than flowers or bamboo. What is so wrong with using them to cultivate the true nature (*dharmatā*)? It simply depends on remaining within words while transcending them, and not grasping at them.
What fault do written words possess? Furthermore, in the Buddha-land of Gandhavyūha, one partakes of fragrances.
When one eats, samādhi is revealed; in the Buddha-land of Ultimate Bliss, right mindfulness is perfected by listening to the wind through the trees.

Thus we know that practicing the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) by relying on words and letters is the definitive teaching (nītārtha) of the Tathāgata. From "All those below" onward, it is explained in terms of the stage of fruition:
sentient beings within the three realms, if deluded regarding this, will sink and wander in the ocean of karma; therefore, this is the root.

The Root. Knowing the root is itself the turning away from delusion and the awakening to enlightenment; therefore, it is called the "Mother of Wisdom. When those who have attained the fruit in the ten directions awaken to this, they transcend and ascend to the other shore;
thus, it is the essence of wisdom (*jñāna*). To penetrate this essence of wisdom is to be wondrously identical with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Before it has fully become the Mother of Wisdom, one relies upon it to be able to give birth to the merits of the Buddha-fruit; once it has fully become [the Mother], it is all... [omitted].
"Wisdom" (jñāna): This refers to that which is capable of thoroughly penetrating and comprehending all phenomena. Therefore, what has not yet been activated is the inherently possessed nature;

what has already been attained is ultimate wisdom. Although the nature of wisdom and [the inherent nature] differ, in reality they are one. △ Second, a further explanation in response to difficulties.
The Prajñā of the Three Vehicles is neither born nor extinguished; its self-nature is eternally abiding. For all sentient beings, this is their enlightened nature (*bodhicitta*).

If a Bodhisattva does not cling to words, yet does not depart from words, being without the mark of words yet not without words—if one can cultivate in this way, perceiving no mark of cultivation, then this is called "one who cultivates words," and such a person is able to attain Prajñā.
If it is true nature, this constitutes the *prajñāpāramitā*.

The first three phrases explain this in terms of the nature of practice: that is to say, while the faculties and capacities of the three vehicles are not uniform and the various practices they cultivate likewise differ, the nature of original enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*) is not produced by causes and conditions;
how, then, could it have arising or ceasing? For it is immutable. Thus it is.
Regarding "permanently abiding," Master Sengzhao stated: "The three vehicles equally contemplate the emptiness of nature and thereby attain the Way. The *Vajracchedikā* states:
"All worthy sages have distinctions based on the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Based on this, it is clear that while the nature is one, the practices differ.
However, this is called a "re-explanation" because what was previously termed the "mother of wisdom" and the "root" is being further elucidated here.

Fearing that others might find this difficult to understand, I have provided this detailed explanation. From the phrase "All things below" onward, the explanation is given in terms of the principle of nature (*li-xing*).

That which is called "awakened nature" (*jue-xing*) is the fundamental, substantial reality inherent in every person. Because one relies upon it to achieve the Way, there is nothing that does not proceed from it as one cultivates the causes.

Because one creates karma through it, there is likewise nothing that does not proceed from it as one undergoes retribution. It is through this very nature that all daily activities and actions are carried out.
All conventional designations depend upon this. Thus, Master Pang said: "The village elder returns home carrying firewood; he urges his wife to weave through the night.
Observe how busy they are with their household affairs—tell me, by whose power do they succeed? How wondrous! This is surely what is meant by sentient beings relying upon the enlightened nature.
As for the section below on "Bodhi," it concludes by manifesting the perfection of cultivation; it does not rely on words and is entirely without text.
The two phrases concerning the "characteristics of letters" conclude that all preceding words and letters are identical to suchness; there is nothing that is not the true mark (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, to grasp at the characteristics of letters is precisely what is not the true mark. The two phrases "not departing from letters" and "yet not being without letters" conclude that those who cultivate the true mark do so in the manner described in the passage on cultivating the true mark through letters. The intended meaning is that one does not become attached [to them].
Detached, the true reality (*dharmatā*) of words and letters is neither one nor two. Cultivating by means of this, though one cultivates, one forgets cultivation;
attaining by means of this, though one attains, there is no attainment. Because this very locus of words and letters is the true nature of *prajñā*, the text concludes with these words.
△ Third, a summary of the preceding text.

"Great King, it is in this manner that Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas protect the fruit of Buddhahood, protect the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and protect the transformation of sentient beings.

Protecting the fruit of Buddhahood refers to the passage in the 'Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata' where the fingers are joined; protecting the practices of the ten stages refers to the joining of the fingers in contemplation..."
This is the text of the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Practice. Since both chapters contain the practice of transforming sentient beings, it further concludes by stating:

"protecting and transforming sentient beings. △ Third, the non-duality of the Dharma gates. [This section has] three parts. First, the question regarding the contradiction between the capacities of beginners and the characteristics of the teaching.
King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying: "The true nature is one, yet the categories of sentient beings, their faculties, and their conduct are immeasurable.
Are the Dharma-gates one, or are they immeasurable?"
The intent of the question is as follows: Sentient beings equally possess a single nature, yet they undergo immeasurable perfuming by karma, whether defiled or pure.

Since the faculties and practices of those who receive the teaching are manifold, are the Dharma-gates that can encompass them one or many? If there is only one, how can a single Dharma reach so many capacities?
If there are many, how can the true nature remain equal? What is the underlying meaning of this principle of "one" and "many"?
"How is this so? △ Second, the answer that the teaching varies according to the capacity of the recipient. This has two parts.
First, the general answer with a dual heading. The Buddha said: "Great King, the Dharma-gates are neither one, nor are they infinite."
The meaning of the answer is that the nature [of reality] transcends number and quantity; in principle, it is formless and soundless.
However, the Dharma-gates accord with this nature, and these boundless teachings manifest according to conditions. One is immeasurable; how could they be limited by signs or numbers? II.
Second, the interrogation and explanation of non-difference, in two parts. First, clarifying the Two Truths in relation to the capacities of sentient beings and their environments.
Why is this? Because for all sentient beings, the phenomena of form and mind—the five aggregates of grasping—manifest as the characteristics of self and person;
their various faculties, conducts, and categories are boundless. Accordingly, the Dharma gates that follow these faculties are likewise immeasurable.
Yet the nature of these dharmas is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics, and yet it is not without measure.
The first phrase poses the inquiry: "The immeasurable" and "the one"—these two designations are distinct. If it is not one, it must be immeasurable; if it is not immeasurable, it must be one.
Why is it that both are negated rather than being definitively established as one? The subsequent passage provides the explanation.

First, it is explained in terms of the actual multiplicity based on the faculties (*indriya*): because the vessels of the faculties differ, the Dharma-gates are likewise immeasurable. [This applies to] form and mind...

The dharmas of the five aggregates and so forth have already been explained as before. However, because sentient beings collectively grasp at and do not relinquish both material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), they are called the "aggregates of grasping" (*upādāna-skandha*).
"Self," "person," "knowledge," and "view" are names for that which is capable of grasping.

"Various faculties and activities": "faculties" refers to the depth or shallowness of what was cultivated in the past; "activities" refers to the excellence or inferiority of one's current practice. "Categories" refers to their various types.

"Things are categorized by their kind; beings are divided into groups. The *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse) states: "Apart from the minds of sentient beings, the fruit of Buddhahood possesses no form or sound, nor any merit.
Only suchness (*tathatā*) and the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) remain alone.

Great kindness and great compassion act as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), causing the Buddha’s form and voice to appear within the minds of those to be converted whose faculties have matured, so that he may preach the Dharma. This is...
Therefore, the holy teachings are merely images within the minds of sentient beings. That commentary states that the substance of the teaching is only the image and lacks an original;

I now say that since the Tathāgata establishes the Dharma in accordance with the faculties [of beings], the Dharma-gates that can thus follow are themselves the predominant conditions of compassion and wisdom.
Those sentient beings who are followed likewise possess mature faculties, within whose minds the Buddha’s form and voice appear.
He preaches the Dharma; therefore, he cites this to substantiate its meaning. Regarding the phrase "these various," etc.:
from the perspective of ultimate non-duality, the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is the true reality (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) upon which the various Dharma-gates rely.

Nevertheless, although there are many kinds of provisional Dharma-gates established throughout a single period [of a Buddha's life], the ultimately true nature is neither with marks nor without marks, yet it is also not without measure. Within this...
"Non-characteristic" means that it is not existent. "Non-non-characteristic" means that having discarded existence, one might cling to non-existence;

yet even non-existence does not exist, and therefore both are negated. Master Pang said, "I only wish to empty all that exists; take care not to reify all that does not exist. This is precisely that meaning.
If one were to correlate this with the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it should be stated as: neither existent nor non-existent, neither both existent and non-existent nor... neither.
Neither existent nor non-existent; this is indeed the true essence of Prajñā. It transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations; therefore, it must necessarily possess [both].
Otherwise, how could it be limited to merely two propositions? △ Second, illuminating the two truths through contemplation.
If a bodhisattva, following after sentient beings, perceives one or perceives two, this is precisely not seeing the meaning of one or two.
To fully know that one and two are neither one nor two is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). To grasp at one and two, or at existence and non-existence, is the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
First, one clearly understands that this is precisely the truth: namely, the Great Compassion that delivers sentient beings.

Because it constantly accords with all things for their sake, the meaning of "one" and "two" involves seeing while not seeing. Why is this? It is because, by following and conforming to sentient beings, it manifests as if seeing;
yet, because its wisdom shines through with total penetration, it forgets the marks of seeing. This is the state where, though there is duality within non-duality, one realizes that it is not two.
Though not one, they reside in a single state; realizing they are not one, one transcends words and severs all marks, becoming purely and solely the reality.
Therefore, it is said that this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This is precisely as described in the *Dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*:

the meaning of "truth subsuming phenomena" and "truth is not the phenomenon. Thus, its analogy states: "The phenomenon is empty while the principle is real," just as water subsumes the waves; the characteristic of the waves—

Because it is self-extinguishing (*svayam-astaṃgama*). This is because one does not grasp or cling in such a manner. Below the section on grasping and clinging, the text next clarifies that grasping and clinging are the conventional (*saṃvṛti*);

that is to say, they are equally [empty] within a single dharma. To fully realize this is the ultimate (*paramārtha*), which subsumes the conventional truth into non-existence. Grasping and clinging—[are thus the conventional].

Thus, the mundane conceals the ultimate truth within existence and non-existence. Therefore, we know that delusion and awakening depend on the person; what concern does the ultimate or the mundane have [with this]?
It is just as benevolence and wisdom differ in their perspectives yet do not divide the Way.

This also refers to the observation that phenomena can conceal principle, and the sense that phenomenal dharmas are not themselves the principle; thus, grasping and attachment occur in this manner. △ Third, the conclusion and response.
Non-dual. Therefore, this Dharma-gate is neither one nor two; the concluding text may be understood accordingly.
△ Second, the exhortation to uphold [this teaching] and its merits, in three parts. First, praising the teaching as being identical to what was spoken.
"Great King, all the Buddhas have taught the Prajñāpāramitā; what I now teach as the Prajñāpāramitā is non-dual and without distinction."
Faith means that the August Heaven has no dual paths and the sages have no double-mindedness. Since that which they realize is the same, that which they teach is likewise the same.
△ Second, citing the benefits to encourage upholding.
"You great assembly, if you receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice according to these teachings, you will thereby be upholding the Dharma of all Buddhas;
for it is because all Buddhas have realized it together and spoken it together. △ Third, the comparison that reveals its excellence, in four parts:
First, presenting that which can be compared, in two parts. First, the inexhaustibility of Buddha after Buddha.
"Great King, the merit of this Prajñāpāramitā is immeasurable. Suppose there were as many unspeakably numerous Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River;
and each one of these Buddhas were to teach and transform unspeakably numerous sentient beings, and each of those sentient beings were to attain Buddhahood;
and all those Buddhas, in turn, were to teach and transform unspeakably numerous sentient beings—[the merit would still not equal that of the Prajñāpāramitā]."
All shall attain Buddhahood.

The first phrase provides the initial heading, manifesting that their merit is immeasurable. "If there are... and so forth below, this cites the Buddhas who perform the transformation, who are exceedingly numerous.
"Each and every one... and so forth below, this cites the boundless multitudes who are transformed, all of whom together attain Buddhahood. These various... [text continues].

"Below. This further raises the point that the many assemblies transformed and produced, as well as the Buddhas thus accomplished, go on to teach and transform immeasurable and boundless sentient beings so that they attain the Buddha-way.
Yet, although the word "Buddha" is mentioned three times here, how could there ever be a numerical limit to Buddhas?
△ Second, the immeasurability of *prajñā*.
The Prajñāpāramitā taught by these Buddhas consists of immeasurable, unspeakable hundreds of billions of verses;
it cannot be fully expounded.
The present sutra consists of only two fascicles and eight chapters;

yet, as for what is here called the "Ineffable Verses," this refers to a teaching that is universally pervasive, where the one and the many are not fixed, and which is a discourse in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), wherein contraction and expansion are both sovereign. II.
Citing the objects of comparison. This has two parts. First, comparing a single part with the whole.

Among all these verses, if one were to take a single verse and divide it into a thousand parts, and then speak of only one part of those thousand parts, the merit of its words and meaning would still be inexhaustible;
how much more so, then, for the merit contained within such immeasurable words and meanings?
If a single verse were divided into a thousand parts, and one were to take but a single part of those thousand, its meaning could be called extremely subtle.

Yet even such a portion possesses merit that is inexhaustible; this is what is meant by the "Dharma-gate of a Single Syllable. Even if one were to write it with ink as vast as the oceans, it would never be exhausted—how could it have any limit?
Just as a great thousand-fold world-system scripture emerges from within a single speck of dust, we know that the mind is inconceivable.
It cannot be fathomed or measured. △ Second, comparing the understanding and upholding through a single thought-moment:

If there is anyone who can give rise to a single thought of pure faith in this sutra, that person will immediately transcend the suffering and difficulties of birth and death for hundreds of kalpas, thousands of kalpas, and hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas;
how much more so for those who copy, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others!
This explains the merit obtained:
a single moment of pure faith is called the ultimate of faith; therefore, one can transcend the suffering of birth and death across many kalpas.
It is just as a single recitation of the Buddha’s name can exempt one from the sins of birth and death for eighty billion kalpas. Because of this one...
That one may escape manifold sufferings through mindfulness is due to a single thought of courageous resolve;
it is not merely a casual thought. Truly, a single lamp can dispel the darkness of a thousand-year chamber.
Those who encounter this sutra should seek liberation from suffering with pure faith; they are by no means ordinary people. △ Third, the conclusion revealing the attainment of Buddhahood.
They shall then be equal and no different from all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
You should know that this person is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and will before long attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
For Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas; it can fully explain and uphold [the truth], and the true reality (dharmatā) resides within oneself.
Thus, cause and effect penetrate one another, being equal and non-dual. Protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, one may swiftly attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment.
How great indeed is the meaning of this sutra! △ Fourth, the benefits gained by the assembly.
When this Dharma was being taught, one billion people attained the patience of the three emptinesses; one trillion people attained the patience of great emptiness;
and immeasurable bodhisattvas attained birth in the ten stages.

"Patience" (kṣānti) refers to the establishment of practice as a name. There are three types of emptiness-patience (*śūnyatākṣānti*). These may refer to the three gates of emptiness of the Hīnayāna—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
If one were to explain them by means of the simultaneous emptiness of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ubhaya-śūnyatā*), I fear it would be too exalted;

for later there is mention of abiding in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When this faculty is first understood, one first attains the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*)," and so forth.

"Clouds and space are both empty and unarisen; such a person immediately attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). This occurs at the stage subsequent to the seventh bhūmi;
therefore, it is known that this refers to the three gates of emptiness of the Hīnayāna. Great emptiness (mahā-śūnyatā) means that all phenomena are empty."
This is because upon hearing the Prajñā once, one realizes that all phenomena are thus, and the benefit gained is likewise thus.

"The ten stages" (daśabhūmi) does not refer solely to the tenth stage, but generally indicates all ten stages. Regarding the term "stage" (*bhūmi*) as "abiding," it refers to what this very sutra states:
"Entering into the wisdom of principle is called abiding. This is precisely it.
Commentary on the *Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll I, Part Three;
Commentary on the *Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll II, Part Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Śramaṇa Amoghavajra of Great Wisdom under Imperial Decree during the Tang Dynasty.
Composed by the founding bhikṣu of Mizuiji Temple, Puzhen-gui of Shudong.
△ Second: The external protection against national calamities and the manifestation of the wondrous benefits of the Dharma. Part two. First: The title of this chapter.
Chapter Five: Protecting the State.

When the World-Honored One emerged from meditative concentration, the various kings, mindful of their invitation and with sincere devotion to protect the state, had already initiated this aspiration within the source of their minds.
Consequently, the profound mirror of true knowledge manifested upon the ground of awakening. Desiring to discourse on this meaning, the Tathāgata first opened the Dharma.
The conditions clarify the profound mystery of the two protections of Prajñā; their essence lies in the non-abiding of dharmic marks.

They open the correct path for the practice of the five patiences, which is wondrously brought about through the transformation of birth by contemplating emptiness. By means of this most profound and subtle principle, one protects both cause and fruit;
thus, through the realization and cultivation of these causes and fruits, one benefits oneself and others—what is called internally protecting the Buddha-dharma and manifesting it.

O Subhūti, the merit and benefits do not exceed these. Nevertheless, although the two forms of protection—internal and external—are distinguished by their differing aspects of principle and phenomena, both the mundane and supramundane rely upon Prajñā-pāramitā as one and the same.

Therefore, following the conclusion of the previous section on internal protection, there is this "Chapter on Protecting the Nation. Now, regarding this land, if we categorize it according to the realized attainments of the sages and worthies:
They are not the same; there are distinctions among the four lands: the Land of Common Residence, the Land of Expedient Means, the Land of Real Reward, and the Land of Quiescent Light.

The Land of Common Residence and the Land of Expedient Means are the bases for ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles. The Land of Real Reward and the Land of Quiescent Light are the bases for the ocean of fruition, from the stage of faith up to the stages of sainthood within the Perfect Teaching.
If one wishes to protect them, one must ultimately rely on the specific doctrines and principles of each respective vehicle when contemplating them.

It is not lost; because it is realized through correct reasoning and severed [of delusion], it is called "protection" (*rakṣā*). This meaning of protecting the country is not essential in the conventional sense;
rather, it is because the land is named after that upon which the noble ones rely, and because the noble ones observe it correctly, it is termed "protected.
Now, this "country" in the present sutra specifically refers to those sentient beings who are produced by the common karma of ignorance. Since...

While these things are induced by collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), calamities, blessings, auspiciousness, and misfortune are likewise transformed by the individual karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*) within the minds of sentient beings.
Therefore, when the hearts of the common people are upright, above, Heaven is clear and the earth is tranquil, and the seasons are harmonious and orderly;

below, families honor loyalty and filial piety, people delight in the worthy and the good, litigation is sparse and punishments are few, transformation prevails and customs are beautiful, and all living beings ascend [to a state of peace].

On the spring platform, they rescue those in suffering and lead them toward the Great Way. Furthermore, in the human realm, sages and worthies appear in succession to support the social order and its constant norms without obstruction;
in the world beyond, Bodhisattvas manifest transformations to guide the lost across the ford of delusion with perpetual renewal.
Even so, sweet springs emerge, ambrosia manifests as an auspicious omen, phoenixes arrive in graceful flight, and qilin descend as portents of good fortune—all of which serve to eliminate evil.
Gods will be majestic and ghosts will hide their traces for five hundred *yojanas*; celestial calamities and timely misfortunes shall not arise in this land of the ten wholesome deeds.
A hundred things will accord in harmony, and myriad blessings will all arrive. Thus we know that the fundamental basis for protecting the state lies in rectifying the mind.

This mind, once deluded, gives rise to ten thousand forms of calamity. One commits the ten evil deeds without awareness or knowledge, inviting ten thousand misfortunes that one must create for oneself and suffer for oneself.
Consequently, heaven rebels and the seasons and things run contrary to principle; harmonious qi is not cultivated within the family.
Virtuous people do not descend upon the land; they do not exhaust themselves in the toil of life within the three realms, nor do they falter within the domain of suffering and its origination.
All persons of this world are bound and fettered within the sphere of the hindrances and entanglements; it is not merely that malevolent planets have descended upon their palaces.
Furthermore, when auspicious stars recede in their courses and wind and dust storms arise frequently, obscuring the sun and moon so they lose their light;
when the planet Mars (Hing-hwok) constantly rises, parching mountains and marshes until they become a single void; or when weapons and conflict erupt repeatedly, causing the common people to perish;

and when calamities and evils arise together, leaving the masses to suffer through turmoil—at such times as these, one must rely on the power of the Buddha to provide silent support and secret protection. Thousand...
Calamities can be forgotten all at once; by relying on the power of the Dharma, they are subtly extinguished and secretly protected, so that myriad evils are unable to invade.
It is like a chronic illness of a thousand days that can still be cured with moxibustion, or various kinds of iron and stone that do not require more than a pinch to dissolve.
Thus we know that Prajñā can protect the nation precisely because it rectifies one's own mind. When the mind is upright, Prajñā resides within me, and [it is able to...]
Protection likewise rests with me. If the mind is not upright, one must rely entirely upon the Prajñā-pāramitā dharma-gate as a great divine power.

If one were to abandon this dharma-gate while wishing to protect the nation, it would be like wishing to cross a river without a boat or oars, or hoping for a harvest without sowing seeds in autumn—is such a thing possible?
Therefore, in the following text, the Buddha clearly and earnestly demonstrates this. △ Second, the formal exposition.
Profound and Subtle. Part Three. First: Admonishing the Audience and Granting Permission to Speak.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit and the other great kings: "Listen attentively, listen attentively!
For your sake, I shall expound the Dharma for protecting the state."
The previous kings, having made their request with the thought, "World-Honored One, you possess great compassion and universally bring benefit and happiness;

how should we, the various kings, protect our kingdoms? thus concluded the section on internal protection. Now, this exhortation to listen permits the teaching of the methods for protecting the kingdom.

Regarding the repeated instruction to "listen attentively": because the divine efficacy of Prajñā is incomparably swift and subtle, it realizes that all phenomena are empty and that their essence and function are void and profound.
Thus, the merit of protecting the nation is likewise not something that can be measured as merely slight; therefore, this admonition is repeated for no other reason than this.
II. Extensive Explanation of the Fundamental Meaning. This has three parts. First, the extensive clarification of protecting the Dharma. This has three parts. First:
The Merit of Protecting the Nation. Fourth. First, regarding the time of protection:
when all lands are about to fall into chaos and encounter various calamities, such as being destroyed by invading enemies.
"All lands" refers to the whole in general. Now, when the single mind is not upright, all affairs fall into neglect;

this is precisely when a hundred wrongs arise and myriad calamities inevitably arrive. At such a time, when virtuous men conceal their brilliance and treacherous flatterers hold the path, how could disorder be avoided?
Therefore it is said: "If one wishes for disorder, [it arises from] water, fire, and wind."
Epidemics are all termed calamities (*āpad*); kings, thieves, and the clash of arms are all termed misfortunes (*vighna*).

Should there be eclipses of the sun or moon, untimely winds and rains, internal rebellions within one’s own realm, or incursions by foreign nations—all these belong to the category of calamities and misfortunes.
If any one of these occurs, what begins as a mere libation of wine ends in a vast deluge; wicked men and treacherous sons will surely seize upon such an opportunity.
They will then cause disturbances. Malevolent ghosts and heterodox deities will also take advantage of this decline to bring about calamity; thus it is said, "When thieves come to destroy.
In such circumstances, were it not for relying on the spiritual power of Prajñā, how could they ever be eliminated? II. The Dharma Capable of Protection. This has three parts.
First, the designation of the dharma and the exhortation to uphold it.
"You kings, you should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā.
All transformations that arise are produced by the mind; therefore, what originates from the mind must likewise cease within the mind. Now, Prajñā is the numinous mind itself.
By receiving and reading this, the numinous mind will not be deluded by worldly dust and afflictions; thus, calamities [will be averted]."
