The affliction naturally dissipates within non-delusion; it is like one who has fallen to the ground rising back up from that very ground—a principle that is certain.
This is the application of medicine and disease in opposition to one another, serving as a method of divine efficacy. Therefore, it is said: "One should regard them as equal.
△ Second, establishing the field of merit.
He adorned the site of enlightenment, arranging one hundred Buddha images, one hundred bodhisattva images, and one hundred lion thrones. He invited one hundred Dharma masters to expound this sutra.
Before each of these seats, he lit various kinds of lamps, burned various kinds of incense, and scattered various flowers.
Extensive offerings—robes, bedding, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, dwellings, seats, and all manner of service—these constitute the adornment of the altar for making offerings to the Sage.
The *do-chang* (place of practice) is the site where the Way is practiced; it symbolizes the ground of the mind (*citta-bhūmi*).
The adornment of the place of practice is simply the purification of the awakened mind. For when the ground of the mind is pure, the world is pure; how much more so this single site?
Regarding the hundred Buddha images: these are the Lord Vairocana, the Benevolent One who Eliminates Calamities, the Guide and Teacher, and so forth.
Regarding the hundred Bodhisattva images: these are the Great Wisdom Mañjuśrī, the Great Practice Samantabhadra, the Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, and so forth.

The reason one must place these within the *maṇḍala* is truly because all Buddhas take the salvation of sentient beings as their primary intent, and the Bodhisattvas take the benefit of others as their purpose.

He is the foundation. If the state faces calamity, the mind’s concern for delivering sentient beings becomes even more urgent; if the people are not at peace, the compassionate vow to benefit others becomes even more expansive.
Thus, when a hundred Buddhas preside over the altar, their divine efficacy is revealed as inconceivable; when Bodhisattvas shed light, their wondrous power is known to be immeasurable.
It is not only that disasters are extinguished and difficulties removed, but it is also able to bring forth blessings and ensure auspicious responses. By means of this—
The True Body is difficult to behold; therefore, physical images are established to manifest a heart of reverence. This is like a crossbow weighing a thousand *jin*:
it hits the mark every hundred times it is fired. It is like the elixir that preserves life: it proves efficacious every ten thousand times it is ingested.

How could these compare to those ghosts and spirits possessed of the three poisons who crave only abundant sacrifices, or to those malevolent essences subject to karmic retribution who derive no benefit from being venerated? [After the hundred masters have finished, they arrange their seats.]
Please perform the exposition. The seat is named "Lion," signifying that the assembly at the place of preaching the Dharma is free from fear.

A Dharma Master is one who serves as a model for humans and devas; in terms of the principles followed by later students, they must possess three qualities: first, to approach the great assembly with solemn deportment;

second, to present the great framework to exhaustively elucidate the great meaning; and third, to possess the eye of the school to demonstrate the objects of contemplation. Thus, one preaches the Dharma.

This also possesses three essential points: first, regarding the pleasant fruits of wholesome karma, one employs gentle and kind speech; second, regarding the painful fruits of unwholesome karma, one employs firm and stern speech;
third, regarding the praise of the good and the censure of the evil, one employs worldly, miscellaneous speech.

Explained in this manner, the wisdom-nature of those who hear it will open and become clear; they will know that karmic conditions arise from the mind, their spiritual consciousness will shine brightly, and they will thoroughly understand the stages of distraction.
This arises from beyond; it is not merely by relying on the Buddha-dharma that calamities are quelled, but rather by observing the numinous mind to ward off misfortune.

The requirement for one hundred seats and one hundred masters is because disasters and afflictions arise in profusion, being the result of karmic inducement over many days and moments, not just a single day or hour.

Thus, if one wishes to bring benefit and fortune to the masses, it cannot be achieved without these one hundred masters and one hundred seats. How much more so, then, regarding the masters themselves?

When a hundred people assemble, precepts and meditative concentration emerge beyond the mundane; they become a fertile field for excellence. Their cultivation and realization approach the realm of the Way, and can they not produce virtuous fruits?
Thereafter, great offerings were made for those below [the assembly]. First, there was the offering of incense, flowers, and lamps.
All acts of offering are fundamentally rooted in the mind. When the mind is sincere and earnest, there is nothing that cannot be provided.
Thus, there are various kinds of lamps, such as lamps with *campaka* oil and the like. To offer lamps is not merely to illuminate and dispel the darkness of ignorance;
it also symbolizes the inexhaustibility of wisdom’s radiance. Furthermore, there are various kinds of incense, such as sandalwood incense.
...and so forth. By offering incense as an act of worship, one not only perfumes away those evil habits, but also symbolizes that the causes of the precepts are inexhaustible.
Furthermore, there are flowers of various colors, such as the *mahāmandārava* flower;

by scattering these flowers as an offering, one not only adorns that which is defiled and impure, but also symbolizes that the causes are wondrous and inconceivable. Therefore, it concludes by stating "vast and great offerings."

This refers to the lamp of the mind, the incense of the mind, and the flower of the mind, used as offerings to the Buddha of the Mind. Who would say that disasters and calamities cannot be extinguished?
Regarding the passage "clothing and so forth," among the four requisites for making offerings to accomplish the work of the Path, nothing precedes the full possession of these four requisites.

In seeking extensively for fields of merit, nothing is more precious than the abundance and excellence of these four requisites; how much more so now, when one seeks the Dharma and restrains disorder, [all] depends on offerings for their elimination.

As for those who perform rites of averting calamity: even if one exhausts all the delicacies of the world, the treasures of the heavens, the finest offerings of the human realm, and provides such sustenance until the end of one's life—even using one’s own body as a seat—it would not constitute a transgression. Thus the sutra says this.

However, if one is stingy with external things and finds it difficult to give them away, or if one is miserly regarding one’s own mind and begrudges expenditure, one will lack the means within oneself to ward off disasters or resist afflictions.

Regarding auxiliary conditions: among people today, there is rarely a constant presence of sincerity and the aspiration for the Way. This is what is meant by "one day of heat followed by ten days of frost.

Is it not likely that one will lack merit? Furthermore, it is a pity that the wondrous response of the Dharma-gate is thus lost in vain. How shameful! △ Third, the difficulty of extinguishing [afflictions] through lecturing and listening.
If twice daily one lectures upon or reads this sutra, and if kings, ministers, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās listen to,
receive, read, and recite it, practicing according to the Dharma, then calamities and disasters shall immediately be extinguished.
The reason one must lecture and recite at two sessions is that this sutra is the true exposition of Prajñā and the sublime method for dispelling calamities.
Since the nature of wisdom is inherently possessed by every person and is never absent for even a moment, one should read and recite this sutra daily, without failing at these two sessions.
In this way, the wheel of Dharma shall be constantly turned and proclaimed even amidst turmoil and disorder.
This is the autumn of [the Dharma]. This boundless field of merit has arisen in an age of decadence.
Thus, to expound and study this sutra is the fundamental principle for rectifying one's own mental faculties and extinguishing the root causes of worldly calamities and chaos.

From the king downward, if the king and his ministers listen and receive [this teaching), it is through the power of the king and ministers that national disasters and difficulties will be quelled; it is through the fourfold assembly that they will be averted.
It is power. Therefore, one should listen to, receive, read, and recite [the Dharma]. However, listening to the Dharma with the spirit constitutes the faculties of the highest vehicle;
listening to the Dharma with the mind likewise constitutes the faculties of the superior vehicle. If one listens to the Dharma with the ears, then the faculties are inferior.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of reading and reciting: it too consists of reading and reciting the sutras with the mind, rather than being read by the sutras.
Recite it. Listen and receive it in this manner; read and recite it in this manner—this is most excellent. By following the Dharma as set forth below, one extinguishes calamities.

Relying on this to make offerings to the Buddha and requesting a teacher to expound it, and relying on this to arrange offerings and listen to its reception, is precisely practicing according to the teaching.
Thus, when light arrives, darkness is dispelled; when wisdom arises, delusion perishes. Therefore, by practicing in reliance upon this, calamities and disasters will immediately [cease].

As for the "Credibility of Extinction," it means that having associated with righteous men for a long time and witnessed their integrity, I venture to transmit these methods based on verified efficacy.
△ Third, the essence of protecting the Dharma: Great King, within all lands there are immeasurable spirits and ghosts, each of whom has immeasurable retinues. If...
Upon hearing this sutra, [it shall] protect your kingdom.
An ancient commentary cites the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-ṛṣi-sūtra* from a foreign land, which states that there are ten fundamental ghosts, each of which is further divided into ten to make one hundred:
first, the Great Deity; second, the Youthful Deity; third, the Mother Deity; fourth, the Brahmā Deity; fifth, the Crane-headed Deity.
Sixth, the dragon spirits (*nāga*); seventh, the asuras; eighth, the *sāra* spirits; ninth, the yakṣas; tenth, the rākṣasas. Based on these, each is further divided into one hundred;
each hundred is divided into one thousand. When linked together, they become infinite in number.

Thus, when the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* has finished reciting the mantra, there are celestial deities, terrestrial spirits, the hundred numinous beings, and ten thousand ghosts who vow to protect and uphold it. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* likewise provides extensive protection.
As for its circulation, there are celestial kings and yakṣas who do not fail to incline their hearts [toward it].
The twelve great yakṣa generals of Bhaiṣajyaguru each have their respective retinues, and they also vow to protect those who uphold this sutra.

This is identical to the meaning of the various ghosts and spirits of the present sutra, along with their retinues, hearing the sutra and protecting the nation. Indeed, the hundred spirits and ghosts each...
Possessing sublime minds, they are able to establish great righteousness. Upon hearing the sutra, each understands their own inherent nature and together receives this profound grace.
Who among them would not protect the state, bring peace to the realm, bless the nation, and aid the people? △ Fourth, manifesting the difficulty of that which is protected; in two parts.
First, it clarifies the six difficulties to be guarded against.
If a country is about to fall into chaos, the ghosts and spirits will first become disordered. Because the ghosts and spirits are disordered, the myriad people immediately fall into disorder.

Robbers shall arise and the common people shall perish. The king, the crown prince, the princes, and the hundred officials will mutually accuse one another, while heaven and earth manifest strange portents.
The sun, moon, and various stars lose their proper times and degrees; great floods, great fires, and great winds—these are the six calamities.
The first two phrases refer to the disturbances caused by ghosts and spirits. Laozi said: "Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
When one presides over the world with the Dao, its ghosts do not manifest their spiritual power. It is not that the ghosts lack spiritual power; it is that their spiritual power does not [manifest].
It harms the people. It is not because their spirits do not harm the people; it is also because the sages do not harm the people.
When neither party harms the other, their virtue is mutually returned. Liezi said that things have no husks or chaff, and ghosts have no spiritual resonance.
As stated in the two preceding accounts, when there is ultimate governance and brilliant clarity, the improper qi that fills the world is entirely melted away without remainder.

Alas! In these times, all at once the Way is obstructed and the world’s path is shrouded in darkness. Thus, ghosts and spirits take advantage of this decline to unleash calamities, and depraved passions exploit this disorder to act as plagues.
This is truly lamentable. Below the section on ghosts and spirits, it is said that bandits and thieves arise like swarms of bees.
Now, when Bai Gui repairs his dykes, he plugs up every hole; when the old man guards against fire, he coats every crack.
Thus, Bai Gui had no difficulty with water, and the old man had no trouble with fire. In both cases, they avoided danger by being cautious regarding what was easy.

This is because one who honors the trivial distances themselves from the great. Laozi said: "When things are secure, they are easy to maintain; when no signs have yet appeared, they are easy to plan for.
Now, ghosts and spirits are in disorder before us, and the masses are in disorder behind us. Furthermore, bandits have arisen and the people are perishing.
Is this not like a golden embankment a thousand *li* long collapsing from the soil of an ant's hole, or like a jade disc of a continuous city bearing a flaw?
This is the first flaw. When discussing causes, one finds that karmic retribution for grievances follows one everywhere and cannot be escaped; thus, there is ruin.

When discussing the evils [of such conduct], each person prizes rare and precious goods, which leads to the day of great loss from excessive hoarding. If this is so, how can the thieves of desire not arise, and how can the people avoid ruin?

From the king below to those above, contradictions have reached their ultimate point. Only when governance is at its most flourishing will there be the union of the enlightened ruler and the virtuous minister.
Joy arises. At such a time, what is called "the administration is obscure, yet the people are simple.
Those above are square but do not cut; they are sharp but do not wound; they are straightforward but do not run wild; they are luminous but do not dazzle.
Those below likewise practice non-action, attend to nothingness, and savor flavorlessness. Fortunately, ruler and minister are now mutually oblivious, as if—

Fish and water are mutually suited to one another. Now, if the wind of valuing profit should rise once more and the source of right and wrong should open again—where those above lack the propriety of governing their subordinates, and those below lack the loyalty of serving their superiors—then they will be like enemies or like strangers to one another.
This would not occur only in times of chaos; when would it occur? Therefore, such mutual accusations of right and wrong arise. Heaven and Earth...
Regarding "mutations and anomalies": this refers to the two polarities reversing their seasons. Now, the position of Heaven is above, and its function is to cover;

the position of Earth is below, and its function is to support. That Heaven and Earth are able to maintain their respective positions above and below, established in their stations without change, is because the participation in and assistance of the transformative harmony depends solely upon the fulfillment of human nature.
Therefore, the *I Ching* says: "The Sage is one with Heaven and Earth..."
The harmony of their virtues is now disturbed by the delusion of the common people regarding their own nature; thus, portents arise from the transformations of Heaven and Earth.
If one seeks that which Laozi described—wherein "Heaven attains unity and becomes clear, and Earth attains unity and becomes tranquil"—how could such a state be achieved?
The *Yinyang Shu* states: "Because the Yang energy is insufficient, Heaven cracks; because the Yin energy is insufficient..."
Therefore, earthquakes occur. For example, during the Yuankang era of Emperor Hui of the Jin dynasty, the heavens split into several sections with a resounding roar.
In the second year of King You of Zhou, the three rivers quaked and Mount Qi collapsed; such are the instances of this kind. As for the two lines concerning the sun and moon:
The three luminaries lose their proper course. The *I Ching* states: "The sage unites his brilliance with that of the sun and moon; he unites his order with that of the four seasons.
If one believes these words, then the sage takes the sun, moon, seasons, and order as his standard.

Thus, the movements of the sun and moon, the orbital positions of the constellations, the waxing and waning that correspond accordingly, and the shifting of the hours and moments cannot be altered. The Buddha said: "Heaven and Earth..."
The sun and moon are the environment of retribution (niśraya-vipāka), brought forth by the collective karma of sentient beings.

It is because living beings have lost their true nature and follow their individual karma that the eternal spiritual luminosity within themselves has become as dark as the long night, and the celestial illumination descending upon the earth has lost its orderly course.
When the summer sun moves southward, the days are long and the heat is intense; in winter...
When the sun moves northward, the days become shorter and the cold intensifies. Regarding the length of these days: sometimes it enters the hour of You (5–7 p.m.

and exits Mao (5–7 a.m.), or it exits Chen (7–9 a.m. and enters Shen (5–7 p.m.). This is also a deviation from the proper measure of the sun. As for the moon, it waxes in the first half of the month and wanes in the second half;
as for the stars, they are arrayed according to fixed laws and appear or disappear according to fixed measures. Now, all of these are contrary to that. Therefore, we know [that this is so].

This is brought about by the disorder of the state. In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, it is said that false perceptions shared by common people include solar and lunar eclipses, halos, comets, rings, crescents, "ears," rainbows, fire-wheels, meteors, and other such calamitous signs among the sun, moon, and stars;
these appear at all times as manifestations induced by the pestilential evils of sentient beings, reaching up to—

With a heart of sacred concern, filled with deep anxiety and silent reflection, [I pray that] you may preserve the imperial destiny for a billion years and offer blessings for the Sage’s longevity for ten thousand years.
This can only be achieved by relying upon the Dharma-gate of Prajñā; only then will there be the wondrous Way to eliminate all calamities. Great!
The first two lines concern water; the latter five lines concern the principles of the Five Elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). The Five Elements can both benefit and harm;
man corresponds to the Five Elements, and thus can also bring about life or death. Therefore, great floods, great fires, and great winds all become disasters. To speak of this by way of illustration:
they cause the various plants to flourish and bring maturity to the hundred grains. All things depend on them for birth, and humanity relies on them for sustenance.

Without water, things wither and dry up; yet when water becomes vast, it overflows rivers and streams, surging across heaven and earth, drowning people and things, and drifting away all existence—who can stem its flow? Such is the water of human wisdom.
It is just like this. When one hits the middle way, it irrigates bodhi and nourishes the spiritual nature, leading directly to the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.
If one misses the middle way even slightly, the water of wisdom becomes the water of craving and attachment;

submerged in the river of torrential currents, one enters directly into the ocean of birth-and-death suffering. There, the raw is transformed into the ripe, and the cold is exchanged for the hot. Yang...
The light permeates and warms; harmonious energy surges forth. Were it not for fire, ice would remain cold and solidified.
Yet when that fire becomes great, it burns down houses and dwellings, scorches the plains and wilds, causes living beings to burst apart, and roasts all manner of things.
Who could save them? Human wisdom-fire is likewise like this. In its state of equilibrium, it burns away delusions.
The firewood matures the seeds of the Path; its radiance reaches directly to the summit of the Peak of Profound Mystery.
Should one lose even a fraction of this levelness, the fire of wisdom becomes the fire of lust and anger, incinerating the wealth of merit and dharma, and burning the seed-nature of Nirvana.
It resonates through the myriad species and fans all things; it is empty yet unbending, moving yet ever-emerging. The power of the wind stirs and inspires it.
It acts like bellows within the space between heaven and earth. Yet, with a single movement of the gale-like wind, it clouds the two polarities of the universe and obscures the three luminaries.
It turbidizes the void and robs it of its luster;

it shakes sentient beings and creatures until they are on the verge of dispersing—not merely causing mountains to collapse and trees to break, nor simply making waves surge and oceans boil. The true wind of the emptiness of human nature is likewise so. Hold fast to this.

Within this very state, welcoming guests and attending to visitors is nothing other than the revolving of the true mechanism; picking up the spoon and raising the chopsticks is entirely the spiritual penetration of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
To lose even a fraction of this truth is for the wind of the True Dharma to transform into the wind of ignorance;
thus it can break down the tree of the Way and stir the source of the mind, causing the waves of the seven consciousnesses to surge upon the power of that wind.
Leaping and revolving, this puppet of the four great elements relies on the power of the wind to stage its illusory performance. It withers the forest of meritorious virtues;
it is solely this single fire of the mind that churns the source of the water of nature. Nor is there any other separate method [to stop it].
Thus we know that the three calamities correspond to karma; wherever one may be, there is no escape. Now, fire, water, and wind are called the "great" [elements].

This is merely a minor matter. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "When sentient beings see the end of the kalpa, when all is consumed by the great fire, my land remains peaceful and secure, ever filled with devas and humans.
This is the vision of one who has realized the ultimate state of the Tathāgata.
Viewed from this perspective, those who wish to escape calamity and avoid disaster, or who seek to prosper their states and protect their nations, cannot do so apart from this.
The wondrous Prajñā has no gate. △ Second, explaining that which can protect Prajñā:
when these various difficulties arise, one should in all cases uphold, recite, and study this Prajñāpāramitā.

When various calamities arise together, one should lecture and recite this present sutra; thus one will know that the essential means for extinguishing calamities does not lie elsewhere than in this ability of Prajñā to protect the state.

Truly, it is like a wondrous elixir that eliminates a hundred ailments, and like a divine wish-fulfilling jewel that responds to every request. Alas! How marvelous is the divine efficacy of Prajñā! △ Two.
To protect and increase the merit of one's blessings:
if one receives, maintains, reads, and recites this sutra, all that is sought—official rank, wealth and abundance, sons and daughters, and wisdom and understanding—shall be attained.
One’s comings and goings will proceed as desired, and the fruits and rewards of humans and devas will all be fully attained.
Becoming exceedingly wealthy and noble, one is able to fulfill the pursuit of official rank and abundance because these are gathered and stored within the Prajñāpāramitā.
A virtuous mind that is sincere and truthful, compassion that is gentle and supple, decisive discernment, and mental realization—all of these are the residual traces of Prajñā;

thus, it is able to respond to the requests for wisdom and understanding from both men and women. Furthermore, the retributions of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions are all cultivated in reliance upon Prajñā;
therefore, one is able to fulfill one's vows regarding the fruits of existence among humans and devas.

This is the fulfillment. The phrase "coming and going according to one's will" means that when one lifts the feet and takes a step, there is nothing that does not accord with one's wishes regarding such karmic fruits and rewards.
