The phrase "possessing the flavors of a hundred rivers" refers to the latter two lines. These clarify that the fruition is perfectly complete and transcends the causal stage;

as the secret treasury of the three virtues (triguṇa) is entirely without deficiency, it is specifically termed "full. Since the state of the Tathāgata’s fruition is inherently and spontaneously accomplished, it is explained in meaning as "abiding."

The so-called three virtues are: first, the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is principle (*tattva*); for it serves as the basis for all meritorious qualities. Second, the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*), which is gnosis (*jñāna*);
for it fully comprehends all causes and effects, and brings about severance and realization. Third, the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*), which is practice (*caryā*);
for it is not bound by the fetters of the three paths of affliction, karma, and birth within the nine realms of the holy and the mundane. These are the three virtues.

To raise one is to manifest three; to speak of three is to manifest one. The three and the one are mutually fused, without mutual obstruction. They are neither vertical nor horizontal; they are neither identical nor separate.
This is like the Tianmu Peak, and like the circular character *ī*: if even one side is missing, it is incomplete. It possesses the three sides and the three circles.
The Buddhas have attained this, whereby they have eternally realized the myriad dharmas; their wondrous functions are as vast as the sands of the Ganges, and their compassion is boundless.
Exhausted. In reality, it is difficult to conceive; thus it is called "the treasury of perfected merit. Regarding the cause:
it is by severing the three paths that the three virtues are revealed. Regarding the fruit: it is by realizing the three virtues that the three bodies manifest. In terms of contemplation:

it is through the perfect cultivation of the contemplations of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle that one perfectly realizes these three virtues. Having thoroughly awakened to the profound source, one suddenly becomes equal to the Buddha.

The realm comes from the path of suchness; it emerges as a true sign of sainthood, manifesting transformations without fixed direction. Therefore, it is said that one "abides in the stage of the Tathāgata.
This is to emulate the footsteps of predecessors, one of the Ten Epithets [of a Buddha]. Reaching this state, one flows against the current and emerges, wondrously identical with all things;
yet this is not yet equal to Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi). Flowing with the current, one has not yet attained the equality of the immeasurable.

The *Ābharaṇa* (瓔珞) says: "Equal Enlightenment is illumination within stillness; Wondrous Enlightenment is stillness within illumination. This is what is meant. △ Third, the summary of the meaning of patience:
"Good son, all these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold, recite, and explain [this teaching] shall all go to the various [lands] in the ten directions."
In the Buddha-fields, they bring benefit and peace to sentient beings and penetrate the true nature of reality; they are equal to me today, without any difference.
Good son, throughout the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm, all Tathāgatas have attained Buddhahood by relying upon this very gate.
If anyone says that one can attain Buddhahood by transcending this, it is the teaching of Māra and not the teaching of the Buddha. Therefore, you all should [practice] accordingly.
This is the knowledge; this is the vision; this is the faith and understanding.
This concluding summary consists of four parts. First, the statement "thus" and so forth refers to the aforementioned practice of the thirteen contemplations.
"Receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting" refers to matters for one's own benefit. "Wandering through lands and manifesting birth" refers to benefiting others.
However, the very nature of words is emptiness, which is itself Prajñā. Thus, it causes those who hear it to penetrate the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Cause and effect share the same path; self and other are non-dual. Since our Buddha has expounded this in this world, the Bodhisattvas have resolutely proclaimed it throughout the ten directions.
This is truly because Prajñā pervades all realms and has never been concealed; there is no one who does not possess it in full.
Because there is no time when one can be separated from it. From "In the ten directions" onwards, it is said that the attainment of Buddhahood follows the same track.
This is because Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of all Buddhas. Furthermore, it is because all worthies and sages possess their distinctions by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Now, since the unconditioned is precisely the wondrous wisdom of Prajñā, it enables all Buddhas to attain Buddhahood by relying upon this very gateway.

Listen! If one speaks thus, one distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox. That is to say, the correct cultivation of *prajñā* is the swift vessel for exiting the sea of suffering and the level path for entering bodhi.
Heterodox teachings deviate from its gateway, whereas orthodox teachings open its bridges and causeways.
Those who enter the profound purport of *prajñā* possess this eye of the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-cakṣus*) in a hidden manner; thus, they may hope not to err in their practice.

Therefore, below, I shall exert effort to instruct you so that you may know: to know, see, and resolve with faith by relying on Prajñā is what constitutes true knowledge, true vision, and pure, singular faith and understanding.
Apart from this, there is only deluded knowledge, heterodox views, and petty faith or partial understanding.
Thus, you should strive in this; let your resolve not falter. △ Second, the repeated verses in praise. This has two parts. First, the general [summary].
The Verse on the Stage of Submissive Patience (Kṣānti):
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva of Submissive Patience Nurtures the Buddha-dharma And makes the thirty minds firm and solid."

The first line, titled "Non-retrogression," provides a general verse for the three stages of the Ordinary Beings (*pṛthagjana*), because they all rely upon the same single patience (*kṣānti*). The subsequent three lines provide verses for the cultivation of the practices of the three stages of the Ordinary Beings:

by giving rise to the ten minds during the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), one nurtures the holy embryo; by practicing the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) during the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), one gives rise to... [the ten transferences].
The antidotes, the ten dedications, the cultivation of the ten dedications, and the arising of the ten kinds of patient acceptance are all for the purpose of reaching the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*).

Having reached the noble stages, they are called "non-retrogressive. All of these verses summarize the meaning of the preceding long prose section; the subsequent parts should be understood accordingly.
△ Second, the separate verses on the four patiences. Eleven [verses]. The first verse concerns the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Having first realized the nature of equality, one is born into the family of the Buddhas;
because of this initial awakening, it is called the Stage of Joy.

The first line of the verse praises the internal realization of *tathatā* (suchness). The second line praises the transcending of the stage of ordinary beings (*bālabhūmi*) and being born into the family of the Buddhas;
because one accords with the principle and is identical to suchness, it is figuratively said that one is "born. The third line praises the wisdom of abandonment and realization.
The fourth line concludes the title as in the text; subsequent lines should be understood by analogy. △ Second, the verse on the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
Far removed from defilements, Such as the various stains of hatred and the like, Possessing the precepts and attaining purity—this is called the Ground of Freedom from Stain (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

The first three lines of this verse describe the abandonment of the habitual tendencies of hatred and so forth, and the cultivation of the ten wholesome paths of action and other practices. △ Third, the verse on the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākari-bhūmi*):
Having extinguished the darkness of ignorance, one attains the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*). The illumination proceeds from the light of wisdom;
this is called the Ground of Emitting Light (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

The first line of the verse praises the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*); because it is obscured by ignorance, one is deluded regarding the three periods of time. The second line praises the eight meditative absorptions. Third...

The verses praise the three types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*), the births within the eight meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and [their attainment] by means of sublime wisdom. 4. Verses on the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
Pure Factors of Enlightenment: Far removed from the view of a self and the view of [extreme] existence, With the flames of wisdom blazing intensely, it is named the Stage of Blazing Wisdom.

The first line of the verse praises the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharma*). The second line praises the permanent abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and other such views.
The third and fourth lines together conclude both the name and the meaning [of this stage]. △ Fifth, the verse praises the Difficult-to-Conquer Stage (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
Knowing the truths as they truly are, And all the various worldly arts and crafts, To benefit sentient beings in manifold ways— This is called the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*).
The first line refers to the Four Truths and the Two Truths. The second line praises the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) and their various treatises. The third [line]...
The verse on the phrase "merely not causing harm or affliction to sentient beings," etc. 6. The Verse on the Present Stage (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*):
Observing the dharma of dependent origination, From ignorance through to old age and death— One who can realize its profound depth Is named the Present Stage.
The first two lines of the verse praise the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

The third line praises the preceding passage beginning with "all [arise] from attachment to a self" up to "because they are non-dual," etc. △ Seventh, the verse on the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).

The first line of the verse, "The samādhi of skillful means manifests immeasurable bodies, skillfully responding to all sentient beings," refers to the passage concerning abiding in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth.
The second line of the verse refers to the passage concerning manifesting entry [into the paths] of the śrāvakas and so forth. The third...
The verses on conforming to the world, etc. △ Eighth: The Ground of Immovability.
Abiding in the ocean of signlessness, sustained by the empowerment of all Buddhas, one who possesses mastery in destroying the armies of Māra is named the Ground of Immovability.

The first line of the verse corresponds to the text on severing all functional efforts (*prayoga*). The second line corresponds to the text on the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas due to fundamental vows.
The third line corresponds to the text on destroying the demonic hosts who are unwilling to benefit sentient beings;
because they retreat without being subdued by the excellence of the great vow, it is called "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*). △ Ninth, the verse on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

Attaining the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), preaching everything with a single sound, and causing all who hear it to rejoice—this is called the stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*).
The first line of the verse concerns the attainment of the analytical knowledges and so forth; the second and third lines concern a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). By means of...
The section on the single voice explaining questions and difficulties, etc.

**Ten Verses on the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma:** Wisdom is like a dense cloud, Pervading the entire dharma-realm; Universally sprinkling the nectar of the Dharma— This is called the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma.

The first three lines of the verse describe a single moment of thought, continuing until it says, "He expounds the Three Vehicles, universally causing them to cultivate the *pāramitās*," and so forth.
This is because the clouds of wisdom contain moisture that pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, and thus the rain of Dharma falls everywhere.
△ The eleventh verse describes the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
Fulfilling the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), it is the eternally pure body of liberation. This state of quiescence and inconceivability is called the "all-knowing one's untainted realm.
It is the perfect severance of the three delusions, a singular purity, and the inexhaustible merit that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, this verse praises the three virtues because they are identical in being untainted (*anāsrava*). Two lines of the verse praise the perfection of the three bodies:
"Eternal" refers to the Dharma-body; "Pure" refers to the Reward-body; and "Liberated" refers to the Transformation-body.

Three lines of the verse praise the passage on being equal to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for the limit of reality is quiescent and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inconceivable. II. Specifically Exhorting to Uphold and Maintain (four parts). First:

Encouraging the Upholding for the Protection of the Nation. Part Two. First, a brief praise of the difficulty of the time. Section Four. First, citing the extinction [of the Dharma] to encourage its upholding.
The Buddha addressed King Prasenajit: "After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is about to perish..."

The preceding section clearly elucidated upholding [the teaching], manifesting practice based upon the *prajñāpāramitā*. Now, by separately exhorting one to uphold it, the text directly clarifies that the wondrous benefits of *prajñā* are inexhaustible.
First, it calls out those who are such as this to clarify that a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter.

This serves to encourage firm faith. Yet, while the Buddha was in the world, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) flourished. Once he manifested the conditions for his parinirvāṇa, the Dharma declined, causing gods and humans to grieve and sentient beings to suffer greatly.
Question: The teachings state that the True Dharma lasts for one thousand years; with the ordination of nuns, it is reduced by five hundred years.

The Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) lasts for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma (*paścimadharma*) lasts for ten thousand years. Does this statement regarding the extinction of the Dharma refer to [the end of] the True Dharma, or...?
"Is it during the ten thousand years of the Dharma-ending age? He replied, "It is indeed as you have said. When the Buddha-dharma first flourished, many attained liberation;

the four aspects of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit were all fully present. By the time of the Semblance Dharma (Sāṃketika-dharma), although there was much cultivation of practice, those who achieved realization were few.

In the Dharma-ending age, however, strife and contention become entrenched and things become hollow and unsubstantial; though the teachings and principles still exist, they are regarded [as mere words]."
To paint a cake is a premonitory sign of the extinction of the Dharma. Who will enter the gateway of the Dharma to believe, accept, and practice it?

Therefore, know that the extinction of the Dharma occurs because of the karmic conditions of sentient beings; they are like the blind who do not see the sun, and thus claim that the sun does not exist.
How could it be said that [emptiness] is truly non-existent? △ Second, clarifying the power and function of Prajñā:
Because all sentient beings create evil karma, various calamities arise in all lands. The kings and others...

To protect oneself, as well as princes, crown princes, queens, consorts, and their retinues, the hundred officials, the common people, and the entire kingdom, one should immediately uphold this Prajñāpāramitā; thus, all shall attain peace and happiness.
The Buddha taught all dharmas in order to deliver all minds. If there were no such minds, why would he have taught all these dharmas?
Now that the True Dharma is about to perish, it is precisely a time when the multitudes of sentient beings are lost in confusion and darkness.
Thus, they construct similar karmic actions, and consequently, such calamitous signs are summoned and manifested. How could one wish for various disasters not to arise? Is this possible?
It is said that when a Buddha dwells in the world, the dragons and devas rejoice; when there is no Sangha to preach the Dharma, the ghosts and spirits grieve.

As for the King—noble as the Son of Heaven and possessing the wealth of the four seas—his person is as precious as jade, his divine mandate is of vital concern, the state and its altars depend upon him, and the billions of subjects look up to him in reliance. Therefore, when encountering calamity, he must necessarily protect [the Sangha] alone.
This is the most essential point. However, as for the method of protection and peace, the Prajñā-pāramitā dharma-gate alone is supreme.

Therefore, it says, "one should immediately receive and uphold [this]," and so forth. Indeed, this dharma-gate, when obscured by delusion, causes the worldly path to become inverted and human life to be without reliance;
yet, through receiving and upholding it, the inner mind becomes upright and external calamities are secretly extinguished. △ Third, the explanation of the entrustment.
For this reason, I entrust this sutra to kings, and not to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. Why is that?
Lacking royal power, they would be unable to establish it.
However, the reason this sutra is entrusted to the king is that the strength of the fourfold assembly is frail and the ways of the world are corrupt;
thus, one must rely solely upon the king so that worldly transformation and Buddhist transformation may shine together, and the sun of the Buddha and the sun of Shun may remain ever bright.

Moreover, the words of a king are like a single strand of silk, yet when they issue forth, they become a thick cord; when subjects and citizens behold such an example, who would not reform their hearts and turn toward the Dharma?
How truly it is like grass bending before the wind! Thus it is said that without the sovereign’s majestic power, [the Dharma] cannot be established.
An ancient text records the Imperial Edict of Emperor Taizong of the Tang Dynasty concerning the *Buddhabhāṣita-śeṣa-dharma-paryāya-sūtra*, which states:

"As for the Dharma, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, because the final age (*mofa*) is turbid and frivolous, [the Buddha] entrusted its protection and maintenance to kings, ministers, and the Sangha. However, as for the monks...

When a nun leaves the household life, she must be fully equipped with the precepts and conduct. If she indulges her passions and engages in licentiousness, she will encounter afflictions at every turn;

by involving herself in worldly affairs, she will constantly violate the sūtras and the vinaya. Thus, she not only loses the profound and subtle intent of the Tathāgata but also fails in the duty of upholding the King’s entrustment.
The *Śāsanānuśāsana Sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching) was spoken by the Buddha as he approached his parinirvāṇa to admonish and exhort his disciples; it is most [important].

Examining the essential points of the final age, both the laity and the monastic community do not revere [the teachings]. The Great Way is about to be obscured, and the subtle words are on the verge of being lost.

Cherishing the holy teachings in my heart, I intend to propagate them extensively. It is fitting that the relevant authorities dispatch ten scribes to transcribe many copies of the scriptures, with the primary goal being their practical implementation.
The necessary paper, brushes, and ink shall be provided by the authorities accordingly. As for the five ranks of officials...
Copies of one fascicle each shall be distributed to those of the fifth rank and above, as well as to the Provincial Governors (Cishi).

If you observe that the conduct of monks and nuns does not accord with the text of this scripture, you should encourage them through both public and private means to ensure they surely follow its teachings. Based on this, the *Bequeathed Teaching* concludes.

The exhortation to the monks and nuns is that this [edict] should be promulgated throughout the empire for all to follow. Moreover, as these scriptures now serve to protect the state and preserve the people, their significance is vast and profound;
it cannot be fully expressed in words, and its ramifications are so extensive that they exceed the power of any individual to sustain.

At such a time, if the Son of Heaven, who embodies the Buddha-mind, upholds and practices them, ensuring they are known by every family and household, then perhaps their merit may provide unseen support.
The seas are tranquil and the rivers clear, bringing silent benefit; ministers are loyal and sons are filial, so that the mandate of the state may endure for long.
May it last as long as heaven and earth, with the ancestral altars firmly established;
may it shine as brightly as the sun and moon. Alas, that it once sank into the dragon treasury and has not yet been widely disseminated!
What, indeed, is the reason for this? △ Fourth, the specific entrustment to King Prasenajit:
"Therefore, you all should constantly receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and disseminate [this teaching].
When the Dharma perishes and calamities arrive, rely upon this to protect the nation. Since its circulation truly depends upon the king, it is fitting that you do so firmly."

Because King Bimbisāra received, upheld, read, and recited [this teaching], it was separately compiled and entrusted to him with such exhortations. △ Second, the extensive praise of various difficulties has four parts;
first, the heading indicating that merit arises from removing difficulties.
"Great King, the great trichiliocosm that I have now transformed consists of ten billion Mount Sumerus and ten billion suns and moons.
On each Mount Sumeru there are four continents, and within this Jambudvīpa continent there are sixteen great nations, five hundred intermediate nations, and one hundred thousand minor nations.
In all these nations, should the seven calamities arise, may all the kings, for the sake of eliminating those calamities, receive and uphold [this teaching]."
When this Prajñāpāramitā is explained, the seven calamities are immediately extinguished and the land becomes peaceful and happy.

The text consists of two sections: first, a general indication of the trichiliocosm; second, a specific clarification concerning Jambudvīpa. Within the section on Jambudvīpa, there are three further parts.

First, the various countries are listed. Second, "these [beings] below" lists those who are difficult to enumerate. Third, from "all" onwards, it clarifies that the benefit of the Dharma is universal;

this is to be understood according to the text. The "trichiliocosm" is the realm where the Tathāgata transforms beings through his sovereign power; hence it says, "that which I now transform. The rest is as explained previously.
However, the reason for specifically clarifying Jambudvīpa is that the Buddha manifested his birth in this world, and furthermore, it is where he is seen.

Because it is heard that this is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* clarifies that within these [continents] there are three thousand small continents and eight hundred large continents.
Among these various continents, some contain one thousand kingdoms, some five hundred kingdoms, and so on, down to even one or two;
therefore, the present enumeration of kingdoms includes the three categories of large, medium, and small, as well as numerous others. Based on this:
Thus, the Middle Kingdom within the great chiliocosm is no more than a minute speck of dust;
within Jambudvīpa, it is no more than a single grain of rice in a vast granary. Truly, the world is boundless! That which lies beyond the six realms is set aside and not spoken of;
yet for the Sage, he has indeed integrated it all and spoken of it secretly to the people of the world. △ Second.
The detailed explanation is found in the *Prasādapratibhodbhava-vaipulya-sūtra* (Bie wenda). Second: First, King Prasenajit’s inquiry.
King Prasenajit said: "What are the seven calamities?
Previously it was said that if the seven calamities arise, they are immediately extinguished. This only indicated their names; it has not yet been explained in detail."
What is its other name? Therefore, I now inquire about it. This is because one who exhausts the waters must seek their source, and one who climbs a mountain must ascend to its peak.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s response. Part three: First, a brief explanation of the seven calamities. Seven [subsections]:
First, the sun and moon losing their proper course.
The Buddha said: "First, the sun and moon lose their regular course; the color of the sun changes, appearing white, red, yellow, or black;
sometimes two, three, four, or five suns shine simultaneously; the color of the moon changes, appearing red or yellow; and the sun and moon undergo eclipses."
There are those with multiple wheels; one, two, three, four, or five concentric wheels appear.
The *Shu* (Book of Documents) states that the celestial sphere consists of three hundred and sixty-five degrees, plus a quarter of a degree.

Therefore, the sun and moon move day and night without ceasing, each having its own specific measure. Although the duration of the days and seasons differs across the four quarters, [the cycle remains constant].
All [the celestial bodies] complete one circuit of the heavens in a single day; there is not even the slightest discrepancy. Thus, the ancients said:

"When it is midnight at the northern continent, it is midday at the southern continent. Is this statement not indeed the true explanation of the celestial bodies following their courses through the heavens?
According to the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra*, the two palaces of the sun and moon are composed of fire and water-crystal respectively; by this standard, the sun is purely of the nature of fire.
Red is fire; the moon is purely water, and its white light is its true nature. Thus, the proverb says: "The true fire of the sun roasts humanity.
Furthermore, a poem states: "Ascending the tower to gaze at the moon, its cold radiance flows on. This now speaks of transformation and impermanence.
In that case, the nature of form would not be its true state. Master Ziyu said: "Heaven has no two suns, and the people have no two kings.
Now, to say that the sun and moon appear with multiple wheels and in layers is to create confusion regarding their sovereign authority. It is the same for the moon. As the *Shijing* says:
"The eclipsing of the sun and moon is a most grievous shame. Now, to speak of the sun and moon being eclipsed is likewise a great calamity. However...
In the *Waishi* (Annals of the Outer Court), the term for an eclipse (*she*) is consistently written as "to devour" (*shi*). Thus, the commentary by Chang Zhao states:
"When a vapor presses against [the sun or moon], it is called 'thinning' (*bu*); when they are impaired or destroyed, it is called 'devouring' (*shi*).

That this must be considered difficult is because the Sage harmonizes his brilliance with the sun and moon and his order with the four seasons; that they now lose their measure and undergo such changes is the reversal of Heaven.
At that time, it was difficult because he responded to people's minds with principles that were contrary [to reason]. △ Second, the loss of the constellations' proper courses.
Second, regarding the loss of the constellations' proper courses: comets, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, Saturn, and all other such stars.
Each undergoes its own transformations, sometimes appearing during the day.
The constellations are suspended as images in the heavens, each presiding over its own domain. Within the Ziwai (Purple Micro) Enclosure, the central image symbolizes the virtue of the sovereign;
thus the Sage said: "It is like the North Star, which dwells in its place while the myriad stars revolve around it. Furthermore, there are twenty-eight...
The constellations (xiù) grasp the coordinates of the four quarters; each has its own astrological division (fēnyě), presiding over and illuminating specific phenomena and affairs.

This is clearly evidenced in the *Móṅgēnǚ Jīng* (Sūtra of the Woman of the Matanga Clan). Therefore, if the numerical calculations are even slightly off, calamities will immediately manifest. As for the comet (huìxīng):
Its shape is like that of a broom; it should remain hidden and must not be revealed. It corresponds to the five stars and governs the principles of the Five Elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*).

When its course is regular, there is auspiciousness; when it undergoes change, misfortune follows. As for its appearance during the day, this is a great omen of ill fortune; therefore, both conditions are considered calamitous.

For example, when the human mind moves toward either anger or joy, then depression or exultation follows accordingly. How much more so in the Way of Heaven, where responses are triggered by what is contrary to principle;
how could calamities, shifts in the seasons, and changes in the luminaries not manifest in alternating succession?

Therefore, one should know that when such events occur in the present, one should uphold this sutra, or the *Mayūra-vyamsaka-sūtra*, or the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* to pray for protection. There will be no thought that is not answered, and [calamities] will be secretly dispelled.
This refers to a time when the night is dark and gloomy, and the sunlight has faded so that only the stars remain, with their positions roughly distinguished as north and south.
As soon as the bright sun appears, the starlight naturally subsides; this is indeed brought about by the power of the mantra. △ Third, the difficulty of the four great fires arising.
Third, there are the fires of dragons and ghosts, the fires of humans and trees; great fires break out on all four sides, incinerating all things.
Although dragons govern water, there are also fire-dragons that preside over fire. Ghost-fire refers to the fire-spirits who preside over the department of fire and manifest calamities.
Human-fire refers to those who bring harm by seizing upon decay and slaughter. Tree-fire arises when aged trees produce flames.
Alternatively, after a long time, malevolent spirits may take up residence, or they may manifest as calamities due to social upheaval and disorder. When four fires converge, they arise suddenly;
they cannot be saved by human effort, and thus it is said they "arise from the four directions. They spread like creeping vines and erupt with explosive violence, burning and scorching without end;
thus it is said they "incinerate the myriad things. In reality, these correspond to the two fires of anger and desire within the human mind.
This refers to transformation through resonance. Otherwise, the four fires would have no basis from which they could arise. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Just as when the elder had barely gone out, fires broke out on all four sides," which is like sentient beings who, in the absence of a Buddha, are simultaneously oppressed by the four sufferings.
According to the *Sou Shen Ji*, during the Three Kingdoms period, Mi Fang served Emperor Yinglie while he was still a hidden dragon; at that time, he was...
Kun was ordered to go to Fengdong Province to seek assistance. Since Feng was a man from the eastern region, Kun took him along.
Receiving the command, Kun traveled by carriage and encountered a woman of beautiful appearance who wished to share the vehicle. Kun granted her request.

Once they were riding together, Kun focused solely on her beauty and voice without being improper, maintaining his self-restraint through propriety alone. After a short while, the woman wished to depart, but Kun earnestly entreated her to stay once more.
She departed. She also felt pity for him. The woman said to Fang, "I am not a human being; I am a deity of the Fire Department.

Your past karma was predetermined, and the High God has assigned you to the household of the Fire Lord. Seeing that your conduct and righteousness are no ordinary, I have come specifically to inform you in advance.
You must act with haste to move all the property in your house. I shall [depart] on such-and-such a day."
"The time has come; I shall simply burn that empty house. This is the decree of the High God, which I dare not disobey.

When Fang returned home, it was indeed exactly as he had said, without error. Based on this, it can be seen that Fang’s merit in his present life spared him from the karmic retribution of his previous cruel deeds.
Otherwise, a single fire would have reduced both the jade and the stone to ashes, leaving both wealth and house in ruins. Now...
If one observes such calamities caused by the planet Mars (Māhendra), it is appropriate either to seek personal exemption through virtue or to rely on the sūtras to pray for their cessation;
this should be recorded. △ Fourth, the alteration of the seasons.
Fourth, the seasons have changed; cold and heat are no longer constant. Rain falls in winter with thunder and lightning; frost, ice, and snow fall in summer.
Mountains of earth and stone, as well as sand and gravel, rain down. Hail falls out of season. Red and black water rains down, and rivers overflow their banks, carrying stones and floating mountains.
The waxing and waning of Yin and Yang cause cold and heat to alternate; thus, following the stage of pure Yang, a single Yin line arises below to form Tianfeng Gou (Wind over Heaven);
following the stage of pure Yin, a single Yang line arises below to form Didun Fu (Thunder under Earth).
As for the principle that Zhen gives rise to Yuan, and Tai is seen before Lin—this is the immutable law of change. Now, however, both have become the reverse; therefore...

The three seasons have lost their order; the timing is no longer constant. In winter, all things hibernate and conceal themselves, and the Yin energy is cold and harsh—this is the time when thunder withdraws and lightning rolls up.
In summer, the hundred grains flourish and grow luxuriantly, and the Yang light is warm and steaming—this is the time when ice melts and thunder falls.
Now, everything is the reverse of this, further manifesting that the seasonal order of cold and heat has become disordered.
In antiquity, there was a master of the lute whose slightest movement of sound revealed inexhaustible subtle functions. Thus, by striking the note of *shang*, he could turn spring into autumn;
by caressing the resonance of *jiao*, he could change cold into warmth. This was merely the lingering sound of the *Tai-xuan* at a particular moment, reaching the sublime realm of manual skill;
yet even such a thing was not the constant order of the Way of Heaven. If it can effect such transformations, how much more so...
Human sentiments fluctuate between warmth and cold; the conditions of the world are unpredictable, ranging from misery to comfort.

Since causes inevitably summon their corresponding effects, what is there to wonder at in the seasonal cycles losing their regularity? Earth, stones, sand, and gravel descend as a result of the arrogance, greed, and anger of sentient beings.

The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states: "When yang reaches its extreme and yin becomes excessive, they clash and transform into hail. To pour down out of season is a transgression of the times that harms things;
it is truly a portentous calamity. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The Dragon King rains in a mere instant, moistening and refreshing all under heaven."
It is said that clear water is appropriate; this is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of people in the world today. Now, that red and black water falls is truly an anomaly and contrary to the Way.
Formerly, when the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng, the Lord of Yuechang came from afar to present tribute.
When the Duke asked for the reason, he replied: "For three years within, the sea has not stirred its waves. From this, it was known that there was [disturbance] in the Central Kingdom.
Because a Sage has appeared, it is now said that the waters have overflowed and the waves surge; thus, the rivers, streams, mountains, and rocks no longer present an image of stability.
Yet, if one wishes to extinguish this calamity, one must be like Yao who obtained the five ministers of Shun, whereby the water disasters of the Nine Provinces were naturally pacified;
or like Tang who cultivated the six matters of self-reproach, whereby the drought-demon was finally quelled after seven years. Furthermore, [one must rely on] the divine power of Prajñā.

Power. There is nothing that cannot be bestowed. Not so. When Yao’s ox gored the sun and Tang’s dog barked at the clouds, although these were indeed times of great peace and prosperity, they were still like flaws within jade. △ Fifth: The violent winds strike repeatedly.
Fifth, violent winds arise frequently, obscuring the sun and moon, tearing down houses, uprooting trees, and scattering sand and stones.

Heaven has four seasons, and the wind likewise changes according to the four times: thus, in spring there is the "harmonious wind" (*huafeng*); in summer, the "pervading wind" (*xunfeng*); in autumn, it is named the "metal wind" (*jin feng*);
and in winter, it is called the "northern wind" (*shuofeng*). The winds that are now described as violent do not follow these seasonal rhythms.

This is the wind [of calamity], for Heaven responds to the human heart through transformations. When even a single degree of cold offends the human heart, how much more so when such occurrences arise repeatedly?
That it darkens the sun and moon is the calamitous omen of obscuring the Three Luminaries;

that it uproots houses and trees is the calamitous omen of striking terror into the myriad people; and that it whirls sand and hurls stones is the calamitous omen of agitating the ten thousand species.
It is like an elephant. However, this too arises with the wind of sentient beings' ignorance as its root and the eight winds as its auxiliary conditions, causing the ocean of the mind to surge.

When praise and blame exceed reality, and honor and disparagement are inappropriate, and gain and loss are indifferent, these calamities arise from the winds because suffering and pleasure do not accord with the Way.
Therefore, one must employ the divine, wondrous, and truly substantial mind of Prajñā.
This is to bring it to rest. △ Sixth, the heavens and earth suffer from excessive drought.
Regarding the sixth: when the heavens and earth suffer from excessive drought, ponds and reservoirs dry up, grasses and trees wither and die, and the hundred grains fail to ripen.
When yin and yang are in harmony, rain and sunshine occur at their proper times; this is the era of Great Peace, which is characterized by the absence of specific signs.

When heaven and earth do not interact, moistening and nourishment remain forever stagnant; thus, the myriad waters suffer the misery of sudden exhaustion, and the hundred grains never reach the autumn of harvest.

To deliberate upon the source of this, it all originates from the fire of anger within the human heart, which is more severe than the drought-demon and its flames more poisonous than the scorching sun.
Day by day, it burns away the seeds of Bodhi and withers the grove of merit. Though the waters of wisdom are vast and expansive, the celestial nectar has not emerged for kalpas on end.
Why, then, would it fail to arrive at its appointed time? "Pō" (陂) also refers to a pond.
This is the place where water is stored. △ Seventh, bandits swarm like bees. Seventh:
bandits come from the four directions to invade the domestic and foreign territories; weapons and war break out in competition, and the common people perish.

Celestial calamities and human transformations rely upon one another; thus, while great disasters manifest above, human affairs undergo transformation below as rebellions arise like swarms of bees—hence it is said that "thieves come from the four quarters.
When treacherous slander secretly permeates, it is said that "the country and the capital are invaded.
Yet, when soldiers and farmers remain in the fields, the common people enjoy the joy of resting on their pillows and singing songs; [to] drive the people [away from this]...
As for warfare, the common people suffer the bitterness of displacement and death;

therefore, it is further said that regarding weapons and the like, whoever encounters such calamitous cycles of destiny is merely reaping what they have sown themselves. How could Heaven bestow these upon them?
△ Second, the summary of their immeasurability.
"Great King, I have now briefly described these various calamities: when the sun does not appear by day, or the moon does not appear by night;

when there are various celestial portents, such as rain and snow falling without clouds; and when there are various terrestrial calamities, such as the earth splitting, shaking, or even flowing with blood."
Spirits and deities appear; birds and beasts become strange and anomalous. Such calamities are immeasurable and boundless.

The first two lines conclude what preceded; the nine lines beginning with "Those who have" point to the detailed exposition; the final two lines beginning with "In this way" provide the general conclusion.
The sun and moon are symbols of the sovereign. As previously stated, that many disks appear with many colors and undergo changes may still be considered tolerable.
But now it is said they do not appear by day and do not appear by night—how can one even speak of such a calamity? Regarding the four lines beginning with "The celestial seeds":

in each case, the first line provides the general description and the second line provides the specific detail. That snow and rain do not occur, and the clouds are perpetually obscured—this is the calamity of Heaven.
The portents of elephants are manifold. Mountains and rivers tremble; cliffs and trees collapse and split—these are the manifold calamitous signs of this land.

Water turns crimson and flows like blood; this is a portent of slaughter and destruction. Ghosts and spirits appear, such as malevolent ghosts raising spears or malefic deities interfering with the righteous.
Birds and beasts act strangely, such as flying squirrels calling out to people or the *shāngyáng* bird.
These are those who dance upon water. All such phenomena are portents of calamity that correspond to an era of misfortune and adversity;

therefore, one must cultivate divine remedies to pacify them, which rely solely on the power of the Buddha and the power of the Dharma. Thus, the following clarifies this point. △ Third, exhorting the holding of the sutra.
Whenever each individual calamity arises, one must uphold, recite, and explain this Prajñāpāramitā.

The preceding section clarified that when disasters and hardships gather like bristles, the causes for their arising lie in the neglect and dust-covered state of the Prajñāpāramitā; therefore, one should [act accordingly] when these various calamities arrive.
One should practice with a single-minded focus; this is indeed Prajñā.

To be deluded by it results in the failure to comprehend the three minds, the proliferation of a hundred delusions, the induction of manifold karma, and the arrival of ten thousand calamities like gathering clouds.

To awaken to it results in the purity of one's inner mind, the concealment of malevolent spirits, the harmony of the Way of Heaven, and the auspicious response of human affairs. It is like a single ingredient in an immortal’s elixir: even a chronic ailment can be cured.
"How peaceful! Like a timely rain falling in a single morning, all that is withered and parched is moistened. How wondrous is Prajñā! How supreme is its divine efficacy!
To protect the state and the people, and to eliminate calamities and quell misfortunes—if one sets this aside, where else could one turn? △ Third, the various kings ask in astonishment.
At that time, the sixteen kings, having heard what the Buddha had said, were all struck with alarm and fear. King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, for what reason have such calamities occurred in heaven and earth?"

The seven calamities are impermanent; thus, when the various kings heard of them, they were struck with alarm and fear. Since these calamities do not arise without cause, this king asked, "For what reason?
This was also a question posed through skillful means, as he already knew the answer, desiring to cause all to understand their source.
△ Fourth, the Buddha answers regarding the causes.
The Buddha said, "Great King, it is because the people throughout all the large and small kingdoms and towns of Jambudvīpa are unfilial toward their parents,
disrespectful toward their teachers and elders, and do not practice the True Dharma toward śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kings, and ministers;
due to these various evils, such calamities arise."
The single mind is the paradigm for all phenomena. Therefore, karmic causes arise from the mind; thus, when retributive fruits manifest, there are none that do not correspond to the mind.
This is what is meant by the saying that blessings and calamities never fail to accord with their causes, following one another like a shadow follows a form.
Though beauty and ugliness differ, they do not exist apart from a single mirror. Hence it is said: "From the continent of Jambudvīpa... and so forth, referring to the various large and small lands.
This refers to the three grades of lands. "All the people" is a general designation for those who create karma.
"Disobedience toward parents," and so forth, clarifies the characteristics of the actions performed. Filial piety is the eternal law of heaven and earth, the supreme virtue and essential path.

While the applications of the five types of filial piety differ, the source of all hundredfold practices is not distinct. When the heart moves heaven and earth, sincerity stirs the ghosts and spirits.

If one abandons filial piety, how can one attain [the Way]? A poem says: "The virtue of one's parents is as vast as the great heavens and has no limit. Therefore, lack of filial piety invites calamity.
As for teachers and elders, they nurture the holy embryo and reveal the path to those who are lost. As it is said: "Those who gave birth to me are my parents;
those who perfected my virtue are my teachers. How could one not revere them? As for a śramaṇa, he diligently cultivates the Way.
Regarding karma: those who seek transcendence are the *brāhmaṇas*, who thus dwell in the ground of goodness.
Those whose hearts aspire to the profound abyss of goodness are the kings, who are as sons of Heaven and as sovereigns of the people, providing a vast and boundless canopy of protection.

The great ministers assist the world and its leaders, harmonizing the cauldron of state affairs and uplifting the common people. Therefore, if one is unfilial or disloyal, the fundamental root is deficient.
If one lacks reverence and respect for the deceased, then the eternal patterns of human relations will be destroyed. There are two kinds of orthodox Dharma:
first, the orthodox Dharma of a nation, which consists of rewards and punishments, granting and revoking, and is characterized by benevolent heart and benevolent governance;

second, the orthodox Dharma of the Buddha, which consists of knowing causes, recognizing conditions, clarifying the mind, and realizing the fundamental source. If either of these two is lacking, then both the worldly and world-transcending Dharmas will fail.
It would be abandoned. Therefore, the conclusion states: "From these various evils, such difficulties arise. How could they be falsely summoned as fruits without a cause?
△ Second, praising the name and exhorting its upholding. This has two parts. First, praising the excellence of the name. This has three parts. First, praising its virtue by way of the Dharma.
"Great King, the Prajñāpāramitā is able to give birth to all Buddhas, the liberating dharmas of all Bodhisattvas,
the unsurpassed dharmas of all kings, and the dharmas of deliverance for all sentient beings."
Laozi said: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows; it is empty yet inexhaustible, moving and ever-yielding.
This refers to the single *qi* as the sovereign master of the myriad transformations.

Yet this single *qi* is also the deluded manifestation of my own mind, subsumed within the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna*. If even this can be so, how much more so is the emptiness of *prajñā*?
Profound illumination is quiescent; it is absolute, numinous, and penetrating, yet it does not consort with the myriad dharmas—how could it stand in opposition to them?
Thus, it is able to give rise to both mundane and supramundane dharmas. Within this, the first phrase designates the name and reveals its excellence.

Regarding "Able to produce the lower": there are four distinct explanations of what is produced. First, the Dharma of the *prajñā*-mind; all Buddhas are identical in this regard, for they have realized entry into the *dharmadhātu*.
Second, the signless nature of *prajñā*; those in the causal stage rely upon this, for their mental wisdom (*citta-prajñā*) is sovereign.

Third, the unequaled nature of *prajñā*; the King of Men holds this, for he protects the nation and is held in high esteem. Fourth, the universal benefit of *prajñā*; the common people [rely upon it].
Li relies upon this to transcend the sea of suffering; thus, there are these four meanings which encompass everything without exception.
Whether ordinary or sagely, cause or effect, noble or base, defiled or pure—none exist outside of this, yet it separately gives rise to wondrous benefits.
△ Second, the illustration by analogy to manifest its excellence.

Like a maṇi jewel, its substance is endowed with manifold virtues; it can subdue venomous dragons and all malevolent spirits, fulfill the hearts' desires of people so that their requests are satisfied, and respond to the needs of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin), thus being named the "wish-fulfilling gem" (cintāmaṇi).

It can cause great dragon kings such as Nanda and Upananda to send down sweet rain, moistening and nourishing the grasses and trees. When suffering from the darkness of night, one places it upon a high banner.
Above, the light illuminates heaven and earth, as bright as the rising sun;

this is found in the explanatory text. There are two parts: first, the initial two lines provide a general indication of the basis and essence (*tattva*); second, from "able to subdue" (*neng zhen*) below, the specific meaning of the essence is revealed.
Regarding the first: Prajñā gives rise to wondrous benefits, which is a matter not yet seen by the ordinary; the maṇi jewel is fully endowed with all virtues.

This refers to matters concerning one's own views; however, as the underlying principle is difficult to clarify, it is elucidated through a metaphor to facilitate understanding, hence the word "like" (yǔ).
*Maṇi* means "as one wishes" (*yìrú*); because it fulfills the heart's desires of all who seek it, it specifically manifests five endowed virtues.
First is the virtue of being able to subdue dragon deities; for the pearl of the black dragon deity shines alone amidst the vast ocean...
In the ocean, venomous dragons were cowed and spirits and ghosts hid their tracks; it was as if a royal decree had been issued, such that all feudal lords yielded the way.

Thus, he possesses the second capacity to fulfill the wishes of the multitude: when people seek wealth or hope for profit, he does not obstruct their intentions, but accords with their hearts with impartiality.
Third, he possesses the merit of being worthy of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), for he responds to the world with a golden wheel;

the seven treasures and a thousand sons appear in succession, auspicious omens emerge one after another, and he transforms beings through the ten wholesome paths of action, for without this, his birth-vow would not be fulfilled.

Fourth, he possesses the merit of being able to pour down nectar, for by means of the jewel he subdues the various dragons, and kings such as Bhadra and Nanda follow him so that rain falls everywhere in torrents, thereby bringing about [prosperity].

Because it truly encompasses all things, the five radiances possess incomparable virtue; they shatter darkness and dispel obscurity so that the two polarities shine together, for the three lights illuminate as one.
It is precisely because the *maṇi* jewel possesses these aforementioned virtues that the analogy for the Dharma is established in its ultimate perfection.
△ Third, the application of the dharma to illustrate:
This Prajñāpāramitā is also like this.
The nature and virtues of prajñā are immeasurable and boundless; now, applying the previous metaphors, five points are briefly shown. First, prajñā.

First is the quality of profound depth: because it is difficult for Bodhisattvas to penetrate, beyond the scope of the Two Vehicles, and a source of delusion for ordinary beings, it is realized only by the Buddha to the ultimate degree.

Second is the quality of vast magnitude: because the Three Vehicles rely upon it equally, it is the single path of Great Enlightenment, the root-source of the myriad practices, and the fundamental nature-ground of sentient beings.
Third is the quality of spiritual responsiveness: because its wondrous essence is identical with all phenomena, its nature...
First, the virtue of being all-encompassing, because it is complete in ten thousand merits and achieves the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Second, the virtue of universal benefit through *prajñā*, because it manifests according to the capacities of beings, teaches the Dharma in accordance with their faculties, increases the seeds of awakening, and nourishes the flowers of the mind.
Third, the virtue of perfect brilliance of *prajñā*, because it illuminates past and present, its light soaring above and below; a single lamp shines upon a thousand lamps, and the torch of wisdom—
Because they are inexhaustible, the five meanings may be understood by correlating them with the metaphors in their respective order. △ Second, the exhortation to offer worship has three parts.
First, the presentation of the method of offering worship.
"You kings, you should construct jeweled banners, pennants, and canopies; burn lamps and scatter flowers for vast offerings.
Place the scriptures within jeweled caskets and set them upon jeweled tables."
Prajñā is the unsurpassed dharma; therefore, one should make offerings in this manner. The banner symbolizes the subduing of the heterodox and the manifestation of the orthodox.

The pennant symbolizes the proclamation of the True Dharma. The parasol symbolizes the shading of all beings with compassion and wisdom. The lamp symbolizes the light of gnosis. The flower symbolizes the true cause.
This is a vast offering; it is an offering made through a vow-power that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), offered to this Dharma-gate that accords with the nature of reality.
The reason all the cases are adorned with jewels is that this [Dharma] cannot easily be manifested except by a single mind.
Furthermore, since the Dharma is supreme, the ritual implements for its offering must likewise be extraordinary. △ Second, a detailed explanation of uninterrupted offering.

Whenever they wish to travel, [the scripture] shall always lead the way before them. In whatever place they dwell, it shall manifest a canopy of the seven precious jewels with a seat made of various gems, upon which the scripture is placed and honored with all manner of offerings.
The *prajñā* of the mark of emptiness, though transcending existence and non-existence, yet emptiness is not different from form, nor does it depart from existence and non-existence.
Therefore, one must strictly admonish the three karmas of body, speech, and mind to be without duplicity; the four modes of conduct must always be in accord.

Covering [the altar] with jeweled canopies and placing jeweled seats therein—through such offerings as these, when one raises the eyes, the nature of wisdom shines forth; when one encounters any path, the light of knowledge is never obscured. Having gathered all this...

The divine efficacy and wondrous benefits not only secretly extinguish the calamities of the state, but also plant the field of merit of the true mark (*dharmatā*) within the human realm, establishing the great foundation for all living beings across vast ages.
As the saying goes: "If one’s words are loyal and trustworthy and one’s conduct is sincere and respectful, one may act thus even among the barbarians;
how much less would one be restricted by local customs? How much more so when Prajñā is one's very original face! It is therefore fitting that the Buddha—

He repeatedly offered such earnest instructions and admonitions, making offerings with a mind that never faltered for a single moment. △ Third, an analogy clarifies the supreme merit of making offerings:
it is like serving one's parents, and also like the various devas serving Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Prajñāpāramitā gives birth to all Buddhas; its true aspect (*dharmatā*) is like a father, and its contemplative illumination (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) is like a mother.

Therefore, those who make offerings do so just as a filial son reveres his parents. Prajñā is the sovereign lord of the myriad dharmas; the true aspect realizes the ultimate truth, while contemplative illumination engages with the conventional world.
Thus, those who serve and honor it are like the various devas attending upon Śakra. Indeed, for a filial son, his parents are...
Parents: a filial son ought to exhaust his sincerity toward them without fail. Śakra, as the greatest among the devas, ought to exercise his reverence toward them without fail.
To revere Prajñā in this way, and to be filial toward Prajñā in this way, then the hundred blessings can be attained immediately.
Therefore, the analogy is explained in this manner, and so forth. △ Third, the explanation of the reasons for exhorting others to uphold [this teaching]. This has three parts; first:

"O Great King, it is because of the power of past merit that I see all the human kings of various lands have become sovereigns by having served five hundred Buddhas and respectfully made offerings to them in the past.
Furthermore, all the holy ones who have attained the fruits of the Path come to be born in their kingdoms and act as great [protectors]."
Benefit. With the Buddha-eye that penetrates all, he clearly perceives the past causes of these kings; this is due to the superior retribution induced by their offerings to the Buddhas.
To say they "offered to five hundred Buddhas" clarifies that the two causes of merit and wisdom have been continuous and far-reaching. Thus, the *Vajra-pradīpa* states:
"One who possesses pure faith for a single thought-moment" refers to one who has already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas;
it is such a person that the Tathāgata knows and perceives as possessing immeasurable merit. The four lines beginning with "All those below" clarify the manifestation of influence and transformation.

When the Perfected One rides upon the opportune moment to respond to the world, he may manifest as a minister or counselor to assist kings and guide the deluded, or he may appear as a response-body or transformation-body.
To open the eyes of the blind and awaken the ears of the deaf—whether abiding in the mundane or the supramundane—all do not depart from Prajñā as their vessel of compassion.
For example, while the Zhou dynasty flourished and the teachings of Confucius and Laozi appeared in succession, our Buddha first manifested his auspicious light in the West;
subsequently, Mencius and Zhuangzi arose, and after our Buddha’s golden image flowed eastward. It was as if true Confucians were arising generation after generation, alongside eminent monks.
He reveals his transformative teachings from time to time; were it not for his manifested appearance, it would be difficult to behold one who transcends the mundane.
It must be that he has displayed his traces in order to bring great benefit to this degenerate age. △ Second, fearing that the merit of his present life might decline.
If the king’s merit is exhausted and he acts without the Way, the sages will depart. Calamities will then arise in competition.
Because those who serve the Buddha have not yet attained the emptiness of mind, their merit and virtue may at times be exhausted. When merit is depleted, it can bring about an era of misfortune;
therefore, the sagely and wise observe the signs of the times and act accordingly. Thus, when the fires of disaster spread, it is precisely the time when karmic calamities arise in competition.

Thus it is. To know this is the true cultivation of Prajñā; to act in accordance with it without duplicity will cause blessings to be as inexhaustible as the vast ocean, and calamities to be as formless as empty space. How true! △ Third, for the sake of bringing benefit to the future.
Third. First, it clarifies that the king’s protection of the Dharma serves as the cause:
"Great King, if in future ages there are kings who establish the True Dharma and protect the Triple Gem..."
These words mean that the Prajñā-dharma serves as a bridge for the future. By establishing the True Dharma, one’s practices and vows will not be deviant;
by protecting and upholding the Triple Gem, the Buddha’s light shall abide in the world. Thus, seeing and hearing it generates merit, and prostrating and revering it increases faith.
The beginning of protecting the nation lies herein; therefore, the subsequent passage describes how it moves the protection of the state. △
Second, it clarifies that the Buddhas and holy ones dispatch guardians as conditions. Third: first, the number is indicated.
"I shall command the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas from the five directions to go and protect that land."
Because the preceding establishment of protection served as the cause, it brought about the result of responding appropriately according to each direction.
Otherwise, even foxes and badgers could not provide warmth for one who is breathless; how much less could they move a Supreme Being (Tathāgata) to come and protect the nation? II.
A detailed listing of the lights and seals, in five parts. First: Vajrapāṇi of the East.
In the east, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, holding a vajra and emitting blue light,
went with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land.
In the east, there is the manifestation of the *Zhèn* (thunderbolt) to benefit all beings; this is one who responds to the world with benevolence and compassion.
His name is Vajrapāṇi, or the "Holder of the Vajra," both of which signify that which is extremely firm and extremely sharp, capable of subduing demons and enemies such that nothing can destroy it.
The blue light signifies his manifestation according to the respective directions. Therefore, the *Zhendì Jì* (Record of the True Meaning) states: "The blue vajra."
It can eliminate calamities and misfortunes; this is analogous to how *prajñā* (wisdom) subdues karmic obstructions.
Furthermore, regarding the mention of "four *koṭis*," this refers to the protection provided by both the principal deity and their retinue; subsequent instances should be understood accordingly.

However, according to the esoteric interpretation, Vajrapāṇi internally represents the possession of great bodhi, while externally he represents the crushing and subduing of afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is further said that he is not overcome by the three māras and destroys them.
It destroys the deluded mind; its own essence is firm and solid, becoming vajra-wisdom established by all Buddhas.

Because it shatters the mountain of false views, those who realize this samādhi always hold it in their palms; therefore, he is named Vajrapāṇi (the later record by Paramārtha and the incomplete Esoteric Scripture merely state "Record" and "Esoteric," respectively). △ Second, the Southern Vajraratna.
In the south is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajraratna, who holds a vajra-maṇi in his hand and emits light with the color of the sun;
together with four koṭis of bodhisattvas, he goes to protect that land.
In the south, he rides upon the void to engage with beings and upholds the rites to bring peace to the world. He is named after the Vajra-jewel;
as for his holding the Vajra-maṇi in hand, these two names are distinct in their Chinese and Sanskrit designations, yet they refer to the same essence.
This collectively clarifies that through emptiness and luminosity, he is honored and precious, giving rise to inexhaustible, wish-fulfilling merits. Separately, he is Fire.
It acts as the sun. Now, as for the emission of solar radiance, it merely manifests colors according to the various directions. The Record states: "Red-colored vajra; facing the sun, it emits fire.
This is because wisdom, facing the original enlightenment (benjue), emits the fire of the knowledge of non-arising. The Secret Text says: "Jewels have six meanings:
first, they are difficult to obtain; second, they are pure and free from defilement; third, they possess great majestic power; fourth, they serve as adornment..."
Because it is worldly; because it is fivefold, extraordinary, and peerless; and because it is unchanging. A detailed explanation is as found therein.
This is the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha. △ Third, West: Vajratīkṣṇa.
In the west, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajratīkṣṇa, holding a vajra-sword in his hand and emitting golden light,
went with four koṭis of bodhisattvas to protect that land.
The West: It takes its cue from the hexagram Dui (the Joyous) to manifest the Sage; it is that which grasps the principles to bring things to completion. It is named for the sharpness of the vajra.

As for holding the vajra-sword in hand, this collectively reveals that expedient governance is appropriate to the occasion. It signifies the heart’s resolve to sever [delusions] with golden sharpness and divine swiftness.
Dui represents the marsh and belongs to Metal; thus, the emission of golden light now serves as a symbolic representation according to the direction. The Record states:
The white Vajra can purify turbid water; Prajñā can purify the turbidity of doubt. The *Mīlun* (Dense Clouds) states:
"The sharp Vajra" refers to the sharp sword of the Prajñāpāramitā, for it can sever the seeds of affliction (*kleśa*).
This is Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. △ Fourth, the Northern Vajra Yakṣa.
In the north is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrayakṣa, who holds a vajra-bell in his hand and emits light the color of lapis lazuli;
together with four koṭis of yakṣas, he goes to protect that kingdom.
In the north, he relies on reality while engaging with the mundane world; he is one who possesses provisional wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*).
He is named Vajra, which carries the meaning of being swift in rescuing the world. As for his grasping a vajra-bell in his hand, it signifies the meaning of summoning and startling the mundane world.
It emits lapis lazuli light. Because humans and devas perceive it differently according to their distinctions, it also carries the meaning of manifesting light according to the various directions.
The Record states: "The azure-colored vajra causes people to eliminate all poisons; this symbolizes that wisdom destroys the three poisons.
Mi-lun (Mīlun) says: "Yakṣa means 'valiant' and also 'exhaustive. This refers to the sixteen [Vajrapāṇis]."
Vajra-wisdom (*vajrajñāna*) is the name of the fifteenth wisdom within the practices of Samantabhadra.
Because this wisdom consumes afflictions until they are completely exhausted without remainder, it is called "Vajra. The vajra-bell symbolizes Prajñā awakening the ignorant;
as soon as ordinary beings hear the sound of the bell, they awaken to the wisdom of Prajñā. This is the Bodhisattva Sarvamārapramardin. (5)
In the center of the Vajra [array] is the central square.
Therein resides the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāramitā, holding a vajra-wheel in his hand and emitting light of five colors.
Together with four koṭis of bodhisattvas, he goes to protect that land.

The four directions each correspond to a specific function and are thus restricted to one type; the center, however, gathers these distinctions and constitutes the Great Achievement of the Samantadhara (Universal Sustainer).
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is named for having reached the other shore through the wondrous wisdom of *prajñā*. Holding a firm and sharp wheel in his hand is its functional manifestation;
all of this symbolizes *prajñā*, which encompasses the myriad practices and serves as the spokes for the myriad virtues.
This is the fundamental basis for their convergence. As for the emission of five-colored light, it likewise symbolizes the light of wisdom, which responds perfectly and illuminates universally.

Furthermore, within this [text], the "Vajra" section subsumes the two types of *vajra* mentioned in the *Zhendi ji* (Record of the True Meaning): the yellow *vajra* and the empty-colored (*ākāśa-varṇa*) *vajra*. That text states:
"The yellow *vajra* accords with what people require, serving as a metaphor for untainted (*anāsrava*) merit; the empty-colored *vajra* enables one to [soar] in mid-air."

"Walking and sitting" is a metaphor for using wisdom (*prajñā*) to shatter attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and abiding in the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); this is it. Míyún [commented]:

"Because this Bodhisattva maintains this wheel, when Vairocana attains Buddhahood, he requests the turning of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). By mounting this Wheel of Dharma, he reaches the other shore.

This is the Bodhisattva who turns the Wheel of Dharma as soon as he first resolves his mind (*cittotpāda*). (The aforementioned identification of specific Bodhisattvas follows the interpretation of the Exoteric Teachings. All.
These five directional Vajras have different names, yet they are all collectively designated as "Vajra" because they are the most adamantine among all that is firm.

They reside in the direction of Śakra and are difficult to behold due to the meager merit of ordinary beings. Now, by virtue of the King’s merit, the Buddha has relied upon the Dharma to summon them here.
That they will protect the nation and bring about sublime benefit can easily be inferred; how could this be anything less than a great boon? △ Third, the conclusion and manifestation.
As for their benefit:
these five bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, each accompanied by such an immeasurable great assembly, will bring about great benefit within your kingdom.
You should establish their images and make offerings to them.
The principal [deity] and his retinue arrive together, fully manifesting the miraculous swiftness of the Dharma-power;

thus, the merit is complete, far exceeding that of minor causes and conditions for goodness. Since the protection of the state and the aid of the people are thus achieved, it is appropriate to enshrine the image and offer worship.
Therefore, the Buddha exhorts and encourages [the assembly]. △ Third, the Bodhisattvas speak mantras to protect the state. Part two: First, the Bodhisattvas arouse compassion. Part one.
One's original vows must be protected. Second: First, protecting the sutra according to its location.
At that time, Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and the others rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, it is our original vow that, by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, throughout the worlds of the ten directions..."
Throughout all realms and all lands, wherever this sutra exists— wherever it is received, upheld, read, recited, or explained— I shall,
together with such retinues as these, arrive at those places in a single thought-moment to protect the True Dharma and establish the True Dharma.
The text consists of two parts. First, from "At that time" onwards, it describes the progression of majestic deportment, which is not limited to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.

Second, from "We [the assembly]" onwards, it sets forth the vow to protect the Dharma. Since the ten directions are vast and boundless, protecting the Dharma is no easy task; therefore, one relies upon the Buddha’s spiritual power.
Only by means of the power of vows can [this] be accomplished. "In the ten directions" below refers generally to wherever this sutra is located.

"We and others" below correctly sets forth the power of the principal and the retinue to protect together. This is because wherever the Prajñāpāramitā resides, it is as if the Buddha himself were present;
a precious stupa should therefore be erected there, and the various devas should make offerings. Thus, in a single thought-moment, [they arrive] through their spiritual powers.
This means to protect and uphold. To guard and protect is to cherish and safeguard the Buddha-dharma, as if protecting one’s own eyes.
△ Second, when the Dharma abides, the country is at peace;
it causes all calamities within that realm—such as warfare and epidemics—to be entirely eliminated.
When the Dharma is present, dragons and devas gaze upon it with reverence, and ghosts and spirits honor it with awe.

Consequently, within the borders of such a nation, the three calamities do not enter its realm, and ten thousand misfortunes are secretly extinguished from without.
