There is no contention. Therefore, the gateway of the letter *ṇa* clarifies this, because by knowing that all phenomena are without contention, one immediately enters into the non-activity of all phenomena.

Therefore, the gateway of the letter *ka* clarifies this, because by knowing that all phenomena are without activity, one immediately enters into non-conceptual wisdom (*avikalpa-jñāna*). Therefore, the gateway of the letter *ra* clarifies that all phenomena are without conceptual differentiation, because by knowing that all phenomena are without conceptual differentiation, one immediately enters into the immovability of all phenomena.
This is clarified by the gateway of the letter *nai*; because by knowing that all phenomena are immovable, one realizes the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. *Paramārtha*.

(Exoteric Teaching: This refers to the Mahāmati reaching the other shore and realizing the Great Prajñāpāramitā, which is based upon non-abiding nirvāṇa. Svāhā. (Exoteric Teaching: This refers to non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Based on this nirvāṇa, one extensively brings benefit and happiness to boundless sentient beings until the end of the future. Now, regarding the commentary on this dhāraṇī, it is found in volume ten of the "Du" section and volume eight of the "Zhong" section of the Northern Canon;

as these are all commentaries by the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra, they are cited here in full to broaden one's knowledge and hearing, so that one may perhaps correspond with the gates of Yogic contemplation. However, regarding Guishan’s commentary on the *Lengyan* [Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra]...
The *Yanzhou* (Severe Incantation) cites the interpretations of Tiantai, which do not exceed the four *siddhāntas*:

first, the *loka-siddhānta*, which provides the benefit of generating joy through teachings adapted to different regions; second, the *pudgala-siddhānta*; third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; and fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
These correspond respectively to the three benefits of producing goodness, destroying evil, and entering into principle. Other meanings are as explained in that commentary (*śāstra*).

Thus it is said: the power of mantras is inconceivable, yet human nature is prone to negligence. Those who witness and hear them with faith and reverence will escape calamities and extinguish misfortunes;

those who follow their ordinary ways and do not maintain the practice will find that they cannot survive when faced with disaster. This is like pouring water from a leaking cup—once it is gone, what can one do to reach back and bite one's own navel?

Do not treat the royal banquet as if it were foul food because of your vulgar perceptions, nor rely on your mundane views to recklessly disparage the sacred mind. We should all exert ourselves most earnestly in this regard.

Do not fail to propagate the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the protection of the nation as spoken by the Bodhisattva through the recitation of mantras. △ Second, the Buddhas and Sages praise the excellence [of this teaching].
This has two parts. First, the collective protection by all Buddhas:
At that time, the World-Honored One, having heard these words, praised Vajrapāṇi and the other Bodhisattvas, saying: "Excellent, excellent!"
Ah! If there be anyone who recites and upholds this dhāraṇī, I and all the Buddhas of the ten directions shall constantly bestow our protection upon them;
and all malevolent spirits and ghosts shall revere them as they would the Buddha.
Since their practice and vows are profoundly identical, they are deeply delighted and praised as virtuous. Since their dhāraṇī is vast and great, all Buddhas provide secret support.
If even the Buddhas grant such protection, how could ghosts and spirits not revere them as they would the Buddhas? △ Second, attaining the fruit before long.
Before long, one shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Since the practitioner constantly protects the Prajñā, they will certainly and swiftly realize Bodhi. That their form is upright reflects its correctness; such is the natural course of principle.
△ Fourth, the entrustment by name.
"Great Kings, I entrust this sutra to you all: the country of Vaiśālī, the country of Kośala,
the country of Śrāvastī, the country of Magadha, the country of Vārāṇasī, the country of Kapilavastu,
the country of Kuśinagara, the country of Kauśāmbī, the country of Pañcāla, the country of Pāṭaliputra, the country of Mathurā, the country of Oḍiviśa, and the country of Puṇḍravardhana."
The kingdom of Ṭakka, the kingdom of Devavardhana, the kingdom of Kāśī, the kingdom of Campā—
all such kings as these should likewise uphold the Prajñāpāramitā.
Although their borders are distinct, their governance of the state is one and the same; therefore, all kings should together uphold this [scripture] to protect the Dharma and the nation.
From "I, from below" onwards, the entrustment is explained in general. From "Vaiśālī" onwards, they are summoned by name.

From "All" onwards, the exhortation to maintain it extensively is concluded. This may be understood according to the text. Question: During the Buddha’s lifetime, the kings were as respectful toward the Buddha as this.
"Is it not excellent? He replied, "Even Śakra-devānām-indra lightened his body to hear the Dharma, valuing the Way and honoring it with reverence;

how much more so for the various kingdoms? Therefore, it is appropriate to act in this way. △ Third, the assembly obtained benefit. Fourth: first, the assembly vowed not to be born in difficult lands.

At that time, the great assembly, including the asuras and others, having heard from the Buddha the account of these various calamities, their body hair stood on end and they cried out in a loud voice:
"May we, in the future, not be born in that land."
The "great assembly" is mentioned collectively, while the *asuras* are cited individually; both belong to the preceding introductory section on the multitude gathering like clouds.

From the phrase "hearing the Buddha" onwards, it refers to the seven calamities, which encompass both celestial portents and human affairs without exception; thus, those who hear them are awakened in mind and struck with awe in body.
In that land, a thousand calamities and ten thousand misfortunes will be gathered and exhausted; therefore, it is proclaimed that "in the future, there shall be no more birth.
This means that before words are even spoken, one becomes dazed and enters a dream-like state; though things are clear, one fails to realize the difficulty of turning back.
When the great assembly heard this, they were struck with alarm and doubt, their hearts unwilling to seek rebirth there. II. The Various Kings Leave Home and Attain Patience.

At that time, the sixteen kings immediately relinquished their royal thrones and cultivated the path of renunciation. They perfected the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and attained the patience of subduing (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), the patience of conviction (*adhimuktilakṣaṇakṣānti*), and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).

While dwelling in the secular world, one instead finds satisfaction; hearing the Dharma, one understands it as the condition for karma. Therefore, one abandons the mundane and seeks the supramundane. Regarding the "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*):
they are so named because they can master the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*), and because they involve the transcendence of craving and desire.
Regarding the "ten totalities" (*daśa kṛtsnāyatana*): these consist of earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, space, and consciousness. [End of] Explanation.

As in the introductory section: *forn* (submissive patience) refers to the patience of the three stages of worthiness (*sādhaka*); *xinren* (patience of faith) refers to the patience of the first three grounds;
and *wushengren* (patience of non-arising) refers to the patience of the seventh, eighth, and ninth grounds. When kings attain these, they become peers among the three worthies and ten sages.
The detailed explanation is as before. △ Third, humans and devas scatter flowers and attain the Dharma.
At that time, the entire assembly of humans, devas, and asuras scattered *māndārava* flowers and *mañjūṣaka* flowers.

With *vāsika* flowers and *sumanā* flowers, they made offerings to the Buddha; according to their respective dispositions, they attained the three doors of liberation, the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*).
*Mandāra* means "pleasing to the mind. *Mañjūṣaka* means "soft and supple. *Vārṣika* means "summer-blooming flower. *Sumana* means "well-pleasing.

Scattering flowers as an offering to the Buddha symbolizes turning away from causes toward the fruit; thus, one attains the three gates of liberation and realizes the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is the lineage of the Śrāvaka.
When both types of emptiness are attained, along with the factors conducive to the path (*mārga-sambhāra-dharma*) and so forth, [one proceeds further].
This refers to the lineage of bodhisattvas; these are humans and devas for whom both the vehicle and the precepts are urgent.

Thus, once they have been moistened by the rain of the Dharma, they receive its nourishment according to their respective capacities, and it is shared equally without limit. △ Fourth, the Bodhisattva Scatters Flowers and Attains Patience. Part Two. First, attaining meditative concentration and abiding in patience.
Immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas scattered *kuṭhaja* flowers and *padma* flowers as an offering to the Buddha;

immeasurable samādhis all became manifest before them, and they attained compliance with patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*) and the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Regarding the phrase "the samādhi of immeasurable manifestation," this refers to the manifestation of the wondrous wisdom in accordance with its true nature (*dharmatā*).

"Accordant Patience" (*anulomikī kṣānti*) refers to the patience of the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages. "Patience regarding the Non-arising of Dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) refers to the patience of the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages.
As for the term "abiding," it means that by correctly entering these stages, one internally realizes contemplation and severs [delusions]. △ Second, benefiting sentient beings.
He attained enlightenment.
Immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attained as many gates of samādhi as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;

they realized the equality of the ultimate and the conventional, possessed unimpeded analytical knowledge, and constantly gave rise to great compassion within as many buddha-fields as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeya worlds.
Manifesting in countless worlds to extensively benefit sentient beings and appearing in person as a Buddha—this is the benefit of the practice of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Because right concentration accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), its number is equal to the sands of the Ganges.

As for the term "gate," it refers to entering or exiting at will, whether in accordance with or contrary to the flow, exercising mastery. The equality of the ultimate and the conventional is itself the Middle Way.
It does not abide in the two extremes. Possessing understanding, practice, and compassion, one opens the Dharma for the benefit of others without interruption.

Through the power of spiritual transformations and the power of loving-kindness, one dwells as a neighbor to the Buddhas; thus, one attains enlightenment within the realms of dust and delivers sentient beings within those very realms.
Were it not for the eleventh stage, how could one reach such a state?
△ Third, the section on the dissemination of the teaching. It has two parts. First, the title of this chapter:
*The Chapter on Entrustment*, the eighth. An ancient master said:
"To entrust by means of words is called 'entrustment' (*zhù*); to bind [the recipient] with the Dharma is called 'cumulative charge' (*lèi*). This refers to the Great Entrustment."

The Dharma is that which relies upon and entrusts itself to those who bear its burden, ensuring that its lineage is transmitted without end. Regarding the three intentions behind the subsequent entrustment to the king:
first, it is so that the Dharma may be proclaimed and expounded through the king’s sovereign power; second, it is so that national calamities may be resolved by relying upon him;

and third, it is so that the True Dharma may be circulated throughout successive generations. Question: Among the previously listed assemblies of the Three Vehicles and the various classes of deities, there are many...
"Why was this not entrusted to him, but instead entrusted specifically to the King? Answer: "This sutra was originally expounded for the protection of the state;
therefore, it is now entrusted solely to the King. Is it not the case that one administers medicine according to the illness?

△ Second, the actual exposition of the profound text. (Divided into two parts: First, the entrustment and admonition. (Divided into three parts: First, the explicit clarification of the entrustment. (Divided into two parts: First, the entrustment.
Regarding that time, the Buddha told King Prasenajit:

"I now exhort you all: after my parinirvāṇa, when the True Dharma is about to perish—in the final fifty years, the final five hundred years, and the final five thousand years—there will be no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Saṅgha."
The Buddha, wishing to entrust the profound gateway of Prajñā to those who would uphold it, therefore exhorted and admonished them repeatedly.
However, this passage differs from the Qin translation; thus, the ancient commentaries explain the Qin text as follows:
"As for the eighty years, after the Buddha’s passing, five persons shall maintain the teaching: first, Kāśyapa; second, Ānanda; third, Madhyāntika..."
Regarding the fields [of practice]: three persons who had seen the Buddha maintained the teachings in succession for sixty years, during which time the practice of the Dharma did not perish.
Next came Śāṇakavāsin and Upagupta; these two had not seen the Buddha, yet they maintained the teachings in succession for forty years.
Because their majestic deportment and the Dharma were then extinguished, it was at that time said that the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha no longer existed. Thus it is said: "Eight..."
Regarding the "one hundred years": within the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), twenty masters maintained the teachings, all of whom were sages; thus, the True Dharma did not perish.
In the sixth century, there was the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; in the seventh century, Nāgārjuna; both were Bodhisattvas.
The Dharma shall not perish. During the eight hundred years [following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa], heterodox schools will flourish; therefore, at this time, it was entrusted to kings.
It is Deva Bodhisattva who beats the drum of King Śabda to proclaim the Dharma. As for the eight thousand years, this refers to the Semblance Dharma (Saddharmapratirūpaka).

When the Final Dharma (Śāsanānta) period ends, the Dharma will perish because sentient beings hold wrong views. Although there are ancient commentaries that provide evidence for this, how can they withstand comparison with this sūtra?

Regarding the "fifty years" and so forth, the chronological sequence does not correspond. Although I, a fool, have not yet extensively investigated the sūtras and śāstras, I shall venture to discuss this.
These three instances all refer to the "later" period because the Buddha, while still in the world, spoke in advance of future events; thus, they are designated as "later.
As for the "last fifty years," this refers to the "later" period by way of anticipation, pointing specifically to the time of the second patriarch, Ānanda. This is because the second patriarch...
Since the succession of Kāśyapa, the True Dharma has been maintained and flourished throughout various lands; yet, as we reach this final age, false teachings have blazed forth.
Thus, there are those such as the "flood-swallowing cranes" who gather in great numbers in the Western Heaven, forming factions and chanting in unison.
The heterodox teacher recited these words: "If a person lives for a hundred years and does not see the cranes at the marsh, it is not as good as living for a single day and being able to see them.
Hearing this, the Second Patriarch said, "Alas! Such false views have entered people so deeply," and he changed the verse, saying:
"If a person lives for a hundred years and does not hear the Dharma of arising and ceasing, it is not as good as living for a single day and being able to..."
He understood this. However, false views are easily contracted, while the True Dharma is difficult to ascend to. Thus, Shuilao mocked the Second Patriarch for his advanced age;
yet he ultimately did not follow the latter’s dharma verses. When the Second Patriarch heard of this, he manifested his passing by dividing [the lineage] into four schools.
At that time, the Buddha-dharma also temporarily ceased. As for the phrase "five hundred years later," it likely refers to a distant future.
In the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, the fifth five-hundred-year period is the final one. That sūtra states: "During the first five hundred years, liberation will be firm;
during the second five hundred years, meditative concentration will be firm; during the third five hundred years, learning will be firm;
during the fourth five hundred years, stūpas and monasteries will be firm; and during the fifth five hundred years, strife and contention will be firm. Thus, it is the fifth.
In an age of turbidity and strife, the Dharma does not flourish; though it exists, it is as if it did not. Yet, the term "vajra" also carries the sense of illuminating through comparison.

Thus, that text states: "After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, in the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit," and so on, concluding with, "regarding this as the reality.
According to the intent of that commentary, Subhūti originally harbored doubts regarding the evil world.
Because there is no faith, I have cited the evil age merely to sever doubts.
As for the "five thousand years later," this refers to the time when the period of the Semblance Dharma has already ended and the Final Dharma (mofa) is manifest; that is what is meant by "later.

At such a time, sentient beings hold false views and are entirely inverted; they do not follow the bequeathed instructions and transgress the precepts and rules. They do not pursue the pure source, and the corrupt customs [prevail].

The eternal fan [of the Dharma] has ceased; the Jetavana grove lies in ruins, and the Deer Park is overgrown with weeds. Among the ninety-six types of heterodox schools, those who descend toward the lower realms consider themselves ascending to heights;

the multitudes of sentient beings within the three realms regard this burning house as a pure land. How could they know that the supreme sages shed tears, and that the gods and humans grieve at the extinction of the Dharma?
Therefore, it is summarized that during these three periods, there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Sangha. Yet, these three points are merely conjectures.
The origin was thus. For now, let it remain as a tentative examination. △ Second, the entrustment of the person and the Dharma:
This Triple Gem of the sutra is entrusted to all kings to establish and protect, so that my fourfold assembly of disciples may [flourish].

They shall uphold, recite, and study it; they shall understand its principles and meanings, and extensively proclaim the essential Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, causing them to practice so as to transcend birth and death.
This sutra refers to the three kinds of *prajñā*. It is the second gate of protecting the Dharma (*dharmapāla*). That which can preach is the Buddha; that which is preached is the Dharma;

and those who listen and receive it are the Saṅgha. Therefore, they are called the Three Jewels (*triratna*). However, as for the propagation and circulation of these Three Jewels, they rely upon kings for great protection;
likewise, those who steadfastly uphold them also rely upon kings. This is because, previously, they relied upon the fourfold assembly, and [the latter] lacks...
It is because the king’s power cannot protect and establish [the Dharma].
If I cause my fourfold assembly—namely, the various kings—to propagate and circulate it, then the fourfold assembly will cultivate their minds and delight in the Way;

thus they will be able to receive and uphold it without loss, reciting it throughout their lives, explaining it through both oral and written means, benefiting both themselves and others, and thereby ensuring that the Three Jewels are sustained. It is not merely for the sake of the Three Jewels’ endurance.

The Buddha-sun shines eternally; moreover, the eight sufferings are all rendered empty, and one reaches the other shore of the ocean of desire. Thus it is said that he causes them to transcend [suffering], and so forth.
All of this relies upon the power of the King’s great protection. △ Second, the specific explanation of the admonitions and commands.
Seven. First, the admonition regarding the faults of the period when the Dharma is extinguished. Four. First, the introduction to the time when the Dharma is extinguished:

"Great King, in the future age of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), when the True Dharma is about to perish, it will inevitably be a time when the five turbidities converge and people lack right view. Thus he speaks of the five turbidities.

These are: first, the turbidity of life-span (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). Consciousness relies upon the four great elements; according to karma, its duration is extended or shortened, such that birth and death cannot be attained with autonomy.

Second, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). It agitates and disturbs one's own mind, clouding and obstructing the principle; it takes the five dull fetters (*pañca-mūrdha-kleśa*) as its essence.

Third, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Greedy attachment and false defilement cloud and obstruct phenomena; it takes the five sharp fetters (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) as its essence. Fourth, the turbidity of the [five] aggregates...

The turbidity of birth (*jāti-kāṣāya*): through false attachments and inversions, one is deluded regarding oneself and pursues external objects; assuming a subtle form within the womb, one voluntarily undergoes the cycle of transmigration.

This is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kāṣāya*), a time when the three calamities intensify, myriad hardships converge, and the ways of the world fall into ruin—a period when the vital energy of the age is shrouded in darkness.
However, the turbidity of the eon has no separate essence; it is merely a name established based on the conflagration of the preceding four turbidities. Therefore, the Dharma...

Huá says: "In times of chaos during the kalpa-turbidity, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy," and so forth. Question: What meaning does "turbidity" (zhuó) convey that serves as the basis for its name?

Answer: The wondrous, pure, and luminous mind is by nature clear, tranquil, and still. When it is further burdened by afflictions, karma, and the four great elements, it is no longer clear but becomes turbid.
As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is like the analogy of clear water and the two substances of ash and sand; their natures are inherently distinct.
They do not correspond. Suppose there were a person who took that ash and sand and threw it into pure water;
the earth loses its obstructive quality and the water forgets its clarity, so that its appearance becomes turbid—this is what is called "turbidity. Your fivefold turbidity is also like this.

However, the meaning and characteristics of those five turbidities differ greatly from those in the present sutra; only the general sense of "turbidity" is the same. Therefore, [the passage] is cited.
As evidence of this: Third, regarding those who destroy the Dharma:
all kings, princes, and ministers, relying on their own high status and nobility, shall destroy my teaching and openly establish restrictive laws.
The Buddha’s wisdom is clear and penetrating. Three thousand years ago, he foresaw the conditions of the Final Dharma (mofa) period;
thus, the seven admonitions that follow are entirely without error, as clear as looking at one's own palm. Their context and reality are manifest.

This is because he desired that the Buddha-dharma should not perish, so that it might continue its eternal course like the two polarities and the three luminaries, or exist like beans, rice, water, and fire. Daily...
It is difficult to find fault with this. Yet those who are deluded are confused by their preconceived views and allow their defiled minds to grow;
they would surely lead the pure companions of an entire age to cast themselves into the deep pit of the three poisons—how truly lamentable this is!

However, the profound principles of the Buddha-dharma cannot be fathomed through ordinary consciousness and emotion. If one insists on relying on one's own noble status to suppress it, [one will surely fail].
Please first examine what the fundamental tenets of the Buddhist school are like. It is for this reason that I have appended these annotations;
I hope that those who wish to preserve the Teaching will take pity on its adherents, and that those who condemn its faults will instead show compassion for its virtues.

Thus, the sages and wise ones employ their benevolent and virtuous minds with the utmost sincerity. "To regulate" (zhi) means to prohibit. △ Third, the refutation of the errors regarding the extinction of the Dharma. Part Two.
At first, he prohibited the four orthodox ones,
forbidding my disciples— monks and nuns— from leaving the household life to practice the Right Path,
and likewise forbidding them from constructing Buddha-stūpas or images.
The path of leaving the household life involves distancing oneself from worldly toil and cultivating pure karma; thus, when the mind suddenly opens wide, the benefit is profound.
Yet, why is it that for some, restraint is required without the need for renunciation? In the practice of cultivation, one must wash away the habitual tendencies of consciousness.
To open the window of the awakened nature, a light arises in profound stillness; yet, how is it that some, having attained entry into the most profound depths, cease their practice?
As for the construction of stupas, one enshrines the Buddha’s *śarīra* therein; whether approaching to pay homage or gazing from afar, the merit is immeasurable.
As for the creation of images, one honors the Buddha’s physical form; by raising a hand or bowing the head, the benefit is vast and far-reaching. Furthermore—

Why does he restrain those who do not wish to practice? It is because, for the most part, their purification of habits has not yet deepened and the seeds of spiritual awakening have not been cultivated;

thus they mistake the correct for the inverted and the good for the evil. Furthermore, how could they know that leaving the household life severs defilement and that practicing cultivation brings one away from suffering? 2. Establishing the Three Deviations.
The layperson occupies a high seat while the bhikṣu stands upon the ground; this is no different from the manner of a soldier or a slave.
Regarding the distinction between the white-robed and the dyed-robed: the white-robed are the laity, whereas the dyed-robed are the Sangha.
To transmit the mind-seal of the Chan Way from a high seat requires one capable of transcendent awakening; for a layperson to occupy such a position is inappropriate. Thus, he stands upon the ground.
To serve with diligence may be appropriate for those among the slaves and servants; yet for a bhikṣu to stand waiting in such a manner is to lose the true principle.
To become as debilitated and weak as a slave, or to act as a soldier in defense, is the ultimate sign of the decline of the Dharma and the decay of the Buddha-way.
For those who preserve a heart of benevolence, it would be excellent to manage matters according to reason; otherwise, there is cause for fear.
"What you send forth shall return to you; what you do will surely come back upon yourself. How can one not stand in awe? △ Fourth, the conclusion on the faults of the extinction of the Dharma:
One should know that at such a time, the extinction of the Dharma will not be long."
The preliminary signs of this Dharma-gate are such that there has never been one that was not subsequently ruined and obscured. Therefore, he concludes this by saying:
△ Second, the admonition against violating the conduct of the fourfold assembly.

"Great King, the causes and conditions for the ruin of your kingdom are all of your own making. Relying on your own power, you have constrained the fourfold assembly and forbidden them from cultivating merit.
These evil bhikṣus accept private invitations; they form close bonds with bhikṣus who are their personal acquaintances, acting with a single mind toward one another in mutual intimacy.
To seek blessings through such ritual assemblies is the dharma of external paths; it is entirely not my teaching. Consequently, the common people suffer from pestilence in immeasurable numbers."
Suffering! You should know that at such a time, the state will be destroyed.
Authority and power will be lost; joy and anger will be indulged according to whim; karmic burdens will increase daily;

and as blessings subtly transform, the end result is that one begins by drinking to excess in negligence and ends with the total ruin of the nation. All of this is caused by one's own actions and is what one must receive for oneself.
"Result. This refers to the present moment. It is not that one fails to examine within one's own mind the cultivation of merit;
rather, it is that the fourfold assembly has encountered prohibitions. Why is this so? Therefore, the Buddha directly clarifies it as such.

"All evils," and so forth, clarifies the thorns of the great forest and the weeds of the great field. "Evil bhikṣus" refers to those who violate the Buddha’s disciplinary rules; they receive [the karmic retribution].
"Please. This refers to those who seek only material offerings. "Knowledgeable and single-minded. This refers to those who band together in evil conduct and practice deception.
"Mutually affectionate and intimate. This refers to those who associate in lewd and frivolous ways. These three phrases refer to the lower grade of assembly.

They are those who appear to be true but are actually false, like coarse stones mixed with jade, or where the music of Zheng (鄭) confuses the refined music of Ya (雅). Therefore, the Buddha directly rebuked them, saying: "This is the dharma of external paths. He further said:
None of these are my teachings. If this is so, then the heterodox and the orthodox will contend with one another, and the true and the false will gather in mutual conflict.
The transgressions of a single mind are difficult to exhaustively describe in words; the calamities that befall those of differing natures may arrive all at once.

The destruction of the land should occur when there are no people who cherish the Dharma. Therefore, the conclusion states: "One should know," and so forth. △ Third, the admonition against non-compliance.
“Dharma, Great King!
In the final age of the Dharma, kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly of disciples will each act contrary to the Dharma, falsely attributing various faults to the Buddha’s teachings.
They will act against the Dharma and the Vinaya, binding bhikṣus like prisoners in a jail. You should know this.”

At that time, when the Dharma has not long been extinguished, the True Dharma flourishes alongside the ways of the world, and the mental faculty is vast and expansive. In the Age of Dharma’s Decline (*mofa*), both the times and circumstances are decadent, and one's perspective and capacity are narrow and shallow;

"Great King, after my parinirvāṇa, it will be the fourfold assembly of disciples, all kings, princes, and high officials who are the very ones entrusted with upholding and protecting the Triple Gem, yet they will bring about its own destruction.
They are like parasites within a lion’s body that eat the lion’s own flesh;
they are not outsiders."

The Three Jewels possess both distinct characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the difference of being a single essence (*ekatva*). Regarding the Three Jewels as distinct characteristics: kings and ministers plant merit by relying on the field of excellence;
bhikṣus cultivate the Way by depending on the forest hermitage (*araṇya*); each fulfills their own aspiration, while the two mutually support one another.
There is no path that can be destroyed. The Three Jewels of identical essence do not exist apart from the single mind of the sovereign and his ministers;
thus, the identical essence manifests through distinct characteristics, while these distinct characteristics rely upon the identical essence as their root and foundation.
To protect the Three Jewels is to sustain the single mind. If the Three Jewels could be extinguished, could the single mind also be destroyed? Reflect on this.

If one reaches this state, one will firmly guard the sacred source and fortify the blessed ground; remaining ever-vigilant throughout the day, this is not an extraordinary matter—how could there be any destruction?
This is clearly illustrated by the analogy of the lion below. Indeed, heaven and earth share the same root as I; right and wrong have originally been one body.
Even those possessing blood and breath are all my fellow citizens and part of the same community with all things; how much more so [is this true for the enlightened]?
The Three Jewels of identical essence are indeed the single source of true nature.

Therefore, to destroy the Three Jewels is to destroy one's own mind, as illustrated by the analogy of the lion and so forth. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-mukha-sūtra* states: "For example, when a lion dies..."
Upon his death, the beings that travel by water, land, and air did not dare to eat his flesh; only the worms born from his body ate it themselves.

This may be understood as being in accordance with the Dharma. As for saying he was not a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), it is because those who destroy [the Dharma] are actually those who inflict perverse harm.

Yet, that the King and his ministers—who ought to have protected and promoted [the Dharma]—instead caused its destruction in such a manner, is this not truly most extraordinary? Therefore, those who read this scripture should take refuge in the Triple Gem and likewise heedfully protect it.

The Way realizes the three bodies, harmonizes with the three virtues, and assists the three fundamental relations. Who could possibly fathom its peerless and wondrous benefits?

They shall fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. If they should obtain human birth, they will be poor, lowly, and deficient in their faculties.

Following the teaching and practicing accordingly. II. First, upholding according to the Dharma. IV. First, the various kings are moved with grief. II.
First, the explicit explanation of their grief.

My Buddha spoke words of truth to admonish against the obscurations of the Dharma-gate. Now, the kings and ministers have never failed to be moved in heart and focused their thoughts;
yet at that time, the sixteen kings alone let out a mournful sound that reverberated afar, shaking the two polarities and the three realms.
The darkness of ignorance is thus dispelled by light; the aspiration for the Way is solemn and majestic, illuminating all eternity.
The breeze of compassion is vast and sweeping, fanning the present day. It is truly capable of cooling the burning heart that destroys the Dharma and awakening the drunken eyes that seek only profit.
△ Second, protecting the Dharma according to the teachings.

At that time, the various kings each received and upheld the Buddha’s words with a sincere heart; they did not prohibit the fourfold assembly from leaving home to study the Way, but rather ensured they would act in accordance with the Buddha's teachings.

If, however, one is negligent and lacks regulation, thereby destroying the teachings and corrupting the Dharma, how can such a person be considered noble for their lack of restraint? △ Second, the Great Assembly’s Lamentation.
At that time, a great multitude as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all sighed together, saying:
"At such a time, the world is empty and void; this is an age without a Buddha."
Hearing the Buddha’s words, he was moved to deep lamentation. As soon as his true mind stirred, he feared only that the Dharma might perish in future lives.
Thus, he sighed again: "This is an age without a Buddha. Dharma Master Lingyu of the Sui dynasty, seeing the destruction of the teachings under the Northern Zhou, was overcome with unbearable grief.
He donned mourning garments of coarse hempen cloth and bound his head with a hair-cord, as if he had lost his own parents. He led his companions to discuss these matters at night.
This is the correct principle. During the day, I read secular books while remaining hidden within these ashes and manuscripts, awaiting the restoration of the Dharma.
Is it permissible for those today who destroy the Dharma to use the Dharma to seek food, clothing, wealth, fame, and profit? △ Third: Inquiry regarding the titles of the scriptures.
At that time, King Prasenajit addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it?
From the beginning of the formal exposition until this point, the standard model of the single sutra is complete; therefore, he requests the title of the sutra and [asks] how to uphold it.
This is the section on upholding the ritual methods. △ Fourth, the Buddha provides the formal response in three parts. First, the direct explanation of the scripture’s title:
The Buddha addressed the Great King, "This scripture is named the *Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā*.
It may also be called the 'Ambrosial Dharma Medicine. If there are those who ingest and practice it, it can cure all ailments."
In the response, there are two types of titles for the sutra. First, the primary titles: protecting the Dharma and preserving the world, both are called *Rājan* (King of Benevolence);

practicing according to the Dharma, all are called *Rakṣā-deśa* (Protecting the Nation); the contemplation of ultimate reality, both are called *Prajñā* (Wisdom); and whether as that which is detached or that which has arrived, it is named *Pāramitā* (Perfection).
Second, the secondary titles: protecting the Dharma and protecting the nation; benefiting oneself and benefiting others; this is the nectar-like Dharma (*amṛta-dharma*).
Medicine: By relying on patience for transformation and teaching, those who immediately take it and practice it will be cured of their illness; this is the benefit of taking and practicing it.
△ Second, praising the vastness of the Dharma.
"Great King, all the merits of the Prajñāpāramitā are like empty space; they cannot be measured.
This single dharma-gate gives rise to wondrous benefits that flow forth inexhaustibly and can be drawn from without end.

Because only a Buddha can exhaust its source, and because those on the causal stages find it difficult to penetrate, it is praised in this manner. △ Third, the protection of the nation through merit."

If there are those who receive, uphold, read, and recite it, the merit they obtain will be able to protect the Benevolent Kings and all sentient beings, like a surrounding wall and like city ramparts. Therefore, you all should receive and uphold it.

Within this, there are four parts: first, clarifying the person who receives and maintains [the precepts]; second, clarifying how their merit protects the nation; third, clarifying the intent of protection through analogy;
and fourth, concluding with an exhortation to maintain them. These are all to be understood according to the text. △ Second, the conclusion correlating the joy of maintaining [the precepts].
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the immeasurable bodhisattva-mahāsattvas such as Maitreya and Siṃhacandra;
the immeasurable śrāvakas such as Śāriputra and Subhūti; the immeasurable devas and humans of the desire realm and the form realm;
the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, asuras, and the entire great assembly—all heard what the Buddha had spoken.
All were greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it.
Regarding "all were greatly rejoiced," the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states that there are three kinds of meanings:
first, the purity of the speaker, who is not defiled by attachment to gain or offerings; second, the purity of what is spoken, [which arises] from knowing reality as it truly is.
The essence of the true Dharma. Third is the purity of attaining the fruit. By means of a single phrase that permeates the spirit, all are aided in reaching the other shore;
therefore, those who hear it believe, accept, and practice it.

From his youth, the Master possessed innate awakening; he traveled to pay homage at all famous mountains, and his spontaneous Zen insights caused veteran masters to stick out their tongues in amazement.
Upon reaching adulthood, he came to the capital, where he gradually concealed his sharp brilliance. He constructed a small hut as a tea hermitage, and his teachings flourished daily.
Prosperous! Both the ignorant and the wise held him in reverence;
he moved the hearts of the former dynasty. A mere inch of land was transformed into a vast earth, and motes of dust were transmuted into golden shrines.

He occupied the lecture seat for over forty years, never wearying even in his advanced age. He received others with impartiality, providing instruction to countless souls. Alas! May the Master’s vows be magnified.

Thus it was. Regarding his commentaries on the sutras, he first produced the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Buddhavaidya*. Among his Buddhist works were the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* ritual manual, the *Dīpa-avatamsaka-sūtra*, and the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*.
These were composed during his final years, close to old age. A separate record of the Master’s meritorious deeds and conduct is extremely detailed.
